**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents to the Board on enrollment projections for the 2018-2019 school year and beyond, with analysis of the district's enrollment history and projections provided by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants.

The enrollment history runs from 11,965 in 2005/06 upward through 12,068 (2006/07), 12,126 (2007/08), 12,165 (2008/09), 12,069 (2009/10), 12,056 (2010/11), 12,328 (2011/12), 12,391 (2012/13), 12,573 (2013/14), 12,556 (2014/15), 12,710 (2015/16), 12,868 (2016/17) to 13,084 in 2017/18 — a gain of more than eleven hundred students over twelve years, and a period in which the district grew rather than shrank.

Projected versus actual enrollment is tabulated by year (projected / budgeted / actual): 2013/14 12,494 / 12,440 / 12,573; 2014/15 12,653 / 12,590 / 12,556; 2015/16 12,612 / 12,560 / 12,710; 2016/17 12,710 / 12,740 / 12,868; 2017/18 12,992 / 12,900 / 13,084; and 2018/19 projected 13,207 and budgeted 13,207 with actual not yet known. In each of the last three years the actual exceeded both the projection and the budgeted figure. The methodology slide explains that future enrollments would be expected to fall between the MOST LIKELY and LOW projections, calculated by adding MOST LIKELY plus the LOW divided by two.

The birth-to-kindergarten ratio table runs 4.65 (05-06), 4.94 (06-07), 5.45 (07-08), 5.29 (08-09), 5.22 (09-10), 5.63 (10-11), 5.67 (11-12), 5.94 (12-13), 6.18 (13-14), 5.82 (14-15), 6.39 (15-16), 6.59 (16-17), 6.53 (17-18) and a projected 6.50 for 18-19. Projected future total K-12 enrollment is 13,207 for 2018/19, 13,274 for 2019/20, 13,320 for 2020/21, 13,325 for 2021/22 and 13,396 for 2022/23.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2018-2019.** Administration has reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools be closed to open enrollment. The district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years; based on current projections for 2018-2019 it is recommended that both be closed again, with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School, applications for those twenty-five spots accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March. The resolution adopts that closure and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2018-2019 school year.

**Curriculum 7.C: the Schools of Choice report.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, summarizes the report shared with the Board at the February 6 Board Workshop.

The elementary enrollment projections from Fred Ignatovich give, for kindergarten and first grade by year, HIGH / AVERAGE / LOW bands: 2015/2016 kindergarten HIGH 791, AVERAGE 763, LOW 733 and first grade HIGH 842, AVERAGE 748, LOW 802; 2016/2017 kindergarten HIGH 839, AVERAGE 811, LOW 784 and first grade HIGH 896, AVERAGE 798, LOW 876; 2017/2018 kindergarten HIGH 863, AVERAGE 823, LOW 782 and first grade HIGH 941, AVERAGE 822, LOW 919; and 2018/2019 kindergarten HIGH 901, AVERAGE 874, LOW 847 and first grade HIGH 927, AVERAGE 874, LOW 909.

The elementary SOC application history records openings advertised against applications received and students enrolled for kindergarten and first grade each year from 2006-2007 (25 and 25 openings, 72 and 42 applications) through 2017-2018 (55 and 5 openings, 150 and 41 applications), totalling 915 kindergarten and 310 first grade openings advertised, 1,592 and 516 applications received, and 941 and 265 students enrolled over the twelve years. Applications have consistently exceeded openings at kindergarten by a wide margin.

The data summary for 2017-2018 gives, by building, SOC students against non-SOC students with the SOC percentage and its year-over-year change: Barnard 73 / 431, 14.48% (-2.42); Bemis 16 / 538, 2.89% (-1.51); Costello 57 / 306, 15.70% (+1.00); Hamilton 62 / 458, 11.92% (-0.28); Hill 64 / 272, 19.05% (-1.75); Leonard 42 / 377, 10.02% (-0.18); Martell 52 / 435, 10.68% (-2.82); Morse 19 / 471, 3.88% (-0.62); Schroeder 5 / 522, 0.95% (-0.55); Troy Union 27 / 447, 5.70% (+0.60); Wass 62 / 360, 14.69% (-2.11); Wattles 21 / 479, 4.20% (-0.20); TOTAL 500 SOC and 5,096 non-SOC, 8.93%, down 0.97 points. By grade: kindergarten 54 SOC / 812 non-SOC, 6.24% (-4.86); first 98 / 845, 10.39% (-2.41); second 104 / 819, 11.27% (+1.47); third 79 / 796, 9.03% (-0.37); fourth 83 / 883, 8.59% (+0.09); fifth 82 / 941, 8.02% (-0.18).

By subgroup, SOC students are 21.80% ELL (109 students) against 30.85% (1,572) among non-SOC; 16.60% free/reduced lunch (83) against 12.85% (655); and 6.20% special education (31) against 9.38% (478). By ethnicity the SOC population is 58.40% White (292), 24.00% Asian (120), 8.60% Black (43), 6.60% multi-ethnic (33), 1.60% Hispanic (8), 0.60% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (3) and 0.20% American Indian (1), against a non-SOC population that is 50.10% White (2,553), 40.09% Asian (2,043), 3.55% Black (181), 3.47% multi-ethnic (177), 2.35% Hispanic (120), 0.31% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (16) and 0.12% American Indian (6). Non-SOC enrollment by grade for 2017-2018 runs 812, 845, 819, 796, 883, 941, 912, 949, 909, 994, 993, 922 and 994 for kindergarten through twelfth, totalling 11,769, an increase of 328.

A survey emailed to current Schools of Choice families asked about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade and grades 6 through 8 in 2018-2019: 40 kindergarten students plan to attend, 3 first grade students, and 14 middle school students — 7 in sixth grade, 2 in seventh and 5 in eighth.

The February 6, 2018 memorandum from Kris Griffor and Mark Dziatczak to Dr. Machesky lists the factors considered: current enrollment across the district; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of SOC students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter in 2018-2019 under a limited program; and available elementary classrooms. They recommend using Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two) as the foundation, and accepting SOC applications for 40 kindergarten, 3 first grade and 14 middle school students — noting that on the prior year's application volume the district anticipates attracting many more than 50 kindergarten applicants, which would allow it to admit 40 initially with the option of admitting more in the third week of August if space allows, and that middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.

**Curriculum 7.D through 7.G: the four Schools of Choice resolutions.** Michigan law requires a district to pass a resolution each school year if it intends to participate in a Schools of Choice program, and Troy adopts four — the same seat counts stated once under Section 105 and again under Section 105c, distinguishing where the applicant's home district sits rather than adding seats.

7.D adopts, under Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, acceptance of applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for 2018-2019 for 40 nonresident kindergarten and 3 nonresident first grade students who attend a school district within Oakland County (total students include non-Oakland County residents – Section 105c). 7.E adopts the same 40 kindergarten and 3 first grade seats under Section 105c for students attending a school district outside Oakland County, if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries (total students include Oakland County residents – Section 105).

7.F anticipates that seats will be available for 2018-2019 in grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools and adopts, under Section 105, acceptance of applications for 14 total nonresident 6th-8th grade students at those buildings with placement based on building availability, for students attending a district within Oakland County. 7.G adopts the identical 14 total seats under Section 105c for students attending a district outside Oakland County whose ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD.

**Business 8.A: fiber maintenance.** An RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for the district's fiber cabling maintenance, reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, and John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's January 29, 2018 recommendation letter on Bid #9851 records that bids and proposals were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 p.m. on January 8, 2018. Three proposals came in: Amcomm at $75,791.00, Fiber Link, Inc. at $45,865.00 and Turnkey Network Solutions at $29,651.62, with several voluntary alternates offered by Fiber Link. All proposals were compliant, but variations in the interpretation of bid items required clarification from several vendors to compare unit items and hourly rates accurately.

At first glance Turnkey appears lowest, but Foster found that Turnkey underestimated the amount of work involved, that its hourly rates are higher, that on a time and material contract those higher rates would use up the allocated amounts faster than Fiber Link's, and that Fiber Link's lower hourly rates will let the district accomplish more and maximize the refunds available under E-rate. He recommends award to Fiber Link, Inc. together with Voluntary Alternates 1 and 2 as proposed, which provide accurate documentation of the fiber routing inside and outside the buildings: base bid $45,865.00, Voluntary Alternate #1 $7,500.00 for CAD prints of the outside fiber cable routes and Voluntary Alternate #3 $2,500.00 for CAD prints of the building fiber cable routes, for a total award of $55,865.00. (The letter's prose refers to alternates 1 and 2 while the pricing table labels them #1 and #3.) Fiber Link is the incumbent contractor for the district's fiber maintenance and has already amassed significant knowledge of the network. The letter stresses that this is primarily a time and material contract, provided on an as-needed basis, put out to bid now because the service has become eligible for reimbursement under E-rate Category 1, under which the district will receive a reimbursement of approximately 40% of its expenditures up to 40% of the approved amount.

The attached Universal Service Funding service provider evaluation worksheet scores each bidder across six weighted factors — cost (30 points maximum), integration and service transition (25), adherence to specifications (15), prior experience with the district (15), financial stability and capability (10) and prior experience providing similar services (5). Fiber Link scores 88.8 of 100 against 65.0 each for Amcomm and Turnkey; Turnkey takes the full 30 points on cost but scores zero on prior experience with the district. No bidders were disqualified. The resolution awards fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. in the amount of $55,865.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund.

**Business 8.B: general trades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on architectural components — roller shades, window sills, platform and ceiling work — at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse Elementary Schools; the bid also included remodel work at Troy Union Elementary and doors at Troy High, Athens and International Academy East. Bid responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and Barton Malow.

Christa Amalio, Barton Malow project manager, writes to Rick West on February 6, 2018 regarding the 2013 Bond Program, Series 2, Bid Package 21A. The first bidder, Titan Retail Industries, was missing an allowance noted in the work scopes, which was reason to disqualify it from award. The second apparent low bidder, R&E Development, submitted a breakdown not in alignment with the other bids received even though its overall amount was second among the bidders. At the post-bid interview the estimator explained that all the work at all of the buildings was included in the base bid total price, and that having received his hollow metal door pricing late he placed the total door cost on the Martell Elementary price line rather than breaking the door pricing out by building. Asked about the new wall at Athens and the low price at Leonard, he admitted he had not spent much time on the bid form and was rushing to deliver the bid on time. Through the interview the contractor proved knowledgeable of the drawings and had received quotes from vendors similar to the other bidders and compliant with the specifications, and was able to provide the necessary information and qualifications to receive a recommendation for award. The recommendation is category 06000 General Trades to R&E Development at $188,971.00, total awards $188,971.00. The resolution awards bid pack 21A to R & E Development in the amount of $188,971.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Other 10.A: 2018 Board committee assignments.** Each year Board members are selected to serve as representatives to committees of state and national board associations, within the community, within the school district and within the Board's own committees. The attached membership list assigns: Oakland Schools' Legislative Committee and Oakland Schools' Designate to Gottlieb and Hauff; Friends of Troy Seniors Advisory Committee, Troy Community Coalition and Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence to Fleming; Troy Parks and Recreation Board and Troy Youth Assistance to Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt across the community slate; Troy Nature Society to Hammond; Troy Historical Society to Hauff; the Continuous Improvement Team 17-18 and Diversity Council to Hammond; the Crisis Committee and District Technology Committee to Miletti; the Wellness Committee to Fleming and Hammond; the Policy Committee to Gottlieb, Hauff and Philippart; and the Superintendent Evaluation Committee to Gottlieb, Schmidt and Miletti.

**Other 10.B: NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition.** Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, provides that any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Vice President Steve Gottlieb has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Annual Conference & Exposition in San Antonio, Texas, April 7-9, 2018, and the resolution approves his attendance as representative of the Troy Board of Education. The packet reproduces the NSBA registration materials, which note that NSBA events are open to U.S. school districts holding membership in their state school boards association and that NSBA reserves the right to cancel the registration of any board member or employee of a district not in good standing, in which event NSBA is not liable for hotel, airfare or other charges.

**Other 10.C: 2018 MASB Board of Directors' election.** Biographical data for the candidates is attached. Region 8 is a three-year term with one seat and four candidates: Donald Hubler of Macomb ISD, Macomb County, the incumbent; Robert McLachlan of Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County; Birgit McQuiston of Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County; and Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. of Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County. The resolution casts the Troy Board of Education's ballot for one candidate.

Cheryl Huffman's January 25, 2018 email from MASB explains the mechanics: seven seats are up for election, one candidate is unopposed and one Region and Group has no candidates, so ballots will be distributed only for Regions 1, 5, 7 and 8. Each district receives one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB. Electronic voting is a two-step process — submit the ballot, then confirm it has been submitted. The ballot deadline is 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 7, 2018; unofficial results will be available on a voicemail recording after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and official results approved at the March 16, 2018 Board of Directors' meeting. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign for anyone running for a seat.

Read as a whole, the February 2018 packet is the district's annual enrollment-policy meeting. A projection of 13,207 students for 2018-2019 — the thirteenth consecutive year of growth off a 2005/06 low of 11,965 — drives the decision to close six buildings to open enrollment while admitting 40 kindergartners, 3 first graders and 14 middle school students under Schools of Choice, essentially the number of siblings already identified in the district's own survey. The two capital awards, $55,865.00 of fiber maintenance and $188,971.00 of general trades work, are modest by comparison and both flow from the 2013 bond program's second series and the district's E-rate posture.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, February 28, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Five items. The 2016-2017 Senior Scholar Athletes and the fall and winter All-State Athletes, both presented by Mike Jolly.

The Mission Moment recognizes **Katarina Tasich, a Troy Union third grader**. During December, Troy Union students wrote opinion pieces and many reached out to principal Michael Cottone; Katarina's essay argued the community should do more to stop bullying. She followed up by presenting her writing to him with concrete steps, one of which stood out — that the entire school wear black around a unified message of **"Blacking out Bullying."** The message caught on at Troy Union and then across the district, with community members wearing black in support. "Katrina is proof that we can all make a difference."

**Schroeder Elementary** is recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School, honored by U.S. Secretary of Education John B. King, Jr. in Washington the previous November. **Just 329 schools nationwide were chosen in 2016.** Principal Brian Canfield and staff receive a certificate. The fifth item adopts the Principal Appreciation Month resolution.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the January 10 workshop, the January 17 special meeting and closed session, the January 17 organizational and regular meeting, and the December 2016 Treasurer's Report.

**What the January minutes record**
The January 10 workshop heard a Section 23 proposal presentation naming two bidders — **Mondrian Properties and JP Acquisitions** — and previewed the January 17 agenda items. It ran to 9:56 p.m.

A special meeting on January 17 at 6:30 p.m., attended by Bill Bowman of Great Northern and Dana Abrahams of Clark Hill, went into closed session on the Section 23 sale (resolution 17-001, unanimous roll call) for two minutes and adjourned at 6:56.

The organizational meeting that followed elected **Dr. Philippart president, Mr. Schmidt vice president and Mrs. Fleming secretary**, all 7-0, and appointed Rick L. West treasurer. It adopted the Employment Dispute Resolution Plan (17-013), the Section 23 purchase authorization (17-015) and the $101,162.00 Global Equipment award (17-016), all 7-0, and the revised committee memberships. Mr. Hauff and Mrs. Hammond both praised the MLK Day event; Hammond thanked the Board for her warm welcome.

**Treasurer's Report — December 2016**
Total check disbursements are $10,842,523.49 — matching the register's own TOTAL REPORT line — with the General Fund group at $9,813,108.65 and the General Fund (101) itself at $9,396,917.30. Adding $1,971,606.70 of wire transfers, $157,549.67 of P-Card purchases and $32,412.94 of ACH debits, less $16,877.52 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $12,987,215.28.

**Personnel — the TEA bargaining team**
The collective bargaining agreement between the district and the TEA/MEA/NEA, representing the teaching staff, **expires on June 30, 2017**. The Board appoints **Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson** with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass as team members, resolving further "that the Board desires to reach a fair and equitable agreement with this Association."

**Curriculum — enrollment**
Dr. Machesky presents projections prepared by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants, dated February 7, 2017. Headcount has climbed from 12,056 in 2010/11 to **12,868 in 2016/17**. Projected total K-12 for 2017/18 is **12,752 excluding** self-contained special education, the early childhood program and GROW, or **12,992 including** them — then 12,751/12,991, 12,781/13,021, 12,799/13,039 and 12,765/13,005 through 2021/22. The current headcount excludes 276 students: 77 in the Early Childhood Program, 137 in self-contained special education and 62 in GROW.

The striking series is Schools of Choice enrollment, which has nearly tripled in six years: **416 (fall 2010/11), 590, 700, 821, 907, 990 and 1,120 in fall 2016/17.**

On that basis administration recommends closing **Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park** on enrollment and space constraints, and closing Athens and Troy High again except for not more than 25 incoming ninth graders from the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens, with applications accepted in a two-week window at the end of March and early April.

**Curriculum — Schools of Choice**
Kris Griffor and Mark Dziatczak present. Of elementary students in 2016-2017, **552 are Schools of Choice against 5,003 non-SOC — 9.9%**, ranging from 20.8% at Hill and 16.9% at Barnard down to 1.5% at Schroeder. The SOC population is 56.5% White and 24.1% Asian against a non-SOC population that is 52.9% White and 38.4% Asian; SOC students are more likely to be Black (10.9% vs 3.6%) and on free or reduced lunch (14.9% vs 10.5%), and less likely to be in special education (3.6% vs 9.7%).

The twelve-year application history shows 860 kindergarten and 305 first grade openings advertised against 1,442 and 475 applications received, with 887 and 260 students enrolled. A sibling survey found 51 kindergarten, 4 first grade and 26 middle school siblings planning to attend.

Four resolutions follow, split between Section 105 (within Oakland County) and Section 105c (outside, where the ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD): **55 kindergarten and 5 first grade** under each, and under each, **20 middle school seats at Baker, 6 at Larson and 1 at Smith**.

**Business**
Ten of the district's buses have reached end-of-life. Using the Michigan School Business Officials cooperative purchasing service, three proposals were obtained and reviewed with Transportation Liaison Dominick Asaro; the low bidder, **Hoekstra Transportation**, is awarded **$885,322.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, under the School Bus Replacement Program funded by 2014 Bond Series 2.

**Recognition 2.A and 2.B.** The Board recognizes the 2016-2017 Senior Scholar Athletes and the fall and winter 2016-2017 All-State Athletes, both presented by Mike Jolly.

**Recognition 2.C: Katarina Tasich and "Blacking out Bullying."** The Mission Moment recognizes a third grader at Troy Union Elementary for her efforts to make the world a better place and to take a stand against bullying. During the month of December, Troy Union students wrote opinion pieces on a variety of topics; the students were excited about the project and wanted their voices to be heard, and many of them reached out to the principal. One topic that caught Mr. Cottone's interest was Katarina's essay — she took a risk and shared that the community should do more to stop bullying. A few days later she formally presented her writing piece to him and outlined the steps that could be taken. The ideas were good, but one really stood out: she suggested that the entire school wear black around a unified message of "Blacking out Bullying." The message caught on at Troy Union and throughout the entire school district, with many community members wearing black to support her message. The item closes: "Katrina is proof that we can all make a difference." Principal Michael Cottone and teacher Jess Bronsteen are invited to describe her efforts, and Katarina receives a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

**Recognition 2.D: Schroeder Elementary, National Blue Ribbon School.** The Board recognizes Schroeder Elementary for its designation as a National Blue Ribbon School, an award that honors Schroeder as one of the very best schools in the United States. U.S. Secretary of Education John B. King, Jr. recognized the school in a ceremony in Washington, D.C. the previous November, and just 329 schools from around the country were chosen for the honor in 2016. The item states that the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents and the Schroeder community, and quotes Secretary King: "National Blue Ribbon Schools are proof that we can prepare every child for college and meaningful careers. Your schools are on the cutting edge, pioneering innovative educational practices — professional learning communities, project-based learning, social and emotional learning, positive behavior systems — making you shining examples for your communities, your state and the nation." Principal Brian Canfield and Schroeder staff in attendance come up to receive congratulations and a certificate.

The recognition sits oddly beside item 7.B in the same packet, which recommends closing Schroeder to open enrollment on space constraints — the school is being honored nationally and declared full in the same evening.

**Recognition 2.E: Principal Appreciation Month.** Throughout Michigan, February has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the outstanding work of building-level educational leaders. The resolution recites that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready, and commends the district's elementary and secondary principals for their exceptional commitment to excellence.

**Consent minutes: the January 10, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:00 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Deputy Superintendent Dziatczak, Harris, Griffor, Gottlieb and West, and approximately 10 other members of the audience. The business services update covered the Section 23 proposal presentation and consideration, with two bidders named in the minutes — Mondrian Properties and JP Acquisitions — followed by the January 17, 2017 agenda items: appointment of treasurer, establishing fund depositories and the investment resolution for 16/17 and 17/18, portable testing tables and chairs, and bus purchases. The teaching and learning update covered special education and an update on the timeliness of IEPs, plus a professional learning update and scorecard. The workshop adjourned at 9:56 p.m., nearly four hours.

Mondrian Properties is the same firm that would go on to buy the district's Section 16 land in March 2018 and the Section 1 front parcel that September; its first appearance in these packets is here, bidding on Section 23.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 special board meeting and closed session.** President Philippart called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. with all seven members present. Superintendent Machesky was in attendance along with Bill Bowman from Great Northern and Dana Abrahams from Clark Hill — the consultant and the law firm named in the Section 23 item — and there were no other members in the audience. Resolution 17-001 provided that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Board shall go into closed session to discuss the sale of Section 23 property, on a roll call in which all seven members voted yes. The Board moved to closed session at 6:31 p.m. and reconvened at 6:33 p.m., adjourning at 6:56 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 organizational and regular meeting.** The organizational business ran 7-0 throughout. Resolution 17-002 had Dr. Philippart serve as acting chairperson to officiate until a president was elected. Resolution 17-003: Dr. Philippart was nominated and elected president of the Troy Board of Education. Mr. Schmidt was nominated and elected vice president. Resolution 17-004: Mrs. Fleming was nominated and elected secretary. Resolutions 17-005 and 17-006 appointed Rick L. West treasurer, and 17-007 adopted the fund depositories and investments resolution. Resolutions through 17-011 continued the designations of legal counsel, the superintendent as deputy secretary, the person for posting notices, and adopted the meeting schedule, each 7-0.

Resolution 17-013 established the Employment Dispute Resolution Plan applicable to all applicants for employment, all substitute employees, all nonunion employees and all nonunion administrators and supervisors, 7-0. The team's composition is notable: the assistant superintendent for employee services leads, with the business services head, the deputy superintendent for teaching and learning, the assistant superintendent for elementary instruction and two others alongside — the district's entire senior administration at the table.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents on enrollment projections for the 2017-2018 school year and beyond, with the analysis provided by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants, the presentation dated February 7, 2017.

The enrollment history, by headcount, runs 12,165 (2008/09), 12,069 (2009/10), 12,056 (2010/11), 12,328 (2011/12), 12,391 (2012/13), 12,573 (2013/14), 12,556 (2014/15), 12,710 (2015/16) and 12,868 (2016/17) — eight straight years of growth after the 2010/11 trough, apart from a single dip in 2014/15.

The birth-to-kindergarten ratio table runs from 4.58 in 99-00 through 4.46, 4.42, 4.58, 4.67, 4.61 (04-05), 4.65 (05-06), 4.94 (06-07), 5.45 (07-08), 5.29 (08-09), 5.22 (09-10), 5.63 (10-11), 5.67 (11-12), 5.94 (12-13), 6.18 (13-14), 5.82 (14-15), 6.39 (15-16), 6.59 (16-17) and a projected 6.18 for 17-18 — a ratio that has risen by better than a third and a half over the series, meaning a steadily larger share of children born in the district's catchment area enroll in its kindergartens.

The methodology notes are explicit about what the headline figures do and do not count. The K-12 head count excludes 276 students: the Early Childhood Program (77), self-contained special education (137) and GROW, post-secondary special education (62). The projections assume 60 Schools of Choice kindergarten and 10 Schools of Choice first grade students, sibling only. Future enrollments would be expected to fall between the MOST LIKELY and LOW projections, calculated by adding MOST LIKELY plus the LOW divided by two.

The Schools of Choice enrollment series is the report's most dramatic single trend: SOC students attending the Troy School District number 416 in fall 2010/11, 590 in 2011/12, 700 in 2012/13, 821 in 2013/14, 907 in 2014/15, 990 in 2015/16 and 1,120 in fall 2016/17 — an increase of roughly seven hundred students in six years. Read against an overall enrollment that grew by about eight hundred over the same period, nearly all of the district's growth in that window is Schools of Choice students.

Projected future enrollment by grade band and year, excluding SCSE, ECP and GROW, then with them included: 2017/18, K-5 5,458, 6-8 2,987, 9-12 4,307, total K-12 12,752 or 12,992 including; 2018/19, K-5 5,370, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,307, total 12,751 or 12,991; 2019/20, K-5 5,320, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,387, total 12,781 or 13,021; 2020/21, K-5 5,369, 6-8 2,984, 9-12 4,446, total 12,799 or 13,039; and 2021/22, K-5 5,364, 6-8 2,916, 9-12 4,485, total 12,765 or 13,005. The projection is essentially flat across five years, with the elementary band shrinking slightly and the high school band growing — the shape of a district whose enrollment bulge is aging upward. The current enrollment comparison for grades K-12, including SCSE, ECP and GROW, runs 12,494, 12,573, 12,653, 12,556, 12,612, 12,710, 12,710 and 12,868.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2017-2018.** Administration has reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools be closed to open enrollment. The district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years; based on current projections for 2017-2018 it is recommended that both be closed again, with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School, with applications for those twenty-five spots accepted during a two-week window at the end of March and early April.

The resolution closes Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2017-2018 with that exception, and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain. The following year's list would add Barnard and Martell to the closed elementary schools.

**Curriculum 7.C: the Schools of Choice report.** Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, Teaching and Learning, present recommendations for the 2017-2018 school year.

The elementary enrollment projections from Fred Ignatovich give kindergarten and first grade HIGH / AVERAGE / LOW bands by year: 2014/2015 kindergarten HIGH 827, AVERAGE 807, LOW 787 and first grade HIGH 915, AVERAGE 817, LOW 899; 2015/2016 kindergarten HIGH 791, AVERAGE 763, LOW 733 and first grade HIGH 842, AVERAGE 748, LOW 802; 2016/2017 kindergarten HIGH 839, AVERAGE 811, LOW 784 and first grade HIGH 896, AVERAGE 798, LOW 876; and 2017/2018 kindergarten HIGH 863, AVERAGE 823, LOW 782 and first grade HIGH 941, AVERAGE 822, LOW 919.

The elementary SOC application history records openings advertised, applications received and students enrolled for kindergarten and first grade in each year: 2006-2007, 25 and 25 openings, 72 and 42 applications, 32 and 23 enrolled; 2007-2008, 40 and 10, 92 and 35, 49 and 11; 2008-2009, 30 and 5, 95 and 29, 46 and 7; 2009-2010, 55 and 20, 84 and 47, 62 and 17; 2010-2011, 100 and 50, 132 and 40, 106 and 30; 2011-2012, 160 and 30, 142 and 53, 110 and 36; 2012-2013, 100 and 30, 188 and 39, 117 and 32; 2013-2014, 100 and 30, 183 and 61, 98 and 27; 2014-2015, 50 and 25, 133 and 55, 74 and 35; 2015-2016, 100 and 50, 156 and 40, 98 and 15; and 2016-2017, 100 and 30, 165 and 34, 95 and 27 — totalling 860 and 305 openings advertised, 1,442 and 475 applications received, and 887 and 260 students enrolled across the eleven years.

The data summary for 2016-2017 gives, by building, SOC students against non-SOC with the SOC percentage and its change: Barnard 84 / 411, 16.9% (+0.3); Bemis 23 / 499, 4.4% (-0.3); Costello 53 / 307, 14.7% (+2.3); Hamilton 63 / 452, 12.2% (+1.3); Hill 67 / 255, 20.8% (+2.0); Leonard 45 / 394, 10.2% (+0.7); Martell 69 / 440, 13.5% (-1.2); Morse 22 / 457, 4.5% (-2.0); Schroeder 8 / 512, 1.5% (-0.2); Troy Union 24 / 443, 5.1% (-0.6); Wass 72 / 356, 16.8% (+1.0); Wattles 22 / 477, 4.4% (+0.3); TOTAL 552 SOC and 5,003 non-SOC, 9.9%, up 0.2 points. By grade: kindergarten 100 / 798, 11.1%; first 113 / 769, 12.8% (+1.8); second 83 / 758, 9.8% (-1.1); third 90 / 864, 9.4% (+0.3); fourth 86 / 920, 8.5% (-0.3); fifth 80 / 894, 8.2% (+0.6).

By subgroup, SOC students are 19.5% ELL (108) against 29.8% (1,493) among non-SOC; 14.9% free or reduced lunch (82) against 10.5% (527); and 3.6% special education (20) against 9.7% (484). By ethnicity the SOC population is 56.5% White (312), 24.1% Asian (133), 10.9% Black (60), 6.3% multi-ethnic (35), 1.3% Hispanic (7), 0.9% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (5) and no American Indian students, against a non-SOC population that is 52.9% White (2,645), 38.4% Asian (1,922), 3.6% Black (181), 2.6% multi-ethnic (132), 2.1% Hispanic (105), 0.2% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (12) and 0.1% American Indian (6).

Kindergarten and first grade enrollment history runs 784 and 811 (2006-2007), 804 and 793, 775 and 830, 739 and 817, 752 and 785, 727 and 832, 768 and 795, 766 and 814, 700 and 787, 755 and 728, and 798 and 769 (2016-2017). Non-Schools of Choice students by grade for 2016-2017 run 798, 769, 758, 864, 920, 894, 927, 903, 985, 875, 887, 914 and 947 for kindergarten through twelfth, totalling 11,441, an increase of 222.

A survey emailed to current Schools of Choice families asked about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade and grades 6 through 8 for 2017-2018: 51 kindergarten students plan to attend, 4 first grade students, and 26 middle school students — 15 in sixth grade, 7 in seventh and 4 in eighth.

The Griffor and Dziatczak memorandum to Dr. Machesky, dated February 28, 2017, lists the factors considered: current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of SOC students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter under a limited program; and available elementary classrooms. Their recommendations are to use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two) as the foundation; to accept SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, anticipating more than 100 kindergarten applicants and allowing the district to admit 100 initially with the option of admitting more in the third week of August if space allows — noting that while this is quite close to the opening of school, some families still welcome the opportunity to enroll; to limit Schools of Choice kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and to accept sibling preference applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where current estimates for next year's enrollment approximate 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial process would bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker while leaving room to admit more in August. The memo text also notes that the actual February Count enrollment for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Ignatovich's Most Likely and Low projections.

The memo's own numbers — 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade — do not match the resolutions the Board is asked to adopt, which set 55 and 5. Portions of the memo also carry "2016-2017" where the subject line and the resolutions read 2017-2018, indicating text carried over from the prior year's document; the operative figures are those in the resolutions.

**Curriculum 7.D through 7.G: the four Schools of Choice resolutions.** Michigan law requires a resolution each school year to implement a Schools of Choice program, and Troy adopts four — the same seat counts stated once under Section 105 and again under Section 105c, distinguishing where the applicant's home district sits rather than adding seats.

7.D adopts, under Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, acceptance of applications for a limited Schools of Choice program for 2017-2018 for 55 nonresident kindergarten and 5 nonresident first grade students who attend a school district within Oakland County, with total students including non-Oakland County residents under Section 105c. 7.E adopts the same 55 and 5 under Section 105c for students attending a district outside Oakland County where that intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries.

7.F anticipates seats available for 2017-2018 in grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools and adopts, under Section 105, acceptance of applications for 20 nonresident 6th-8th grade students at Baker, 6 at Larson and 1 at Smith, for students attending a district within Oakland County. 7.G adopts the identical building-by-building allocation under Section 105c for students outside the county. The middle school seats are allotted per building rather than as a pooled total — the practice the district would abandon by 2018, when the resolutions read simply "14 fourteen total" across the three schools with placement based on building availability.

**Business 8.A: bus purchase.** Ten of the district's school buses have reached end-of-life. The Michigan School Business Officials School Bus Purchasing Program was used to obtain competitive pricing, which was compared and reviewed by Mr. Dominick Asaro, Transportation Liaison.

Todd Hensley's January 5, 2017 memorandum to Rick West, headed School Bus Replacement Program – 2014 Bond Series 2 – 2016-17 School Year, records that ten of the district's bus fleet have reached their end-of-life cycle; that MSBO offers a cooperative bus purchasing service to obtain competitive pricing from bidding dealers; that this service was used to obtain pricing for several different models matching the district's needs; and that after analyzing three proposals and reviewing them with Dominick Asaro, they collaboratively recommend the low bidder, Hoekstra Transportation, in the amount of $885,322.00 as detailed in the attached bid tabulation. The resolution awards the bid for school buses to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $885,322.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. (The memo attributes the funding to 2014 Bond Series 2 while the resolution names the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.)

Read as a whole, the February 2017 packet is the district's annual enrollment-policy meeting, and its central fact is the Schools of Choice line: 1,120 nonresident students in fall 2016/17 against 416 six years earlier. Nearly all the district's growth over that period came from outside its boundaries, which is why the same meeting closes three elementary and middle schools and both high schools to open enrollment while carefully allotting 55 kindergarten, 5 first grade and 27 middle school seats building by building. The Board also opens its teacher contract negotiation with a June 30 deadline, replaces a tenth of its bus fleet, and honors a school it is simultaneously declaring full and a third grader who talked an entire district into wearing black.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education's organizational and regular meeting of January 19, 2016 at the Services Building. The organizational half elects officers and re-designates the treasurer, depositories, counsel and meeting schedule. The regular half honors Troy High students who raised over $31,500 for a classmate with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma, appoints David Pass Director of Employee Services from a field of more than fifty applicants, receives the district's first M-STEP results showing Troy ranked #1 in Oakland County on combined ELA and mathematics, and approves a memorandum of understanding with Beijing Weiming Education Group bringing ten Chinese students to Troy for their senior year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Organizational and regular meeting, January 19, 2016, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**The organizational half**
The familiar sequence: elect an acting chairperson to officiate until a president is elected, appoint a temporary secretary, then elect president, vice president and secretary; appoint the treasurer; establish fund depositories and the investment resolution; designate board and district legal counsel; designate the superintendent deputy secretary; designate a person for posting notices; and adopt the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition — "Caring for Karen"**
The Board recognizes Troy High students and staff "who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease." The school-wide effort was spearheaded by **Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government**, and raised **over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund** — Karen being an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma. Principal Remo Roncone describes the effort; participants shake hands with the Board and a folder of certificates goes to the teacher for distribution. Dozens of students are named, among them Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng.

The first recognition item is Board Recognition Month.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the December 1, 2015 special meeting and workshop, the December 15, 2015 meeting, and the November 2015 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report — November 2015**
Total check disbursements are $5,375,669.60, the General Fund group $3,477,732.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $3,172,152.99. Adding $1,962,353.96 of wire transfers, $157,790.88 of P-Card purchases and $17,422.93 of ACH debits, less $1,983.19 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $7,511,254.18.

**Personnel — Director of Employee Services**
**David Pass** is appointed. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary for the past four years and was asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Before Troy he was assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and was then enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated April 2016 graduation.

Unlike the 2017 appointments, the packet publishes the **full applicant list rather than a funnel** — more than fifty names including Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard and Kellie Cunningham. (Pass would appear a year later on the Board's TEA negotiating team.)

**Curriculum — the first M-STEP results**
Mark Dziatczak reports the district's spring 2015 M-STEP results with an Oakland County comparison. M-STEP tested ELA in grades 3-8 and 11, mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11, science in grades 4, 7 and 11, and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

Troy's county rankings, combined and then grade by grade:

| Subject | Combined | By grade |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ELA (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #1 #1 #1 #1 #1 #2 #1 |
| Mathematics (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #3 #1 #2 #1 #1 #4 #1 |
| Science (4, 7, 11) | #7 | #11 #11 #2 |
| Social Studies (5, 8, 11) | #2 | #1 #5 #4 |

By subgroup, Troy ranks **#2 in ELA and #1 in mathematics for special education students**, and #2 in ELA for economically disadvantaged students. The report's conclusions note that **test standards — the cut scores for proficiency levels — increased for 2015**, the first year of the new assessment.

The science result is the outlier: #11 in the county at both grade 4 and grade 7 against #1 or #2 nearly everywhere else. It is the same relative weakness the 2018 gap analysis would still be tracking.

**Curriculum — the Weiming pilot**
Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding with **Beijing Weiming Education Group** for a Chinese and American student exchange. Eligible Chinese students would take part in a **three-plus-one year program** — three years at Weiming schools in China, then transferring to Troy for one year. Troy students would have the opportunity to study at a Weiming high school for summer or winter camps or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators "in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy," and the item notes the program aligns with **recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China**. The resolution approves the MOU and provides that in the first year of the pilot, **a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled in the Troy School District**.

**Other**
Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt is approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute, under Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences — the earlier policy numbering, before the district renumbered it 1000.01.

Agenda packet for the organizational and regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, January 19, 2016, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Election of Acting Chairperson; 3. Appointment of Temporary Secretary; 4. Annual Organizational Meeting of the Board of Education — A. Nomination and Election of Officers (President, Vice President, Secretary), B. Appointment of Treasurer, C. Establish Fund Depositories and Investment Resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17, D. Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel, E. Designation of Superintendent to be Deputy Secretary, F. Designation of a Person for Posting Notices of Meetings, G. Meeting Schedule for 2016 Calendar Year; 5. Recognition — A. Board Recognition Month, B. TSD Mission Moment: Troy High Students' "Caring for Karen" Fundraising Efforts; 6. Additions & Deletions; 7. Public Communication (agenda items); 8. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Special Board of Education Meeting, B. Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Board of Education Workshop, C. Minutes of the December 15, 2015 Board of Education Meeting, D. Treasurer's Report – November 2015; 9. Personnel — A. Consideration: Elementary and Secondary, B. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Director, Employee Services; 10. Curriculum — A. M-Step Results & County Comparison, B. Weiming International Student Pilot; 11. Business; 12. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 13. Other — A. 2016 NSBA Advocacy Conference; 14. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools. (The two curriculum items carry the section header "10. BUSINESS" on their item pages while the agenda index lists section 10 as Curriculum.)

**The agenda memo and organizational items.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board setting out the organizational sequence, beginning with the election of an acting chairperson who will conduct the meeting until a president has been elected. The organizational items follow the pattern used in the 2017 packet: nomination and election of president, vice president and secretary in turn; appointment of the school board treasurer; establishment of fund depositories and the investment resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17; designation of board and district legal counsel; designation of the superintendent to be deputy secretary; designation of a person for posting notices of meetings; and adoption of the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition 5.A: Board Recognition Month.** The annual January item recognizing the work of the Board of Education.

**Recognition 5.B: "Caring for Karen."** The Board recognizes a special group of Troy High students and staff who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease. The item records pride in "the all-out school wide effort spearheaded by Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government," which raised over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund. Karen is an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma.

Mr. Remo Roncone, Troy High's principal, is invited to describe the efforts, after which the staff and students who organized the projects come up to receive recognition. The staging is specified: participants shake hands with the Board, and a folder containing all the certificates is presented to the teacher or administrator for distribution to individuals — a practical accommodation for a group too large to hand certificates to one by one. The students named include Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng, among many others.

Harriet Clark, who taught the Personal Communication classes that led the effort, appears again in the April 2017 packet among the 35 Outstanding Teacher nominees, listed as teaching communications, debate and English at Troy High.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 1, 2015 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 15, 2015 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2015.

**Treasurer's Report, November 2015.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $3,172,152.99, with Total General Fund of $3,477,732.82 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $5,375,669.60. Adding ACH debits of $17,422.93, outgoing wire transfers of $1,962,353.96 and P-Card purchases of $157,790.88, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $1,983.19, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $7,511,254.18. The middle sections of the packet are the November check register run by fund. The totals here run materially below the equivalent months in the 2017 and 2018 packets, which is what one would expect a year before the 2016 bond program began spending.

**Personnel 9.A: elementary and secondary.** The routine personnel recommendations item.

**Personnel 9.B: Director of Employee Services.** The recommendation is Mr. David Pass. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary School for the past four years, and was additionally asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Prior to coming to Troy he held several positions including assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education from Oakland University and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and is currently enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated graduation date of April 2016. The resolution approves his employment as Director of Employee Services without tenure in the administrative position.

The packet's treatment of the search differs from the practice the district would adopt a year later. Rather than the staged funnel published for the 2017 and 2018 appointments — applications received, first-round interviews, finalists, final selection — this packet simply prints a list headed "Troy School District Applicants for Employee Services" naming more than fifty people: Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard, Kellie Cunningham and others. Every applicant is named in a public document, with no indication of who was interviewed — a more exposing disclosure than the later funnels, which name only those who reached an interview.

David Pass appears again in the February 2017 packet as a member of the Board's negotiating team for the TEA contract talks, alongside Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson.

**Curriculum 10.A: 2015 M-STEP results and county comparison.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, provides the district results of the spring 2015 M-STEP testing along with a comparison of scores with other Oakland County school districts. The presentation is dated January 12, 2016.

M-STEP in spring 2015 tested English language arts in grades 3-8 and 11; mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11; science in grades 4, 7 and 11; and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

The presentation reports Troy's rank among Oakland County districts for each subject, first combined across grades and then grade by grade. In ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #1, #1, #1, #1, #1, #2 and #1. In mathematics combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #3, #1, #2, #1, #1, #4 and #1. In science across grades 4, 7 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #7; by grade, #11, #11 and #2. In social studies across grades 5, 8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #2; by grade, #1, #5 and #4.

Two subgroup breakdowns follow. For special education students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined and #1 in mathematics. For economically disadvantaged students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA combined.

The conclusions note that test standards — the cut scores that define proficiency levels — increased for 2015. This was M-STEP's first administration, replacing the MEAP, and the higher cut scores meant proficiency rates statewide fell sharply from the prior assessment; the county-rank framing the presentation uses sidesteps that discontinuity by comparing Troy against its peers on the same new test rather than against its own prior-year numbers.

The science result is the one clear weakness in an otherwise dominant showing: #11 in the county at grade 4 and again at grade 7, against #1 or #2 almost everywhere else, recovering to #2 by grade 11. The same relative pattern persists into the 2018 gap analysis, where science remains the subject on which Troy's margin over the county and state is narrowest.

**Curriculum 10.B: Weiming international student pilot.** Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding between the Troy School District and Weiming Education Group, outlining a Chinese and American student exchange program between Beijing Weiming Education Group and the district.

The MOU outlines the opportunity for eligible Chinese students from Weiming Education Group — referred to as Chinese Foreign Students — to participate in a three-plus-one year program, in which they study for three years at Weiming schools in China and subsequently transfer to the Troy School District for one year. Students from the Troy School District would also have the opportunity to study at one of Weiming's high schools for summer and winter camps and/or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy. The item further notes that the program is aligned to recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China and to promote opportunities for Oakland County businesses and ventures in China — an unusual justification for a curriculum item, tying a student exchange to county economic development policy.

The resolution approves the Memorandum of Understanding under the terms of the agreement and provides that in the first year of this pilot program, a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled as students in the Troy School District.

The structure is worth noting for what it is and is not. It is not a Schools of Choice arrangement — those resolutions, adopted every February under Sections 105 and 105c, govern nonresident Michigan students and turn on which intermediate school district the applicant's home district sits in. This is a separate instrument entirely, admitting foreign nationals for a single senior year under a negotiated MOU, capped at ten students in the pilot year.

**Other 13.A: 2016 NSBA Advocacy Institute Conference attendance.** As required by Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences, expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference.

The policy citation is itself a small marker of time: by May 2017 the same requirement is cited as Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, following the policy renumbering the Board adopted in December 2016 when it approved the revised Board of Education Bylaws and Policies.

Read as a whole, the January 2016 packet is the district at a quieter moment than the years that follow — no bond program yet spending, monthly disbursements running at half what they would reach by 2018, and an organizational meeting with no change in the Board's composition. What it does contain is a district looking outward in two directions at once: a first set of M-STEP results establishing Troy at or near the top of all Oakland County districts in ELA and mathematics, and a memorandum of understanding with a Beijing education group that would bring ten Chinese seniors into Troy High classrooms, justified partly by Oakland County's own economic ambitions in China. Between them sits a fundraiser in which one high school's communication classes and student government raised over $31,500 for a classmate with cancer.

Special Board of Education meeting, Thursday, May 15, 2014, 4:45 PM, Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, phone 248.823.4000. Agenda: Pledge of Allegiance; Public Communication; Business items A through C; Other item A; Adjournment.

3.A SECURE ENTRANCES (BID PACKAGE 1 / 9777)
Bid responses for secure entrances at 12 elementary sites, Baker Middle School and International Academy East were reviewed by Kenneth Miller, Executive Director of Maintenance and Operations, and Ronald Curtis, Senior Project Manager, Barton Malow. Awards are to be charged to the 2014 Capital Projects Fund.

| Category | Contractor | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 061000 General Trades | Construction Solutions, Inc. | $1,892,300.00 |
| 230000 Mechanical | Miller-Boldt, Inc. | $636,815.00 |
| 260000 Electrical | Metro Electric Engineering Technologies, Inc. | $559,000.00 |
| Total Bid | | $3,088,115.00 |

BUDGET
The bond application allocated $2,669,975.00. The bids equaled $3,088,115.00, which was $418,140.00 over the projected cost, to be funded from variances in other packages. The end budget amount of $51,360 from the roofing project at Larson and Boulan Park Middle Schools can be applied at this point. Barton Malow states an intent to manage the over/unders to at least a net zero add to the bond issue.

BIDDING NOTES
Proposals were received May 1, 2014. Only one bid was received for general trades; three of four committed contractors dropped out citing inability to staff the project. Firms that backed out are listed as Arjac Inc., M.L. Schoenherr, NACE and Precision Contracting. The apparent low electrical bidder, Ecker Mechanical, asked to withdraw claiming its bid was incomplete; Barton Malow recommends allowing withdrawal and awarding to second low bidder Metro Electric, noting a bid bond claim would delay the project and might recover approximately $10,000. Group 1 buildings are Costello, Hill Leonard, Martel, Morse and Wattles; Group 2 are Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Baker MS and IAE.

3.B / 3.C IPAD CASES
On April 22, 2014 the board awarded a portion of the bid for Computer Equipment, Mobile Devices and Accessories for Gumdrop Tech iPad cases to CDWG in the amount of $153,000. Mark Washington, Director of Technology, learned of the MaxCase Shield case at a Michigan School Business Officials conference. The Shield costs $23 per unit compared with $30 per unit for the Gumdrop, a savings of $35,700, and has two open slots in the back for barcode and ID labels. The resolutions rescind the $153,000 CDWG award and award 5100 iPad MaxCase Shield cases at $23 each for a total of $117,300.00, expensed from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund.

Resolutions may be adopted no earlier than May 12, 2014 and copies are due to Oakland Schools by Friday, May 30, 2014.

ITEM 3.A, SECURE ENTRANCES. Bid responses for secure entrances at 12 elementary sites, Baker Middle School and International Academy East were reviewed by Mr. Kenneth Miller, Executive Director of Maintenance and Operations, and Mr. Ronald Curtis, Senior Project Manager, Barton Malow. The suggested resolution awards the bid and approves the amounts as an expenditure of the 2014 Capital Projects Fund: Construction Solutions, Inc., General Trades, $1,892,300.00; Miller-Boldt, Inc., Mechanical, $636,815.00; Metro Electric Engineering Technologies, Inc., Electrical, $559,000.00; Total Bid $3,088,115.00.

A memorandum dated 12 May 2014 from Kenneth D. Miller, Executive Director, Facility Operations and Purchasing Department, 1140 Rankin, Troy, Michigan 48083, phone 248 823-4050, fax 248 823-4077, addressed to Mark Rajter, Assistant Superintendent Business Services, and subject-lined Secure Entrance under the Bond Renovation Project, states that after analyzing the proposals and attending the post bid reviews Miller concurs with Barton Malow's recommendation on bid package 9777, Secure Entrance at all 12 elementary sites, Baker and International Academy East, listing Construction Solutions, Inc. (General Trades) $1,892,300.00, Miller-Boldt, Inc. (Mechanical) $636,815.00, and Metro Electric Engineering Technologies, Inc. (Electrical) $559,000.00. Based on the bond application the funding allocated was $2,669,975.00; the bids equaled $3,088,115.00, which was $418,140.00 over the projected cost. Miller attributes part of the overage to the tight timeline needed to start the projects during summer 2014, noting that projects of this magnitude would normally be bid 6 to 8 months before construction kickoff but that the bond did not go up for vote until November of 2013, leaving only a couple of months to process. General Trades firms that initially planned to provide proposals but backed out due to a last minute addendum and other obligations already scheduled for summer 2014 are listed as Arjac Inc., M.L. Schoenherr, NACE and Precision Contracting. Copies went to Pat Orczykowski, Business Department, and the Purchasing Department file.

A letter dated May 12, 2014 from Barton Malow Company, 26500 American Drive, Southfield, Michigan 48034, phone 248.4365000, fax 248.436.5001, to Mr. Kenneth Miller, Executive Director, Troy School District, 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083, covers the 2013 Bond Program, Series 1, Bid Package 1, Secure Entrance Remodeling at 14 Buildings, and contract award recommendations. The project scope describes a Welcome Center/secure entrance concept in which a visitor enters the main building entrance vestibule through exterior doors left open to permit vestibule-only access for shelter in inclement weather, sees a glazed wall and door leading from the vestibule directly to the main office, and finds the inner set of vestibule doors locked to prevent further passage into the school. The visitor communicates with the main office secretary from the vestibule over an audiovisual station, is identified and permitted access to the main office, completes identification and sign-in with the secretary, and then enters the school through a separate door beyond the secure entrance.

Proposals were received on May 1, 2014. Barton Malow recommends contracts as follows: category 061000 General Trades, Construction Solutions, Inc., $1,892,300; category 230000 Mechanical, Miller-Boldt, Inc., $636,815; category 260000 Electrical, Metro Electric Engineering Technologies, Inc., $559,000; total $3,088,115. Under Special Considerations the letter notes that only one bid was received for the general trades category, that four contractors were committed to bidding until the last days of the bidding period, and that the three that dropped out cited inability to staff the project if awarded a contract. Barton Malow states that although it would typically not recommend making an award from a single bid, in this case it does not see the situation improving because most contractors have their work load set for the summer this late in the bidding season, and that with the bond issue approved in November the architect/engineer was not able to start design work and produce bid packages for the January/February time frame the firm would prefer. The letter also reports that the apparent low bidder for electrical work, Ecker Mechanical, requested that its bid be withdrawn claiming the bid was incomplete, and recommends allowing the withdrawal and awarding to the second low bidder, Metro Electric, because attempting to recover damages from the bid bond would delay the project and may only result in a recovery of approximately $10,000. Under Budget, the letter states the budget for this work is $2,669,975, resulting in an overage of $418,140 which will be funded from variances in other packages, that the end budget amount of $51,360 from the roofing project at Larson and Boulan Park Middle Schools can be applied at this point, and that going forward Barton Malow intends to manage the over/unders to at least a net zero add to the bond issue. The letter is signed by the Senior Project Manager, with a bid tabulation attached and a copy to Ms. Nichol Bruno, BMC.

The attached bid tabulation is headed Troy School District, 2013 Bond Program, Series 1, Bid Package 1: Secure Entrances at 14 Buildings, with columns for Base Bid (Group 1), Base Bid (Group 2), Combined Bid (Group 1 and 2), Alternate 1 (Group 2), Alternate 2 (Group 1), Alternate 2 (Group 2), Addendum 1,2,3, Bid Bond, Family Disclosure Form, Clarifications Included, and Comments and Voluntary Alternates. Notes define Group 1 as Costello, Hill Leonard, Martel, Morse and Wattles, and Group 2 as Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Baker MS and IAE. In bid category 061000 General Trades, Construction Solutions bid $1,137,600 for Group 1, $774,700 for Group 2, $1,892,300 combined, $156,700 for Alternate 1 (Group 2), $41,000 for Alternate 2 (Group 1), and no bid on Alternate 2 (Group 2). In bid category 230000 Mechanical, Miller-Boldt bid $371,315 and $265,500 with no combined bid and a voluntary alternate to deduct $10,000 to use Carrier equipment and Carrier fan coils; Ecker Mechanical Contractors Inc. bid $398,600 and $296,100; Johnson and Wood bid $431,540 and $326,790 with a combined bid of $744,100; Contrast Mechanical bid $443,133 and $319,605 with a combined bid of $762,738. In bid category 260000 Electrical, Ecker Mechanical Contractors Inc. bid $218,500 and $244,100; Metro Electric Engineering Technologies bid $291,000 and $268,000; Great Lakes Power and Lighting bid $292,000 and $296,000.

ITEM 3.B, IPAD CASES BID RETRACTION. On April 22, 2014 the Board of Education awarded a portion of the bid for Computer Equipment, Mobile Devices and Accessories for Gumdrop Tech iPad cases to CDWG in the amount of $153,000. The district subsequently learned of a newly introduced iPad case, the Shield, from MaxCase, which provides the same level of protection as the Gumdrop cases and offers other benefits at $23 per unit compared with $30 per unit for the Gumdrop case, a savings for the district of $35,700. The suggested resolution rescinds the $153,000 CDWG award. A supporting memorandum dated May 8, 2014 from Mark Washington, Director of Technology, to Dr. Barbara Fowler, Superintendent, explains that he learned of the Shield after attending the most recent Michigan School Business Officials conference, that the case has two open slots in the back usable for barcode and ID labels so a case can be inventoried and identified without turning the device on, and that the case costs $23 per unit instead of $30 per unit for a savings of $35,700. The Gumdrop cases had been selected off the National Joint Purchasing Association (NJPA) bid vehicle; Gumdrop had not been notified of the award, so there were no vendor issues. All cases are in stock from MaxCase of California and MaxCases are also available via the NJPA bid vehicle. Lansing Public Schools has used an earlier model for two years with success, and another MaxCase product was named by District Administration Magazine readers as one of the Top 100 Products of 2013. Washington recommends 5100 iPad MaxCase Shield Cases at $23 each for a total of $117,300, expensed from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund.

ITEM 3.C, IPAD CASES PURCHASE. The companion resolution awards the bid for iPad Shield cases to MaxCase in the amount of $117,300.00 as an expenditure of the 2014 Capital Projects Fund.

ITEM 4.A, BIENNIAL ELECTION FOR OAKLAND SCHOOLS BOARD OF EDUCATION ON JUNE 2, 2014. In accordance with Public Act 419 of 2004 the Troy Board of Education must elect members to the Oakland Schools Board of Education and select a designate to cast a ballot on its behalf. The board is to designate a representative and discuss the candidate, Mr. George Ehlert, an incumbent running unopposed for the one open seat. The resolution recites that Public Act 419 of 2004 amended election procedures for intermediate school districts, requires a constituent board to designate its representative and identify the supported candidate by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election, and requires consideration at not less than one public meeting before adoption, with the Troy board considering the resolution at an open meeting under the Open Meetings Act on May 15, 2014. The operative paragraphs designate a representative to the 2014 electoral body, state support for a candidate for one position for a term of six years ending June 30, 2020, and direct the representative to vote for that candidate at least on the first ballot taken at the June 2 election. A certification block is provided for the Secretary of the Board of Education of Troy, Michigan.

An attached email dated Thursday, May 08, 2014, 9:29:43 AM from Kathy Boike, Executive Assistant, Office of the Superintendent and Board of Education, Oakland Schools, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, MI 48328, phone 248.209.2123, fax 248.209.2206, reports that one individual filed for the one open seat, Mr. George Ehlert for a 6-year term. Attachments include a Local Board Resolution Template, the OS BOE 2014 Election Timeline Revised, and MCL 380.614. The email explains that Oakland Schools board members are elected by an electoral body composed of one person designated by each constituent district board, that designated electors must cast ballots in person between 5:30 and 7:30 PM on Monday, June 2, 2014 in Conference Room A of the Oakland Schools building at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road in Waterford, and that absentee ballots are prohibited. It describes three options districts have used to consider and adopt resolutions, notes that resolutions may be adopted no earlier than twenty-one days prior to the election, that is, no earlier than May 12, 2014, and asks that adopted resolutions be faxed to 248.209.2206 by the end of business on Friday, May 30, 2014. Questions may be directed to Sherry McMillan at 248.209.2062. Because the candidate is an unopposed incumbent, no Meet the Candidates forum will be scheduled.

The attached Oakland Schools Board of Education Election 2014 Timeline lists: March 12 to May 5, candidates may pick up nominating petitions and affidavit forms at the Oakland County Clerk's office, Elections Division, 1200 N. Telegraph Road, Dept. 417, Pontiac, 48341; Monday, May 5, 4 PM, last day to file nominating petitions, filing fees and affidavits of identity; Thursday, May 8, Oakland Schools receives the list of qualified candidates and forwards it to constituent district superintendents and board secretaries; May 12 to May 29, each constituent board designates its representative, identifies supported candidates, and considers and adopts a resolution, with consideration at not less than one public meeting before adoption; Friday, May 30, copies of district resolutions due via fax 248.209.2206 or email to Kathy.Boike@oakland.k12.mi.us; Monday, June 2, 5:30 to 7:30 PM, representatives cast ballots at the Oakland Schools Board of Education open meeting with no absentee ballots accepted; Tuesday, June 3, notification of results sent to district superintendents and the Oakland County Clerk; Monday, July 14, successful candidates take the oath of office at the Oakland Schools Board of Education Organizational Meeting.

ITEM 6.A, ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, PRINCIPAL, BARNARD ELEMENTARY SCHOOL. The superintendent recommends the appointment of Ms. Melanie O'Neil as Principal of Barnard Elementary School. O'Neil comes to the Troy School District from the Grosse Pointe Public School System, where she has been the Principal of Kerby Elementary School for 2 years. ITEM 8.A, RESOLUTION TO HOLD A PUBLIC HEARING ON THE PROPOSED 2014-2015 SCHOOL YEAR BUDGET. The resolution provides that a public hearing shall be held on June 17, 2014 at a regular board meeting beginning at 7:00 p.m. at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, Troy 48098, for the purpose of receiving testimony and discussing the proposed 2014-2015 budget, and authorizes and directs the Secretary of the Board of Education to publish notice substantially in the form of the attached Exhibit A in a newspaper of general circulation within the school district at least six days before the hearing.
