ITEM 3.A, ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, ASSISTANT SUPERINTENDENT, SECONDARY INSTRUCTION. The recommendation is for the appointment of Mark Dziatczak as Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction. Dziatczak comes to the position from Principal at Troy High School, where he has worked since July 2005, and previously worked as an Assistant Principal and Interim Principal at Athens High School. He received his undergraduate degree in Physics from Wayne State University, his Master's Degree in K-12 Educational Administration from Michigan State University, and his Education Specialist Degree in Educational Leadership from Oakland University, and is currently enrolled in the Doctoral Program in Education Leadership at Oakland University. The suggested resolution provides that the Board of Education issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Mark Dziatczak, who will begin duties as Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction effective July 1, 2014.

ITEM 3.B, SUPERINTENDENT'S CONTRACT APPROVAL. At its May 6, 2014 meeting it was moved by Mrs. Fleming and supported by Ms. Underwood for the Troy Board of Education to offer the position of Superintendent of Troy School District to Dr. Richard Machesky, and the resolution was approved unanimously. Following successful negotiation of a contract, the board is asked to approve the agreement, which provides a contract through June 30, 2017 commencing July 1, 2014. The suggested resolution approves the contract of the Superintendent of Schools, in effect from July 1, 2014 through June 30, 2017, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to the provisions of the written agreement.

SUPERINTENDENT OF SCHOOLS EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENT. The agreement, entered into on June 10, 2014, is between the Board of Education of the Troy School District and Dr. Richard M. Machesky. Paragraph 1, Employment Term, sets the period commencing July 1, 2014 and terminating June 30, 2017, renewable at any time prior to its expiration date of June 30, 2017 by duly authorized written agreement. Paragraph 2, Qualifications, requires the educational qualifications of Section 1246 of the Michigan School Code of 1976 (Public Act 451 of 1976), as amended. Paragraph 3, Duties and Responsibilities, requires the superintendent to serve as directed by the board and as required by Michigan law and to obey and fulfill board policies, rules and regulations. Paragraph 4, Performance Evaluation, requires the board to provide a written evaluation no later than June 1 of each calendar year, with the instrument and evaluation format made known to the superintendent by November 1 of the immediately prior calendar year. Paragraph 5, Salary, sets an annual salary of One Hundred Seventy-Eight Thousand Dollars ($178,000), with the board retaining the right to adjust the salary prospectively but not to reduce it below that figure. Paragraph 6, Work Year, requires performance of duties over the full fifty-two weeks of the district's fiscal year, July 1 through June 30, less applicable vacation, leave and holidays, including attendance at board and committee meetings and district and civic functions, with no additional compensation for such attendance. Paragraph 7, Fringe Benefits, incorporates the attached Fringe Benefit Supplement, subject to annual review for modification by the board. Paragraph 8 bars outside employment or self-employment without prior board consent. Paragraph 9, Conflict of Interest, requires full disclosure of any questioned interest, with the board's disposition controlling, and includes the superintendent's representation that he possesses no interest adverse to the district. Paragraph 10, Residency, states the board prefers district residency but that it is not required.

Paragraph 11, Discipline and Termination, permits discipline, suspension or termination for reasonable and good cause with notice and a fair hearing, defines good cause to include an act of moral turpitude, any misdemeanor or felony criminal conviction or plea of nolo contendere, violation of the agreement, or disability as provided in Paragraph F of the Fringe Benefit Supplement, and requires thirty days written notice and opportunity to cure any curable violation plus opportunity to attend any board meeting at which a termination vote is taken. Paragraph 12, Arbitration, commits all disputes to arbitration under the Employment Rules of the American Arbitration Association, conducted in Oakland County, Michigan, with the parties equally sharing arbitrator fees and hearing room rental, and limits the arbitrator's opinion in a termination case to whether the board had good cause. Paragraph 13, Non-Renewal, leaves the renewal decision solely within the board's discretion but requires at least ninety days written notice of non-renewal prior to expiration; the superintendent may terminate on at least ninety days written notice, which the board may waive in whole or part. Paragraph 14, Tenure Exclusion, provides that no continuing tenure is granted under the Teachers' Tenure Act, Act 4 of the Public Acts of 1937 (Extra Session), as amended. Paragraph 15, Medical Examination, requires an annual medical examination with a written fitness statement provided to the Board President, reimbursement of examination costs not covered by insurance, and reserves the board's right to direct an examination to verify physical or psychological competence, with reports shared by the President with other trustees but otherwise kept confidential. Paragraph 16, Indemnification, requires the board to defend, hold harmless and indemnify the superintendent from claims arising within the scope of employment, excluding criminal proceedings at the board's sole discretion and claims or actions of the district, and excluding alleged intentional tortious actions or inactions; the board must provide public liability insurance at reasonable cost in an aggregate amount of not less than three million dollars ($3,000,000.00) and reimburse expenses and judgments not covered by insurance, with no individual board member personally liable. Paragraph 17, Entire Agreement, states the agreement and Fringe Benefit Supplement contain all terms and that the Administrative Handbook of the Troy School District is not applicable to the superintendent. Paragraph 18, Applicable Law, makes the contract subject to Michigan law with a severability clause. Signature blocks are provided for Dr. Nancy Philippart, Board of Education President, Karl Schmidt, Board of Education Secretary, and Dr. Richard M. Machesky, Superintendent.

FRINGE BENEFIT SUPPLEMENT. Paragraph A provides health, dental and vision insurance on the same single, two-person or full family basis as other administrators, subject to modification. Paragraph B provides long-term disability insurance on the same basis as other administrators, with benefits of sixty-six and two-thirds percent (66-2/3%) of monthly earnings for inability to work due to extended sickness or injury, payable until age seventy (70); monthly earnings include compensation subject to board-paid retirement contributions to the Michigan Public School Employees Retirement System (MPSERS) at the time of disability divided by twelve months, and the coverage has a 365-day waiting period, with insurance amounts reduced by primary remuneration from the board, the Michigan Public School Employee's Retirement Fund and the Federal Social Security Act. Paragraph C provides a group term life insurance policy paying a designated beneficiary a sum equal to $500,000. Paragraph D provides accidental death and dismemberment insurance in the sum of $1,000,000. Paragraph E, Worker's Compensation, requires prompt notice of on-the-job injury and provides that if the superintendent is absent due to a job-related accident he will be paid, for a period not to exceed sixty days from the date of the accident, the difference between full salary and worker's compensation benefits, with no district supplement after entry into long-term disability coverage. Paragraph F, Income Protection, continues salary for temporary incapacity due to illness or disability but not beyond any continuous period of one calendar year, crediting board-paid disability insurance and statutory worker's compensation amounts; after incapacity exceeding twelve calendar months the board may terminate on written notice, after which insurance benefits continue for the remainder of the first year of long-term disability benefits. Paragraph G provides payment of one state, one local and one national association dues at the superintendent's discretion, plus tuition and registration reimbursement for required professional development on the same basis as other administrators. Paragraph H allows reimbursement of reasonable and appropriate business expenses in accordance with the Internal Revenue Code, Internal Revenue guidelines and Michigan Department of Treasury guidelines, with valid receipts and expense reports. Paragraph I provides 25 paid vacation days per fiscal year which may not be carried forward, with payment on termination or non-renewal for prorated unused earned vacation at the pro-rata daily rate (salary divided by 365 days) using the formula number of total vacation days divided by 12 times number of months worked minus used vacation time. Paragraph J provides twelve (12) paid holidays: July 4, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Friday after Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Good Friday, Memorial Day, and two floating holidays during the winter recess, with pay included in salary. Paragraph K permits a tax-sheltered annuity as added compensation but states no annuity will be provided for the 2014-15 fiscal year.

Called to order at 7:36 p.m. with all seven members present; administrators Machesky, Ms. Birmingham, Mr. Dziatczak, Mrs. Haezebrouck, Mr. Carson and Mr. West attended along with approximately 20 other members of the audience. The agenda listed public communication, an Innovations presentation, a Summer Success Academy update for Grades 3 and 6, a Michigan Merit Curriculum update, a district property update, and a budget update covering millage renewal, the 2014/2015 final budget amendment and the 2015/2016 budget. Adjourned at 11:05 p.m.

PERSONNEL (6). A. New hire recommendation for a probationary contract for 2015-2016: Michael Denyes, 1.0 FTE Counselor, Smith/Boulan Park Middle Schools. His biographical sketch dated July 7, 2015 lists a B.A. from Oakland University, Rochester, May 2010, majoring in Psychology and Anthropology; an M.A. from Oakland University, December 2012, in School Counseling; a Michigan School Counselor Certificate issued January 2013; service as Counselor at Holly Area Schools, Holly, MI from August 2013 to June 2015; Guest Counselor with PESG, Caledonia, MI from February 2013 to June 2013; resident community Troy, Michigan. B. Superintendent's contract extension. The Board reported that Dr. Richard Machesky completed his first year as a HIGHLY EFFECTIVE superintendent, meeting or exceeding expectations in all evaluation categories, having articulated a clear vision and launched the concept of One Troy, introduced a customer service mindset into Central Office, engaged the community, kept the district fiscally strong, successfully negotiated all labor contracts and filled staff positions. The Board authorized a $5000 bonus and, consistent with average total compensation increases for other staff groups, a 3.5% base salary increase, with the contract extended through June 30, 2018. The suggested resolution states the contract will be in effect from July 1, 2015 through June 30, 2018, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to the provisions of the written Agreement.

CURRICULUM (7). A. Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2015/2016, enrolling the six (6) secondary schools under the direction of the Troy Board of Education, City of Troy, County of Oakland, as members of the MHSAA, a voluntary nonprofit corporation, and enrolling them to participate in approved interschool athletic activities; the authorization is effective from August 1, 2015 until July 31, 2016 and may not be revoked during that period. The Board delegates supervision and control to the Superintendent or designee and adopts the MHSAA Constitution, By-Laws and current HANDBOOK rules as minimum standards. B. High School Cooperative Team Agreement: the District seeks MHSAA approval to operate a cooperative team in Boys' Ice Hockey with Athens and Troy High Schools, Troy High as the primary school and Athens as the secondary, for the 2015-16 and 2016-17 school years. C. Athletic Code of Conduct, reviewed at the annual "Vision" meeting, with the revised Code of Conduct for Student Athletes attached (Revised December 2004; Revised July 2015) and to be posted on the District website once approved. The Code contains twelve sections. Section I eligibility requires enrollment by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester; high school participants must be under nineteen (19) years of age, seventh and eighth graders under fourteen (14) and fifteen (15) respectively; a physical examination by an M.D., D.O., physician's assistant or nurse practitioner taken after April 15 of the previous school year; a maximum of four (4) seasons of a sport and four (4) first semesters and four (4) second semesters in grades nine through twelve; and academic eligibility requiring passing grades in a minimum of five (5) classes (Niles 4 classes, Intersect 5 classes, IA 6 of 8 classes), with transfer students new to the district meeting the MHSAA minimum of four (4) classes. Section II limits awards to symbolic or merchandise items not exceeding twenty-five dollars ($25.00) in fair market value and bars cash or negotiable documents. Section III on amateur status applies to baseball, basketball, cross country, football, golf, gymnastics, soccer, softball, skiing, tennis, track, volleyball, wrestling, ice hockey, competitive cheer, swimming and diving. Section IV on outside competition imposes ineligibility for a minimum of the next two (2) days of competition for middle school and three (3) days for high school, reflecting Section 13(A) Limited Team Membership of the MHSAA handbook. Sections V through VIII address school attendance, practice attendance, travel to and from away contests, and responsibility for uniforms and equipment. Section IX on tobacco, alcohol and other drugs sets penalties: a first tobacco violation costs a minimum of the next interscholastic event or one week of a season, capped at 10% of regular season contests; a first alcohol or drug violation or second tobacco violation costs two (2) consecutive events or two (2) weeks, capped at 20% of regular season contests, with a mandatory drug workshop consortium at family expense; a second alcohol or drug violation or third tobacco violation brings dismissal from the team, and if less than 50% of the season remains the student is ineligible for the first half (50%) of the next sport, with professional assessment for chemical dependency at a Michigan State Department of Substance Abuse Services approved agency required; a third alcohol or drug violation or fourth tobacco violation brings exclusion from all interscholastic participation for three hundred and sixty-five (365) days; a fourth alcohol or drug violation or fifth tobacco violation forfeits any remaining eligibility in the Troy School District. Seventh and eighth grade athletes are removed from the team on any violation. Sections X and XI cover voluntary summer and off-season programs and supplemental team rules approved by the building principal. Section XII permits appeal within two (2) school days to the building principal, who must convene a meeting within two (2) school days and respond in writing within two (2) school days, with further appeal to the Deputy Superintendent, whose decision is final.

A, Troy, MI 48083, Attn: Carol Miller), NBS Commercial Interiors (2595 Bellingham, Troy, MI 48083, Attn: Natalie Kosnik) and American Interiors (30553 S. Wixom Rd., Wixom, MI 48393, Attn: Jen Malia). Rick West's July 15, 2019 memorandum to Dr. Rich Machesky quotes the Friday, June 28th Communique and estimates $1,300,000 to renovate Niles without demolition, $1,900,000 to renovate after removing the early childhood wing and adding 30 parking spaces, and $500,000 to demolish the building entirely; none include flooring or casework. District administrative offices are at 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.4000; meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

RECOGNITION. Mr. Jolly read biographies of the Spring 2014 all-state athletes: Craig Bazin, Justice Bigelow, Nicholas Boynton, Jay Darish, Deepthi Devireddy, Jill Dougherty, Kyle Fietsam, David Fracassa, Amanda Harris, Sydney Heath, Lillian Liang, Ashley Messina, Sally Muller, Jacob Nelson, Kunal Tangri and Sarah Troccoli, representing Troy High School and Athens High School in boys and girls lacrosse, girls tennis, girls soccer, softball and boys track. Coaches named include Justin Suarez, Nate Reynolds, Brian Miska, Rob Holder, Todd Heugh, Tom Calnen, Scott Player and Brian Zawislak.

The Michigan Association of School Boards recognized the Troy Board of Education for its Honor Board achievement and a Standard of Excellence Award, President Nancy Philippart for the Master Board Member Award and the Advocacy Skill Specialty Award, and Secretary Karl Schmidt for MASB Level One Certification and the Award of Merit.

The Association of School Business Officials International awarded Troy School District its Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2013, recognizing Mark Rajter, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services. The August 4, 2014 letter from Executive Director John D. Musso, CAE, RSBA, says the engraved plaque will be mailed in approximately 6-8 weeks. Review comments address page ix (duplicated debt information in the transmittal letter; GASBS 34:8 footnote 7; 2012 GAAFR pages 591-592), page 10 (construction in progress reported separately from land), disclosure of commitments in construction in progress (NCGA-I6:4j; 2012 GAAFR page 372), page 43 (basis of budgeting note; 2012 GAAFR page 580), pages 55-58 (remove an unneeded note), and pages 67-70 and 79 (principal property taxpayers and principal employers for the current fiscal period and the period nine years prior; GASBS 34:37; GASBS 44:19-20 & 34). GASB updates cover Statements No. 65 and No. 66 (March 2012), No. 67 and No. 68 (June 2012), No. 69 (January 2013), No. 70 (April 2013) and No. 71 (November 2013). The certificate is signed by Terrie S. Simmons, RSBA, CSBO, President, and John D. Musso. The award is sponsored by VALIC, which as of August 30, 2013 had more than $79 billion in total assets under management and managed plans for nearly 25,000 groups serving nearly 2 million plan participants. ASBO, founded in 1910, is at 11401 North Shore Drive, Reston, VA, 20190.

The TSD Mission Moment honored the Boulan Park Middle School LINKS program, which pairs students with different learning styles; an ASD class and its 8th grade mentors, led by Ms. Sandy Ford and Mr. Joe DeVault, collected 1,022 personal letters and 2,790 items such as snacks, bath items, gloves, CDs and games, plus cash totaling $142, assembled into care packages for troops in Afghanistan.

CONSENT AGENDA. Item A was the minutes of the August 5, 2014 Board of Education meeting at the Administration Building. President Philippart called that meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; present were Board members Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Schmidt and Underwood, Superintendent Machesky, administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Keeling, Machesky, Rajter and Witt, and approximately 8 members of the audience. Resolution 14-087 approved consent items A (minutes of the July 8, 2014 meeting), B (Treasurer's Report for April and May 2014) and C (copy paper), 7 Yes / 0 No. Resolution 14-088 approved new hires Kaitlin Bucchare, Ross Burdette, Aguib Diop, Lauren Field, Johnathan McNurlen, Tanya Myre, Laura Rasmussen, David Recker, Krystal Renton, David Russo, Noelle Wald and M. Kelsey Witt, 7-0. Resolution 14-089 issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure to Ms. Kris Young as Director of Technology effective August 11, 2014, 7-0. Resolution 14-090 exercised the option under Section 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, to accept applications for the 2015-2016 school year for an unlimited number of 9th grade students attending districts in another county whose Intermediate School District is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District, for the International Academy East program, 7-0. Resolution 14-091 awarded the Smart Board Widescreen Interactive Whiteboard System and LED Touch TVs to VSC for $185,012.50 from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund, 7-0. Resolution 14-092 awarded Athens High School addition and remodeling work to North American Construction Enterprises (general trades) $483,750.00, Contrast Mechanical (mechanical) $190,000.00, McNulty Electric (electrical) $137,700.00 and Nagle Paving (site work) $72,500.00, total bid $883,950.00, 7-0. Resolution 14-093 awarded food services equipment and installation to Stafford-Smith, Inc. for $90,140.00 from the 2014-2015 Food Services Fund, 7-0. Resolution 14-094 certified Paula Fleming, Todd Miletti, Nancy Philippart and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2014 Delegate Assembly, November 6-9, 2014, 7-0. Dr. Machesky reported secure entrances would be completed by October 2014, discussed Larson and Boulan Park roofing and weather concerns, elementary site work and high school renovations, an administrator retreat, and an August 26th staff kick-off at Athens High School. The Board was asked to approve and set the millage rate. Rates are set every June on the best information then known and are therefore estimates, after which the Michigan Department of Treasury requests districts to certify rates on state-approved forms. Because operating Non-Homestead taxable values grew greater than the rate of inflation, it is necessary to amend Form L-4029 to officially set the rate for the 2014 tax year; the suggested resolution directs that the Tax Rate Request Form L-4029 be amended and forwarded to the appropriate tax jurisdictions. The attached Michigan Department of Treasury Form 614 (Rev. 04-14), 2014 Tax Rate Request, must be completed and submitted on or before September 30, 2014 under MCL Sections 211.24e, 211.34 and 211.34d, with penalty for non-filing under MCL Sec 211.119; taxable value is stated as of 5-27-14. Instructions reference MCL 211.36 and 211.37, State Tax Commission Bulletin 3 of 2014, STC Bulletin No. 11 of 1999 as supplemented by letter of 6/7/2000, Form 2166 (L-4034), MCL 380.1211(3) on Supplemental (Hold Harmless) millages, an October 26, 2004 memo to assessors, and the 18 mills levied by districts without a Supplemental millage.

OTHER. Ron Curtis of Barton Malow presented a 2013 Bond Program Series 1 summer 2014 construction update prepared by Barton Malow and TMP. Summer scope comprised, at elementary schools, 14 secure entrance projects, 7 sitework projects and 7 site lighting projects; at middle schools, 2 roofing projects, 1 locker room replacement and 2 secure entrance additions; at high schools, 1 secure entrance and auditorium upgrade project, 1 LGI room renovation and 3 additions; and corridor door replacement at the Niles Continuing Education Center. Scheduled completion dates: secure entrances 09/30/14; Boulan and Larson roofing replacement 08/22/14; bus/parent drop-off modifications 08/15/14; site lighting 08/15/14; Troy Athens HS 08/18/14 thru 12/19/14; Troy HS 08/20/14 thru 08/14/15; Boulan and Larson additions 08/11/14 thru 07/17/15; Troy HS entrance/auditorium 07/21/14 thru 11/3/14. Building-by-building work is listed for Morse, International Academy, Barnard, Wattles, Hill, Costello, Wass, Troy Union, Leonard, Martell, Hamilton, Bemis and Schroeder. Boulan Park and Larson office additions and the Troy High School classroom and storage additions carry an August 2015 completion date, the Troy High School secure entrance a November 2014 date, and the Boulan Park/Larson roofing is marked complete. Upcoming 2015 work: Athens HS mechanical/electrical/plumbing upgrades; Larson and Boulan mechanical/electrical/plumbing upgrades; Hill and Troy Union roofing; International Academy East pool to LGI conversion; Schroeder and Troy Union bus loop and canopies; Smith MS and Niles gym/locker room upgrades; and Larson and Boulan window replacement. Finally, the district reported a successful Opening Day gathering for all staff at Athens High School the previous Tuesday, where the OneTroy concept was unveiled as a renewed commitment to a unified district that values every employee's role, accompanied by a video.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, May 21, 2019, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Five items: a Mission Moment on the Wass Wolves' Wellness Night sponsored by the Wass PTO in January; the TSD Athletics Coach-Athlete-Parent Pact; the Outstanding Support Staff Person of the Year; the district's retirees; and Teacher Appreciation Week.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the April 9 workshop and April 16 meeting, the March 2019 Treasurer's Report, approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget, and a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2019/2020 budget.

**Treasurer's Report — March 2019**

General Fund expenditures stand at $97,584,514 of a $155,009,522 budget, 62.95 percent, leaving $57,425,009. State sources are the laggard on the revenue side at 55.32 percent collected and federal sources at 20.05 percent, against local sources at 97.86 percent. The Debt Service fund shows principal redemption of $10,565,000 not yet paid and half the interest disbursed, which is why its balance sits at $15,126,662 mid-year.

**Personnel — four appointments, all effective July 1, 2019**
William Turner becomes Director of College & Career Programming after a 19-year career: teacher at Utica High School, counselor at Jeannette Junior High and Stevenson High School in Sterling Heights, then counselor at Troy High, night supervisor for Adult Education and principal for Summer School, and the last seven years as Assistant Principal at Athens. Kristin Martin and Michael Munaco become assistant principals at Athens, she from Clarkston Junior High and Clarkston High School where she was also a behavioral interventionist and restorative practice coordinator, he currently Career Focused Education Department Chair at Seaholm. Christine DiPilato becomes Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction on a 17-year career. Each is a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure.

**Curriculum and business**
A report on high school science materials is followed by adoption of the recommended materials for grades 9-12 in the amount of $631,107.36 for the 2019-20 school year. The five business items are: authorization to finalize a Chartwells food service agreement for 2019/20 with options to renew through 2023/24, contingent on Michigan Department of Education approval, after bids opened April 18, 2019 from Aramark, Chartwells and Sodexo; playground loose fill surfacing material for all 12 elementary schools and the preschool playground at Athens High School awarded to Rolar Property Services, Inc. at $145,603.00 from the Capital Maintenance Fund; preschool technology — projectors, paging and classroom audio systems, reviewed by Director of Technology Beth Soggs with Convergent Technology Partners — at $117,601.85 from the Early Childhood Center Fund; flooring replacement bid alternates to Conventional Carpet at $94,883.00; and Troy Preschool trim and door frames to Barton Malow at not more than $949,000.00 from the Early Childhood Capital Projects Fund.

**Other**
Two resolutions close the agenda. The first commemorates the ratification of the 19th Amendment at the request of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners: districts submitting resolutions receive a 19th Amendment Suffragette Victory Flag to be flown June 10-14, 2019 for the centennial of Michigan's ratification, and again countywide from August 24-28, 2020 for the centennial of federal ratification. The second supports proper funding of education in Michigan.

**Personnel: four administrative appointments.** Each resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure.

Item 6.A recommends Mr. William Turner as Director, College & Career Programming, beginning July 1, 2019. His 19-year career began as a teacher at Utica High School; he then served as a counselor at Jeannette Junior High School and Stevenson High School, both in Sterling Heights, before joining Troy as a counselor at Troy High School. He has also been Night Supervisor for the district's Adult Education Department and Principal for Troy School District Summer School, and has spent the last seven years as Assistant Principal at Athens High School. He served as a district team member for the New Pedagogies for Deep Learning Cohort, headed the District Vision Team for Career and Technical Education, and mentored five teacher leaders aspiring to administration. He holds a Bachelor of Science in English from Michigan State University, a Master of Arts in School Counseling from Sienna Heights College and an Education Specialist Degree in Education Leadership from Saginaw Valley University.

Item 6.B recommends Ms. Kristin Martin as Assistant Principal, Athens High School. She began as a Social Studies Teacher at Brandon High School in Ortonville and is presently a Social Studies Teacher at Clarkston Junior High and Clarkston High School, having also served as a Behavioral Interventionist at Clarkston High School and Restorative Practice Coordinator at Clarkston Junior High School. She has been part of a Trauma-Informed Champions Learning Group, a Teaching and Learning Council member, and has held various coaching positions. She holds a Bachelor of Liberal Arts and Education from the University of Detroit-Mercy, a Master in the Art of Teaching from Marygrove College, and an Educational Specialist Degree in Leadership from Oakland University.

Item 6.C recommends Mr. Michael Munaco as Assistant Principal, Athens High School. He began as a Computer Technology Teacher at Fitzgerald High School in Warren, moved to Chatterton Middle School in Warren as a History and World Languages Teacher, then became a Business Teacher at Seaholm High School in Birmingham, where he is currently Career Focused Education Department Chair. He has been involved with School Improvement and 5D+ Staff Evaluation. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Marketing and Management from Northwood University, a Master in the Art of Teaching from Wayne State University, and an Educational Specialist Degree in Leadership with Administrator Certificate from Oakland University.

Item 6.D recommends Ms. Christine DiPilato as Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, on a distinguished 17-year career in education.

**Curriculum.** Item 7.A is a report on recommended high school science materials; item 7.B adopts them, resolving that the recommended science materials for grades 9-12 in the amount of $631,107.36 be approved for the 2019-20 school year.

**Business.** Item 8.A concerns contracted food service. Bids were opened on April 18, 2019 for Food Service Management, submitted by Aramark, Chartwells and Sodexo. The resolution authorizes Administration to proceed with finalizing an agreement with Chartwells to provide food services for the 2019/20 school year, with options to renew for 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24, contingent upon final approval by the Michigan Department of Education, the contract to be consistent with the terms and conditions of the original Request For Proposal dated March 18, 2019 and subsequent addendums.

Item 8.B awards playground loose fill surfacing material — sought by RFP for all 12 elementary schools and the preschool playground at Athens High School, with bids reviewed by the TSD Operations Department — to Rolar Property Services, Inc. in the amount of $145,603.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.

Item 8.C awards preschool technology for the Troy School District Preschool, an RFP for projectors, paging and classroom audio systems reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, with Convergent Technology Partners, in the amount of $117,601.85 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund.

Item 8.D awards flooring replacement bid alternates to Conventional Carpet in the amount of $94,883.00. Item 8.E awards Troy Preschool trim and door frames to Barton Malow in an amount not to exceed $949,000.00 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Capital Projects Fund; the attached bid material is prepared by Barton Malow Company of 1274 Library St, Detroit, with Stephanie Buhagiar as bid package lead, under project 180281, Troy School District ECC Wood Trim & Frames.

**Other.** Item 10.A is a resolution commemorating the ratification of the 19th Amendment. The Oakland County Board of Commissioners asked school boards to help commemorate the passage of the amendment guaranteeing and protecting women's constitutional right to vote; districts submitting resolutions receive a 19th Amendment Suffragette Victory Flag to be flown June 10-14, 2019 in honor of the 100th anniversary of Michigan's ratification, with the flags flown again countywide from August 24-28, 2020 in honor of the 100th anniversary of federal ratification. The resolution recites that women of every race, class and ethnic background across America have made historic contributions to the growth and strength of the United States in countless recorded and unrecorded ways, and that the women of this nation initiated the most significant women's movement in history. Item 10.B is a resolution in support of proper funding of education in Michigan.

The attached Superintendent Evaluation System, prepared by Collins & Blaha, P.C., notes that the Michigan Revised School Code requires boards to evaluate superintendents annually and evaluates performance across six components — Visionary Leadership, Policy and Governance, Instructional Leadership, Communication and Community Relations, Organizational Management, and Professionalism and Ethics — with an optional seventh component for statutory factors including proficiency with the teacher evaluation tool under section 1249, progress on school improvement plans, pupil attendance, stakeholder feedback and goal achievement. Board members rate each component highly effective, effective, minimally effective or ineffective and submit individual forms to the Board President; those forms are not retained and are exempt from disclosure under MCL 15.243(1)(m), though the Board's final evaluation is subject to FOIA, and the decision to adopt an overall rating must be made in open session under MCL 15.263. Under MCL 380.1249b(1)(b), 25% of the annual evaluation must be based on student growth and assessment data, the aggregate data used in teacher year-end evaluations district-wide. Ratings convert to numerical scores of 4, 3, 2 and 1; the overall rating is 75% of the performance evaluation tool rating and 25% of the student growth and assessment rating, computed by multiplying the tool score by 7.5 and the assessment score by 2.5, with sums of 40-35 highly effective, 34-25 effective, 24-15 minimally effective and 14-10 ineffective.

**OCSBA legislative priorities.** Oakland County School Boards Association resolutions covering mental health (MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50), local control (A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70), evidence-based decision making (G 11.01), unfunded mandates (A 10.20), the School Finance Research Collaborative, school aid planks A through E (A 10.25 subsections, A 10.55, A 10.05), accountability and transparency (A 6.65), lame duck parameters, universal preschool for four year olds (A 6.15 (c)) and full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which initially promised 40 percent of excess cost (A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA). Plank E asks that the annual School Aid Budget be enacted no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget adoption requirement. The cover letter from Birgit McQuiston, Secretary of the OCSBA Board of Directors, sets a voting window of August 1 through September 15, requires approval by at least nineteen member school districts, and reports results at the September 24 OCSBA meeting; Resolutions and Bylaws Committee members are Carol Finkelstein (248-321-7999), Marc Katz and McQuiston.

**Personnel.** Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky completed his fourth year as a highly effective superintendent and exceeded expectations in all evaluation categories, the item citing his support of oneTROY and Troy as a destination district on its journey to world class; the resolution extends his contract from July 1, 2019 through June 30, 2024 without tenure in the administrative position. Item 6.B covers Rick West (Business Services), Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Jordan Harris (Employee Services), whose contracts expire June 30, 2019; the text describes both one-year extensions and two-year successor contracts commencing July 1, 2019 and terminating June 30, 2021, without tenure.

**Meeting schedule and closed session.** The January 14, 2020 Organizational and Regular Meeting was inadvertently scheduled for the second Tuesday; the resolution moves it to January 21, 2020, consistent with third-Tuesday practice. The attached 2019 schedule lists regular meetings at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, at 7:00 p.m. on January 15, February 26, March 19, April 16, May 21, June 4 (at Athens), July 16, August 20, September 17, October 15, November 19 and December 17, and workshops at the Administrative Center, 4400 Livernois, at 6:00 p.m. on January 8, February 5, March 5 (Troy Center for Transition), April 9, May 7, June 11, September 3, October 1, November 12, December 3 and January 7, 2020. The closed session resolution, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), would take the Board into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege by roll call vote of trustees Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson.

OAKLAND ISD BUDGET. Item 8.A presented the Oakland Schools FY 2014-2015 proposed budgets, noting that effective in 2004 Section 624 of the Revised School Code (380.624) requires each ISD to submit its budget to local districts no later than May 1 and each constituent board to adopt a supporting or disapproving resolution no later than June 1. Property tax forecasts show FY 2014-15 up 1.75%, FY 2015-16 up 2.75% and FY 2016-17 through FY 2018-19 up 3.50%, with a decline from the FY 2008 base of $(50.2)M in FY 2014-15; annual collections declined 24.5% from FY 2008 to FY 2014, a cumulative loss of $194.4 million and an estimated $244.6 million through FY15, against an FY 2008 base year levy of $216.9 million and an expected FY 2015 levy of $166.7 million. Assumptions include interest earnings of $300K for all funds combined compared with $7.7 million in FY07, stable state aid, no personal property tax loss in FY15, a QSCB interest subsidy reduced by 7.2%, a 1% pay increase subject to bargaining, a retirement rate of 25.62% adding $326,000 in cost under MPSERS retirement reform, and health insurance hard-cap employee contributions averaging 20% of premium. Total FY 2015 revenue of $287.8 million comprises property tax $166.7 (58%), other financing sources $7.8 (3%), new grant award funding $73.4 (25%), estimated grant carry-over $8.4 (3%), state revenue $8.1 (3%) and other local revenue $23.4 (8%). Total expenditures of $298.1 million comprise transfers to LEAs and other funds $128.8 (43.2%), grant related expenditures $81.8 (27.5%), personnel $56.7 (19.0%), purchased services, supplies and dues/fees $21.9 (7.4%), debt service $4.0 (1.3%), capital outlay and other $3.9 (1.3%) and utilities $1.0 (0.3%). The General Education Fund five-year forecast shows 2014-15 revenue $23.8 million and expenditures $24.1 million, an operating deficit of (.3), end-of-year fund balance $2.6 million and unreserved fund balance at 10.7% of expenditures, declining to $1.3 million and 5.3% by 2018-19. FY 2015 special education program support and subsidies total $112,844,000: PA-18 base distribution $110,264,000, Section 24 subsidy and other $220,000, group homes $1,910,000, Havenwick $150,000, and assistive technology equipment $300,000; the PA-18 base distribution increased $2.36M from FY14, and from FY13 to FY15 the increase equals the SEF revenue increase of $2.1M. Special education forecasts 2014-15 revenue $129.6 million and expenditures $129.5 million with total end-of-year fund balance $2.2 million and restricted fund balance at 5.00% net of LEA transfers. Career Focused Education forecasts 2014-15 revenue $32.4 million and expenditures $34.2 million, a deficit of (1.7), and restricted end-of-year fund balance $3.1 million at 9.1% of expenditures. Grants and funded projects total $81.8M ($73.4M new awards, $8.4M carry over), including a $5.5M MiCRSI grant under appeal by another applicant, $63.2M in direct transfers to districts and $18.6M in ISD-administered grants including JobLink at $5.7M. Item 8.B resolved that the Troy Board of Education received and reviewed the proposed budget and expressed its support, stating that support is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624, with a copy to be forwarded to the Oakland Schools Board of Education no later than June 1, 2014; the certification cites the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267.

POLICIES. Second readings and adoption followed first readings on April 1, 2014. Board Policy C-1402, Smoking, was revised to Tobacco-Free Schools, prohibiting use or sale of tobacco products and non-tobacco nicotine products, including e-cigarettes, shisha or hookah, snus and dissolvable products, by any person, at any time (24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year), in any location and at any event, excluding physician-prescribed nicotine replacement therapy; adopted February 2, 1999, revised September 2003, April 20, 2010 and February 12, 2014. Board Policy G-1005, Nondiscrimination, cites Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the Age Discrimination Act of 1975 and the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, and adds sexual orientation, gender identity, socioeconomic status, perceived religion and association with a protected person to the protected class list, naming the Assistant Superintendent, Human Resources as coordinator at 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098-4799; adopted July 10, 2007, revised February 12, 2014. Board Policy J-2012, Anti-Bullying, defines prohibited conduct, bars retaliation and false accusation, requires prompt reporting to the building principal, investigation, parent notification, annual reports of verified incidents to the school board, designates the superintendent as Responsible School Official, and adopts definitions of telecommunications access device and service provider from Section 219a of the Michigan Penal Code, 1931 PA 328, MCL 750.219a; adopted June 5, 2012, revised March 6, 2014.

**Notice and format.** The Troy Board of Education issued a Board Meeting Agenda for a special meeting on February 2, 2016 at 5:00 PM in the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, telephone 248.823.4000. The notice states that items do not have to be taken in the order shown and that items identified within the consent agenda will be acted on at one time unless removed. Readers are directed to www.troy.k12.mi.us; when school is in session, meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m., and can also be viewed at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Agenda.** Four items: (1) Pledge of Allegiance; (2) Public Communication; (3) Closed Session - Consideration: Mid-Year Superintendent Evaluation & Negotiations; (4) Adjournment.

**Item 3.A, Closed Session (dated 02.02.16).** The backup states the Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss mid-year superintendent evaluation and negotiations, and that following passage of the resolution the Board of Education will go into closed session, with no additional business taking place after that time other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The recommended action is to adopt the resolution: "Be it therefore resolved that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss mid-year superintendent evaluation and negotiations." Blank lines are provided for "Moved by" and "Supported by," and a roll call vote is called for with trustees listed as Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood and Edmunds.

**Superintendent's Goals 2015-2016, February 2016 Update.** The attached presentation organizes the Superintendent's goals into five focus areas: Operational, Business Services, Communications & Strategic Planning, Employee Services, and Teaching and Learning.

*Operational.* The Superintendent will provide leadership so that each central office executive leader maintains purposeful visibility, responsiveness and promotes collaborative decision making. Measures listed are weekly building visits measured via the Central Office scorecard, monthly updates on collaborative decision making identified and measured via the Central Office scorecard, and an annual survey measuring visibility, responsiveness and collaborative decision making. The update refers to the attached WIG Scorecard for building visits and collaborative decision making for Central Office team members.

*Business Services.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to develop a world-class Business Services Department, establishing a formal process integrating day-to-day front end and back end central office tasks involving budgeting, administration of collective bargaining agreements, and payroll/fringe benefits, and establishing best practices and workflow within Central Office to maximize efficiency and accuracy of employee services and business operations. The update reports that training on the eFinance system is scheduled for both Employee Services and Business Services staff, with the goal of learning how best to utilize the software to gain efficiencies in all functions of both departments; additional modules within the software were initiated in the last year, cited as cash receipting and ACA compliance, and diligent implementation of additional modules is expected to assist in improving data integrity.

A second Business Services goal is to create a transparent and efficient process in the development of the 16/17 FY budget, including a structured budget development timeline with stakeholder meetings to educate and gather input, and a process to inform and gather input for the Board to monitor the impact of current and future decision making. The updates report that a schedule of budget events was developed and implemented for presentation to the Board of Education in June and December, with budget events also communicated to administration and union leadership; and that implementation of providing a Cash Position Report, a General Fund Budget to Actual Report, and a Treasurer's Report on a monthly basis to the Board of Education was established. A Board Retreat has been scheduled for March 17th to discuss current and future budget issues.

*Communications & Strategic Planning.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to continue implementation of world-class communications media and community support for strategic District initiatives, with goals of successful passage of the November millage renewal in order to maintain full funding, and identifying and supporting the Facility Review Committee. The update states the District's millage renewal was very successful and passed with 73% of the vote, and that the Facilities Study Team continues to meet every Tuesday evening with a formal report to the Board at the February 16th Board meeting.

*Employee Services.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to develop a world-class Employee Services Department, with the same formal-process goal covering budgeting, administration of collective bargaining agreements, and payroll/fringe benefits. The update lists collaborative integration with Employee Services; monthly meetings currently conducted between the Employee Services and Business Services departments; and successful collaboration during the months of October, November and December on the design and implementation of the ACA reporting module within eFinance to generate novel data and reporting forms within the eFinance database.

A second Employee Services goal covers developing policies, procedures and protocol for basic operational duties, including standardization of handbook and policy manuals for employee payroll and fringe benefit administration, an advanced calendar of payroll activities, and employee directory information. Updates: an alternate data source/master spreadsheet of all District teaching positions independent of eFinance is currently being developed; the Activity Calendar for payroll activities is completed through February 2016 with the complete calendar expected by the end of 2016, developed over the course of the school year using a 60-day advance window; and standardization of employee benefits tasks and employee leaves is ongoing, with new systems and procedures to be in place for the start of the 2016-17 school year.

A third Employee Services goal is a comprehensive all-employee audit of payroll and fringe benefit accounts within the Sungard eFinance database to ensure accurate administration and reporting of employee information and wage/benefit data. Updates: a healthcare audit was completed for all employees, over 1,200, in November and December 2015, with employees audited for healthcare and fringe benefit elections/enrollment; employee directory information was validated in the eFinance database; periphery data such as teacher certification areas and expiration dates is currently being refined in eFinance; and a longevity audit of all TEA members was to be conducted February 1st for accuracy.

*Teaching & Learning.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to improve student performance and further the status of TSD as World Class, with goals to identify ambitious learning outcomes for all students with corresponding performance assessments to measure growth; develop a sustainable teaching and learning network through creation of Content Area Teams (CAT) in K-2 writing, K-12 math, 6-12 ELA, Science and Social Studies; and further implement Cultures of Thinking K-12. Each update directs the reader to the PowerPoint.

**OneTroy Collective Commitments to Ensuring Learning for All 2015.** Commitment 1, Deep Learning as Our Fundamental Purpose: schools will build collective knowledge regarding state standards to clarify what all students must know and be able to do as a result of each unit of instruction (evidence: Essentials by Unit for Mathematics PreK-5), and will provide a system of interventions based on examined evidence guaranteeing each student additional time and support until agreed-upon standards are met, monitored and adjusted using a regular cycle of data analysis (evidence: Multi-Tier System of support design for each building). Commitment 2, Building a Collaborative Culture through High-Performing Teams: schools will work in collaborative teams interdependently to clarify what students must learn, gather and analyze evidence of student learning, identify the most powerful teaching strategies/best practices, and transfer these strategies across team members (evidence: List of Collaborative Teams). Commitment 3, A Focus on Results: schools will analyze data from common assessments to identify students needing additional time and support, discover strengths and weaknesses in individual and collective teaching, and measure team progress (evidence: Common Assessments aligned to Essentials; TSD Balanced Assessment Calendar). The document notes latitude at the school site in how teams are organized - by course, grade level, department, interdisciplinary, vertically, partnered with other schools, or electronically - while stating schools do not have the discretion to allow teachers to work in isolation.

**Secondary Principals Collective Commitments 2015-2016.** States the mission - the purpose of the Troy School District is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; the vision - the Troy School District will be a world-class learning institution; and the values - Deepening Learning, Focusing Direction, and Cultivating a Collaborative Culture. Secondary principal collective commitments are to work with the Building Leadership Team to deeply implement CI Plan Cultures of Thinking objectives and to actively support the Teaching & Learning CAT Process to establish Ambitious Outcomes in 4 core areas and a Sustainable Teacher Leadership Network. Timeline: by November 30, 2015 principals will submit a report of their plan for the year for deep COT implementation and a report of actions to be taken to actively support CAT work at their building and by their assigned subject area, if applicable; by June 1, 2016 principals will submit an evaluation of the COT plan for the year and a report of actions actively supporting CAT work. Possible plan items listed include membership and size of the COT Leader Team, percentage of teachers attempting and regularly utilizing COT routines, summaries of professional development opportunities and building resources supporting the initiative, the Building Leadership Team implementation plan, meetings dedicated to CAT building level collaboration, administrative team participation in CAT meetings, promotion of T&L Department work at staff meetings, and additional supports for building level CAT leaders.

**Department of Teaching & Learning.** Goals are to ensure ambitious outcomes for all students and to create a sustainable leadership network. Slide titles cover CAT Facilitators for Elementary ELA and Elementary Math, Middle School ELA and Math, Middle School Science and Social Studies, High School ELA and Math, and High School Science and Social Studies; CAT Meetings at elementary, middle and high school; Sustainable Leadership Network at each level; and Guaranteed and Viable Curriculum slides for elementary, middle and high school.

**Recognition**

**Business 8.F: district-owned property.** This is the meeting's substantive act. The district has been conducting pre-sale investigations of district-owned vacant property and offers the resolution for consideration.

The recitals: the Board's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; the Board appreciates and values the real property owned by the district; the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to service its preschool programs; the Board desires to explore and consider the sale of certain surplus, vacant real property in order to offset long term debt for the development of an Early Childhood Center; and the Board desires to authorize the district's administration, its legal counsel Clark Hill PLC, and its real estate consultant Great Northern Consulting Group to explore, market and analyze the sale of certain surplus vacant real property as outlined below, with the understanding that any offers or agreements will be brought before the Board for approval.

The six resolved clauses:

1. The district authorizes administration to further investigate the preservation of the Section 1 property, with the exception of the frontage on Square Lake, which will be split into its own parcel and marketed for sale. The remainder of the land may be preserved in perpetuity either by the district or through a conservation easement or other similar form of agreement.
2. The district authorizes the marketing of Section 11 property for purposes of sale.
3. The district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16 and preserve the balance of the subject property.
4. The district appoints TMP Architecture as the architect of record and authorizes TMP Architecture to commence the design process for an Early Childhood Center in accordance with their submitted proposal for services dated March 10, 2017. The cost of services is not to exceed $933,716 to complete phases 1 through 4 of the proposal and is approved as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.
5. The cost associated with the selling of property is an approved expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund Professional Services Budget.
6. Revenue generated from these property sales shall be restricted in the Capital Maintenance Fund for the purposes of using toward the development of the Early Childhood Center.

John Waldrop, AIA, principal and project manager at TMP Architecture, Inc. of Bloomfield Hills, writes to Rick West on March 10, 2017 with the proposal. He thanks West for the opportunity and notes it has been a pleasure to work with him to develop the project scope and initial concepts, and includes a breakdown of proposed fees by phase based on their previous agreement for the 2013 TSD Bond projects. The fee for architectural and engineering services is $1,167,144.00, based on 6% of an estimated construction cost of $19,452,406, and includes architectural, furniture, mechanical, electrical, civil and landscaping design services but not technology consulting services or design.

The fee by phase is: 1, schematic design, 15%, $175,072; 2, design development, 20%, $233,429; 3, construction documents, 40%, $466,858; 4, bidding, 5%, $58,357; 5, construction, 18%, $210,066; and 6, close out, 2%, $23,343 — totalling $1,167,144. The Board's authorization covers phases 1 through 4 only, at not to exceed $933,716, holding back the construction and close-out phases until the project is actually built.

This resolution is the origin point for most of what the district would do with land and buildings over the next two years, and it is worth reading against what actually followed. The Section 1 disposition described here in a single sentence — frontage split off and marketed, remainder preserved in perpetuity or by conservation easement — is exactly the structure the Board would adopt in three separate resolutions in March 2018, over two dissenting votes and after months of public comment. The Section 16 land is here designated as the Early Childhood Center site on approximately 8 acres, with the balance preserved; in the event, the entire 19.43-acre Section 16 parcel was sold to Mondrian Properties in March 2018 and the preschool was built at 205 Square Lake Road instead. And the financing premise stated here — selling surplus land to offset long term debt, with proceeds restricted toward the center — is the plan that the December 2017 construction resolution and the 2018 bond issue would ultimately supersede.

The estimated construction cost TMP works from, $19,452,406, is also close to what the project ultimately cost when bid 9855 was awarded in March 2018.

Read as a whole, the March 2017 packet is a district converting real estate into a building. Item 8.F sets the whole chain in motion — the consultants, the architect, the parcels, and the rule that the money must stay restricted to the preschool — while the four construction items around it, totalling roughly a million and a half dollars of site work, doors, painting and lockers, are the ordinary maintenance of the buildings it already has.

It also awards $1,847,628.40 of network equipment to Presidio and $393,635.73 of musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies.

**Meeting**

**Business 8.A — selling Section 16**
The district issued an RFP to purchase 19.43 +/- acres of surplus vacant land south of Long Lake, east of I-75 and west of Livernois (Sidwell 20-16-401-002) and received six proposals, examined with Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. **Business 8.G — borrowing without a vote**
Having resolved in December 2017 to build an early childhood center, the Board authorizes **2018 School Building and Site Bonds (Limited Tax General Obligation) of not more than $11,000,000**. The authority is Section 1351(2) of Act 451, which lets a board issue bonds without a vote of the school electors so long as total outstanding bonded indebtedness is under 5% of the district's state equalized valuation. Final maturity is capped at 22 years; the bonds sell at public sale between 99% and 110% of par; PFM Financial Advisors LLC is financial advisor. PFM's presale runs a **3.57% NIC** on a 20-year structure at a 3.500% coupon, $11,000,000 of principal against $2,625,963 of interest on each side of the year for $16,251,925 of total principal and interest, with the required millage peaking at 0.20 mills.

**Business 8.H — building it**
Bid 9855 covers complete construction of a **72,000 square foot preschool building** in 19 separate bid categories, of which 3 — joint sealants, roller shades and casework — drew no acceptable bids and will be re-bid in fall 2018. Rob Carson recommends the low qualified bidder in each remaining category: total awards **$17,107,803.00** plus a 5% contingency of **$855,390.15**, for **$17,963,193.15** from the Early Childhood Center Fund. The largest packages are Titan Retail Industries general trades/exterior carpentry $3,204,000.00, Site Development sitework $2,535,000.00, Contrast Mechanical mechanical $1,658,000.00, City Contracting interior carpentry $1,348,800.00, Goyette electrical $1,324,287.00, Men of Steel $1,267,000.00 and Amalio Corporation concrete $1,017,600.00.

**Recognition 2.A: outreach to Parkland students.** The Mission Moment honors students and staff at Troy High School, Athens High School, Boulan Park Middle School and Larson Middle School who took it upon themselves to reach out in a show of support to students at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, the scene of a deadly school shooting the previous month. At Troy High and Boulan Park, students, staff and teachers wrote hundreds of letters and cards to their counterparts in Florida, sending messages of love, prayers and positive thoughts. At Athens, students and art teachers sent student artwork and uplifting messages. At Larson, the Craft Club made a banner that could be hung at the school to let Stoneman Douglas students know that people as far away as Troy were thinking of them. The item observes that though there is no way to take away the pain students in Florida are feeling, the district is proud that its students and staff took the initiative to be part of the healing process. Certificates go to Boulan Park teachers Ann O'Neill and April Reem and student Britta Pingree; Larson teachers Amanda Fisher, Laura Garver and Katy Stanley; Athens teachers Jennifer McLellan and Melissa Velk; and Troy High teacher Jen Opalewski and students Emma Bossenberger, Quinn Kelly and Josiah Willis.

**Recognition 2.B: Larson Middle School, State School of Character.** A select few schools across the country are chosen each year as a State School of Character through the implementation of 11 core principles, which include promoting good character, culture and ethics; fostering student self-motivation; giving students the opportunity for moral action; and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building efforts. Larson was praised for the high quality of its work in all 11 principle areas, and its application has been forwarded for consideration as a National School of Character, to be announced later that spring. The item also commends Wass Elementary School, named a 2018 Honorable Mention School of Character and strongly encouraged to re-apply for the state designation the following fall. Larson Principal Joe Duda and teacher Charlie Tull receive the certificate.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the February 6, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Special Board of Education Workshop; C. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Board of Education Meeting; D. Treasurer's Report – January 2018.

The February 6 workshop, called to order by President Schmidt at 6:04 p.m. with Mrs. Hammond and Mr. Hauff absent, covered board professional learning — Diversity & Inclusion Part III with Dr. Jay Marks, Diversity Consultant from Oakland Schools, and a Technology Integration 4-Year Plan — a business services update on WAN fiber maintenance and the general trades package, a teaching and learning update on Schools of Choice 105 and 105c, the superintendent's update on enrollment projections, board committee assignments, and other items including the NSBA conference, the MASB Region 8 election, Five Dysfunctions of a Team next steps and a code of conduct update. It adjourned at 10:02 p.m.

The February 27 special workshop began at 6:34 p.m. with all seven members present, along with cub scouts from Wass Elementary, Troop 1708, and approximately 20 other members of the audience. In public communication, Britta Pingree, an eighth grade Boulan Park Middle School student, addressed the Board to share that she was organizing the March 14 student-led walkout at 10:00 a.m. related to the recent Parkland shooting. She indicated the walkout would be held indoors, encouraged students and the community to write letters to the families of the victims in Florida, and asked the Board to continue to promote keeping guns out of schools. The workshop adjourned at 6:58 p.m.

**The February 27, 2018 regular meeting minutes.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Birmingham, Canfield, Cottone, Dziatczak, Jolly, Griffor, Harris and West, and approximately 150 members of the audience. Every resolution that evening carried 7-0.

The Board recognized the 2017-2018 senior scholar athletes, who maintained a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while participating in an athletic program, and the fall and winter All-State athletes. For the Mission Moment the Board honored Mr. David Easterbrook, benefactor of the new Auto Lab at Troy High. Troy High Principal Remo Roncone described Easterbrook's involvement: the owner of a Troy-based company providing facility design services and equipment to auto dealers across the country, he led the effort to engage outside help to develop a world-class instructional center. The new auto lab is the first phase in updating the high school's facilities to further enhance its STEM curriculum, with future plans for additional classes in automotive technology, engineering, robotics and the skilled trades. Resolution 18-016 adopted the Principal Appreciation Month resolution.

Resolution 18-017 approved the consent agenda. Dr. Machesky reported on enrollment projections, reviewing the district's history and the projections provided by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants, explaining the data collected and analyzed for projecting enrollment for public school districts, the impact of Schools of Choice on current enrollment, the three projection scenarios — low, most likely and high — and how the projections are calculated, and comparing the projected 2017/2018 figures to the actual enrollment. Resolution 18-018 closed Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2018-2019, with the exception of not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens, and allowing students with siblings in grades 9 through 11 at Athens and Troy High to open enroll to remain.

Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent for Teaching & Learning, reported on the Schools of Choice recommendations, noting the factors weighed — current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter in 2018-2019; and available classroom space — and that the information had been reviewed in detail at the February 6 workshop. Resolution 18-023 awarded fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. in the amount of $55,865.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund. Resolution 18-024 awarded bid pack 21A to R & E Development in the amount of $188,971.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. Resolution 18-025 adopted the 2018 Board Committee Memberships. Resolution 18-026 approved Mr. Gottlieb's attendance at the NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition in San Antonio, April 7-9, 2018. In Board comments, Dr. Philippart congratulated the athletes and thanked Mr. Easterbrook, but noted there were no females in the video and asked how the district could help girls see this as a possible career; Mr. Gottlieb echoed her, recalling that he had only 7 female students in his class during his teaching career and wondering what should be done to open the program to more students; Dr. Machesky agreed more work is needed to make the program more viable in the future.
