She attended Oakland University, receiving her Bachelor's degree in teaching in 2003, her Master's degree in Reading Instruction in 2005, and her Educational Specialist degree in Educational Leadership in 2007. With Board approval, Ms. Griffor will begin her duties as Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction effective July 1, 2015. The recommended action is acceptance of a suggested resolution (with Moved by / Supported by and Yes / No lines) reading: BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Board of Education issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Kristine Griffor, who will begin her duties as Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, effective July 1, 2015.

ITEM 3.B — ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT, DIRECTOR OF ELD, FEDERAL GRANTS & STATE ASSESSMENTS. The Superintendent recommends the appointment of Ms. Christin Silagy to the position of Director of ELD, Federal Grants & State Assessments. Ms. Silagy came to the Troy School District in 2001 from the Burbank Unified School District in Burbank, California, where she served as a fourth grade teacher for 2 years. During her 14 years with Troy, Ms. Silagy taught Science, Language Arts and English as a Second Language at Baker Middle School for 2 years. She then moved to Bemis and Schroeder Elementary Schools as the Program for Accelerated and Creative Education Resource Teacher for a year. In 2004 she moved to Morse Elementary School, where she currently serves as an Elementary ELD Coordinator. Ms. Silagy attended Oakland University, receiving her Bachelor's degree in Elementary Education in 1999, her Master's degree in Curriculum, Instruction and Leadership in 2003, and her Educational Specialist degree in School Administration in 2005. With Board approval, she will begin her duties as Director of ELD, Federal Grants & State Assessments as of July 1, 2015. The suggested resolution states that the Board of Education takes action to approve the aforementioned personnel recommendation as stated above, with Moved by / Supported by and Yes / No lines.

ITEM 3.C — TESPA CONTRACT RATIFICATION. A tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association/MEA/NEA (TESPA) was reached on June 5, 2015. The TESPA membership, comprised of paraprofessionals and skilled-trades employees, voted to ratify the agreement on June 10, 2015. The new one-year contract is for the period commencing July 1, 2015 and ending June 30, 2016. The agreement includes a 1% increase in the existing salary schedule, step movement for all eligible members, and a 4% off-schedule payment to members on the tier 1 schedule who are currently on step 5 or higher. The agreement also includes additional language changes that do not have significant monetary impact. The suggested resolution states that the Board of Education hereby ratifies and adopts the tentative agreement reached on June 5, 2015 between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association/MEA/NEA for the period of July 1, 2015 through June 30, 2016, with Moved by / Supported by and Yes / No lines.

SUPPORTING MEMORANDUM ON THE TESPA TENTATIVE AGREEMENT. A memorandum dated Friday, June 12, 2015 is addressed to Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent, and the Board of Education, from Larry Lobert, Interim Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, and Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, regarding the TESPA Tentative Agreement. Contact details shown on the memorandum are the Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.4022 and fax 248.823.4013. The memorandum announces that a tentative agreement has been reached with TESPA and that it is recommended for Board action at the June 16, 2015 meeting since member ratification has occurred. It states the agreement allows for a net increase (new dollars over 2014/2015) of less than 1.5%, attributed to changes in the pay structure explained in the memorandum and outlined in the attached signed Tentative Agreement. The agreement is described as providing modest improvements to the salary structure while retaining portions of the increase as off-schedule (non-compounding) payments; a clear understanding is expressed in the agreement that such payments are for 2015/16 only and are not to be considered as a basis or starting point for a successor contract, which the memorandum says will help the district retain some flexibility if the district's financial condition requires modifications next year.

The memorandum states the total dollar net increase over 2014/15 is approximately $30,000, comprising the following economics: a 1% across-the-Board increase to the existing salary schedule, including longevity steps; step movement for all eligible members; a 4% off-schedule payment for employees on the tier 1 schedule (those hired prior to February 14, 2012) who are currently on step 5 or higher; premium costs for an additional $20,000 in life insurance coverage for the 5 skilled trade employees; and a $200 reimbursement for work boots for the 5 skilled trade employees. Readers are directed to contact either Larry Lobert or Rick West with questions, comments, or concerns. Attachments listed are the signed Tentative Agreement and the Board Resolution.

ITEM 4.A — CLOSED SESSION, SUPERINTENDENT EVALUATION. The packet notes the Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss the Superintendent Evaluation, and that following passage of the resolution the Board of Education will go into closed session, after which no additional business will take place other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The recommended action is adoption of a resolution stating that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss Superintendent Evaluation. A roll call vote is required, with named lines for Hauff, Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood, Edmunds, and Fleming. The agenda concludes with item 5, Adjournment.

**Meeting identity.** Regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, November 11, 2014, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. District address 4400 Livernois, phone 248.823.4000, www.troy.k12.mi.us. The meeting fell a week later than usual because of the November 4 elections.

**Recognitions.** Lisa Carruthers, a third-grade teacher at Leonard Elementary School, was to receive a certificate for implementing "Peer to Peer Mediation," described as an evidence-based practice that positively affects students with Autism Spectrum Disorders. Tracey Kinney, TSD Assessment Coordinator, was presented a certificate for the NUMATS (Northwestern University's Midwest Academic Talent Search) Outstanding Educator Award; in 2014 only 18 educators from the United States received this recognition.

**Minutes of October 7, 2014.** President Dr. Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. with Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Schmidt and Underwood present, plus Superintendent Machesky, administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Keeling, Mull, Whan and Witt, four high school student representatives (Dalia Ibrahim of Athens, Alexandra Levin and Avirath Kumar of International Academy-East, Sylvester Hanna of Niles, Patty Durell and Bobby Hahn of Troy High) and approximately 75 audience members. Resolution 14-102 honored one National Achievement Scholarship semifinalist, Noah McNeal, and sixty-seven National Merit Scholarship semifinalists; nationally, more than 160,000 students entered the National Achievement program and only 1,600 became semifinalists, while more than one million students from some 22,000 high schools entered the National Merit program and 16,000 became semifinalists, scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT (Yes 7, No 0). Resolution 14-103 approved the September 2 minutes, the September 16 workshop minutes and the June 2014 Treasurer's Report (7-0). Resolution 14-104 accepted the resignations of Kenneth Miller, Executive Director of Maintenance and Operations, and Mark Rajter, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services (7-0). Resolution 14-105 approved new hires Meredith Adkins, Taylor Firman, Rebecca Johnson and Holly White (7-0). Resolution 14-106 seated the 2014-2015 Sex Education Advisory Board, co-chaired by Amy Buchanan and Nicole Jenkins, with teachers Lisa Danhoff, Karen Wakely and Kevin Wilson, Rev. David Huseltine of Big Beaver United Methodist Church, and nurse Lois Winer of the Oakland Health Department (7-0). Resolution 14-107 awarded the food services wireless temperature monitoring system equipment and installation bid to SMART Temp, LLC for $38,504.00 as an expenditure of the 2014-2015 Food Services Fund, carrying 6-1 with Schmidt opposed. Resolution 14-108 appointed Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky temporary Treasurer of the Board until an Assistant Superintendent of Business Services is appointed (7-0). Resolution 14-109 awarded masonry work for the Athens High School addition and remodeling project to Efficient Design, Inc. for $73,482.00 from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund (7-0). Resolution 14-110 adopted the 2014/2015 board committee assignments (7-0). The meeting adjourned at 9:58 p.m.; Karl Schmidt signed as Secretary. Reports covered the 2013-2014 teacher and administrator evaluation summary (Jasen Witt), professional development (Anne Mull), and Advanced Placement results (Mark Dziatczak), in which TSD students exceeded both the state and national average AP pass rate by more than 20%. A new Superintendent's Student Advisory Board drew 55 applications and seated 24 students — 6 seniors, 7 juniors, 7 sophomores and 4 freshmen — with a first meeting on October 22. Wattles and Bemis were congratulated for National Blue Ribbon awards, and Doug Madden of Barton Malow flagged a possible delay to the Troy High auditorium because seats might not arrive on time.

The Board formally names the new preschool building the Troy School District Preschool, awards $5,313,940.00 of Bid Pack 23 work across five buildings, and finally settles the Early Childhood Center casework at $662,570.00 after two failed bid rounds. **Meeting**
Regular meeting, December 18, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment recognizes the group developing "a world-class foundation for a comprehensive pre-kindergarten education experience for our youngest learners" — Kris Griffor and Erin Keyser share a video of the Early Childhood Center.

The second item is **Todd Miletti's 12 years of service**, this being his final meeting. The write-up notes that aside from being an elected position, serving on the Board is also a volunteer position requiring a great deal of time, effort and commitment, and that Miletti "has done a remarkable service to past and future generations of Troy students."

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the November 13 special meeting, closed session and workshop, the November 20 meeting, and the October 2018 Treasurer's Report.

**The millage, after the vote**
The November 13 special meeting existed to true up the tax levy. The 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted June 19, 2018 had authorized **17.6840 mills** on non-homestead property. At the November 6, 2018 election the district's electors approved a replacement non-homestead operating millage of **21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy**, effective for the 2018 calendar year. Resolution 18-085 amends the appropriations resolution to authorize a levy of **18 mills**, and authorizes the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2018 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) with **9.158 of the 18 mills levied on the December 1, 2018 levy date**, for submission to the Oakland County Clerk. It carried 5-0 with Miletti and Philippart absent.

**Also from November**
The November 13 workshop covered the Troy High sign, the Consumers and DTE easements at Boulan Park, the Boyd Street property sale and sidewalk, and board professional learning on **school start times**; Judge Kirsten Hartig and Dr. Nicole Wilson were in the audience.

The November 20 minutes record 18-087 through 18-092, all 6-0 with Miletti absent: the consent agenda, Cornelissen's appointment, the Signarama sign award at $21,739.30, the Boyd Street sale to Delmar Homes at $10,000.00, and — added to the agenda at Mr. Gottlieb's request — **resolution 18-091 directing Dr. Machesky and Human Resources to develop a succession plan** to maintain continuity and consistency of the district into the future and share it with the Board. The Troy College & Career High School Mission Moment described a Trunk or Treat event, a book drive that collected and delivered **more than 2,000 books** for students in Pontiac Schools, and a partnership with Oakmont Senior Living where students help with iPads, call bingo and perform skits for residents who often have no family nearby.

**Treasurer's Report — October 2018**
Total check disbursements are $9,173,492.59, the General Fund group $4,711,884.58 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,479,154.93. With $2,045,278.46 of wire transfers, $267,995.65 of P-Card purchases and $29,426.83 of ACH debits, less an unusually large $369,076.31 of prior period void disbursements, total disbursements in period are $11,147,117.22.

**Business 8.A — the casework, third time**
The Early Childhood Center casework and millwork had failed to draw acceptable bids in March and again in September. On this third attempt RFP 9864 produced 5 bidders in each category — but the bids came in over the construction budget. Rob Carson's November 29 memo records that collaborative efforts between the bond construction team and the low bidders identified **options which created cost savings while maintaining intent and function of the original design**. The award is Mica-Tec interior architectural millwork at $442,920.00 — reduced from a $515,000.00 base bid by three options totalling deductions of $24,180.00, $41,314.00 and $6,586.00 — and Architect Systems Group prefabricated casework at $219,650.00, for **$662,570.00** from the Early Childhood Center Fund. Mica-Tec's base bid was already well below the next bidders at $574,121.00, $576,400.00, $615,810.00 and $714,000.00.

**Business 8.B — Bid Pack 23**
The largest single award of the year after the preschool itself. The scope covers mechanical/electrical upgrades and window/door replacements at Schroeder, Troy Union and Smith; the Smith kitchen renovation; kitchen equipment for Barnard, Bemis and Hamilton; renovation of the Troy High auto and wood shop classrooms; conversion of the closed swimming pool area into classrooms at International Academy East; and bathroom renovation plus a new office suite for the TCT program at the International Academy building.

Thirteen contracts total **$5,313,940.00**, split by funding source: **$2,979,173.00 from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, $1,725,961.00 from the Sinking Fund, $608,806.00 from the Food Service Fund** (the Smith kitchen), plus **$504,744.50 of contingency** paid from the appropriate fund as determined by the Business Office.

**Other — naming the building**
The naming resolution recites the district's mission, its strategic plan built on four characteristics of world class, and that one of the four is to **Invest in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten Students through increasing access to a high quality, literacy-rich preschool experience**. The building is scheduled to open in the fall of 2019; Board Policy 6000.09 leaves the selection of future school names to the Board's discretion. Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, December 18, 2018, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: Early Childhood Center, B. Board Member 12 Years of Service on Board – Todd Miletti; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the November 13, 2018 Special Board of Education Meeting, B. Minutes of the November 13, 2018 Closed Session Meeting, C. Minutes of the November 13, 2018 Board of Education Workshop, D. Minutes of the November 20, 2018 Board of Education Meeting, E. Treasurer's Report – October 2018; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Bid Pack #3 – ECC, B. Consideration: Bid Pack #23 – Schroeder, Troy Union, Smith, IAE & THS, C. Consideration: Athens and Troy High Wireless Audio Systems; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. Consideration: Troy Preschool Naming, B. Consideration: 2019 MASB Board of Directors Nomination; 11. Adjournment. (The consent agenda page lists item D as the November 13 meeting minutes; the minutes reproduced are the November 20 regular meeting, as the index states.) Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: the Early Childhood Center.** The Mission Moment takes the opportunity to recognize the group of individuals who have been dedicating their time and energy into developing a world-class foundation for a comprehensive pre-kindergarten education experience for the district's youngest learners. Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction, and Erin Keyser, Director of Early Childhood Programs — appointed to that role in May — share a brief video with the Board.

**Recognition 2.B: Todd Miletti, 12 years of service.** The Board recognizes one of its own members, Todd Miletti, who is retiring from the Troy Board of Education, this being his final meeting. The write-up notes that he is leaving after selflessly giving 12 years of service to the district's students, staff and families; that aside from being an elected position, serving on the Board of Education is also a volunteer position requiring a great deal of time, effort and commitment; that Mr. Miletti has been an exemplary trustee and has done a remarkable service to past and future generations of Troy students; and that while this is not goodbye and he will no doubt remain active in the greater Troy community, the Board will miss him. A certificate is presented. Miletti had been absent from several of the fall meetings, including the November 13 special meeting and the November 20 regular meeting recorded in this same packet.

**Consent minutes: the November 13, 2018 special board meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 5:33 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond and Hauff were present; Mr. Miletti and Dr. Philippart were absent. Administrators in attendance were Superintendent Machesky, Harris, Carrier and West, with one member of the audience.

The single business item was resolution 18-085, the L-4029 amendment. Its recitals set out the sequence: the Board, pursuant to a 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted on June 19, 2018, approved the district's operating, debt and sinking fund millage rates for the 2018-19 school year, which included the authority to levy 17.6840 mills for general operating purposes on non-homestead property; at the November 6, 2018 election the district's electors approved a replacement non-homestead operating millage in the amount of 21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy, to be effective for the 2018 calendar year; and the Board desires to amend the approval in the 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution to approve and authorize the district to levy 18 mills for general operating purposes on non-homestead property for the 2018-19 school year.

The resolution approves that amendment and further authorizes the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2018 Tax Rate Request, Form L-4029, with a non-homestead operating millage request for the levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes, and further with 9.158 mills of the 18 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2018 levy date, and the submission of the amended 2018 Tax Rate Request to the Oakland County Clerk. The vote was YES 5 — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Schmidt — NO 0, ABSENT 2, Miletti and Philippart.

This is the completion of the work begun at the July 17 meeting, where the Board certified the ballot language for a replacement of the 18 mills approved by voters in 2015 and eroded by the Headlee Amendment. The 21-mill authorization with an 18-mill cap is the standard structure: the excess exists solely as headroom so that future Headlee rollbacks do not again cut the levy below the 18 mills the state's school finance formula assumes the district will collect. The levy actually restored — 18 mills against the 17.6840 the June appropriations resolution had authorized — is a difference of a fraction of a mill, which is what a rollback of that magnitude costs and what the election was called to fix.

Resolution 18-086 took the Board into closed session on an attorney-client privilege under Section 8(c) of the Michigan Open Meetings Act, on a roll call of Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Schmidt voting yes with Miletti and Philippart absent. The Board moved to closed session at 5:37 p.m. and reconvened at 5:39 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the November 13, 2018 workshop.** President Schmidt called the workshop to order at 6:36 p.m. with Mr. Miletti and Dr. Philippart absent. Present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Carrier and West; Judge Kirsten Hartig and Dr. Nicole Wilson were also in the audience. The agenda: public communication; a business services update covering the Troy High School sign, the Consumers and DTE easements at Boulan Park, and the Boyd Street property sale and sidewalk; and board professional learning on school start times. It adjourned at 8:48 p.m. Two items foreshadow later work — the DTE easement is not among the resolutions the Board acted on in November, and school start times would remain a live topic.

**Consent minutes: the November 20, 2018 regular meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:03 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart were present; Mr. Miletti was absent. Three high school student representatives attended, along with Superintendent Machesky, administrators Griffor, Mueller, Harris, Jansen, MacDonald-Linford and West, and approximately 40 additional members of the audience. Christian Mueller appears among the administrators as the Smith principal appointed in May, and Deb MacDonald-Linford as the Troy College & Career presenter.

The Board recognized the Troy High counseling team for their investment in the Class of 2022. Jesse Allgeier, Anne Young and Tommy Keegan described the new program: the counselors have been meeting with every 9th grade student during the school day to help the newest Colts feel welcome and at home at Troy High School, with students joining in group discussions and activities. The counselors want students to know that when they leave for the day, they see them as a caring team, eager to help them for any reason at any time during their journey through high school. A brief video highlighted some of their interactions.

The second Mission Moment brought teachers and students from Troy College and Career High School to share new initiatives connecting with their community. Their video highlighted a Trunk or Treat event held in the community and a book drive in which they collected and delivered more than 2,000 books for students in Pontiac Schools. They are also partnering with the Oakmont Senior Living Community, where students visit and help with iPads and technology devices, call bingo and perform skits; many of the residents do not have family and enjoy spending time with the TCCHS students.

Under additions and deletions, Mr. Gottlieb requested that a resolution for Succession Planning be added to the evening's agenda under "Other." Resolution 18-087 approved the consent agenda 6-0. Resolution 18-088 issued the two-year probationary administrative contract to Ms. Kimberly Cornelissen as Assistant Principal, Smith Middle School, effective December 3, 2018, 6-0. Resolution 18-089 awarded the Troy High School sign refurbishment to Signarama of Troy in the amount of $21,739.30 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, 6-0. Resolution 18-090 authorized the sale of the easterly 6.00 feet of Lot 27, "Beaver Run Subdivision," to Delmar Homes for $10,000.00.

Resolution 18-091, the item Mr. Gottlieb had added, resolved that Dr. Machesky along with Human Resources develop a succession plan to maintain continuity and consistency of the district into the future and share that plan with the Board of Education. It carried 6-0, and the minutes record some discussion among Board members and Dr. Machesky regarding the current process in place and plans for developing a more formal process in the near future. Coming a month before a twelve-year trustee's departure and six months after the Board extended the superintendent's contract to 2021 and every senior administrator's to 2020, the item reads as the Board asking to see on paper what it had just been voting on piecemeal.

Student representatives reported: Mackenzie Malinowski of Troy College & Career High School, and Grant Vivian of Athens filling in for Jenna Doyle, on a StuCo and Project Lead coat drive with the Oakland County Sheriff's department and the Athens Marching Band's appearance in the Thanksgiving Day Parade. In Board comments, Dr. Philippart said the Mission Moment was very inspiring and gave a shout out to the district's weekly videos; Mrs. Hammond said how thankful she is for the community; Mrs. Fleming announced the TFEE Book Fair on December 11 from 4 to 8 p.m. at the Barnes & Noble at John R and 14 Mile; Mr. Hauff, a member of Troy Beaumont Volunteer Services, shared a poem on gratitude through the holidays; Mr. Gottlieb described the TCCHS Thanksgiving meal and the students' enthusiasm for their school; and Dr. Machesky reported on the AdvancED Engagement Review coming the first week of December, when reviewers would visit buildings and interview stakeholders "to be sure we are doing what we say we are doing," and pointed to the district Fine Arts Calendar for holiday events. Resolution 18-092 took the Board into closed session on attorney-client privilege at 8:52 p.m.; it reconvened at 8:55 and adjourned at 9:40 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report, October 2018.** By fund: General Fund (101) $4,479,154.93; Grant Fund (120) $515.95; Special Education Fund (122) $232,213.70; Durant Funds (140) nil; Food Service Fund (520) $18,253.29; Troy Career Center (529) $17,243.43; Community Education Fund (530) $61,382.63. Total General Fund check disbursements are $4,711,884.58 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS $9,173,492.59. Adding ACH debits of $29,426.83, outgoing wire transfers of $2,045,278.46 and P-Card purchases of $267,995.65, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $369,076.31, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,147,117.22. The void figure is far larger than in any other month of the year — the district's other monthly void lines run from nothing to about $35,000 — indicating a substantial reversal of previously issued checks in the period. The middle sections of the packet are the October check register run by fund.

**Business 8.A: Early Childhood Center Bid Pack 3.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the casework and millwork for the Early Childhood Center project, reviewed by Rob Carson and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Carson's November 29, 2018 memorandum on RFP 9864, Bid Pack 3, records that this was a rebid due to lack of response from an earlier RFP, and that this time the RFP resulted in 5 bidders for each category.

The bids received exceeded the construction budget for these categories. Collaborative efforts from the bond construction team and the low bidders resulted in identifying options which created cost savings while maintaining the intent and function of the original design; the attached bid results summary identifies those options, cost savings and bid pricing. Carson recommends, on low bid for each category: 064023 interior architectural millwork, Mica-Tec, $442,920.00; and 123204 prefabricated casework, Architect Systems Group, $219,650.00 — total recommended awards $662,570.00, with a separate purchase order for each bid category and funding from the ECC Fund. The resolution awards the casework and millwork in the amount of $662,570.00 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund.

The bid tabulation shows how the reduction was achieved. Mica-Tec's base bid was $515,000.00, against MOD Interiors at $574,121.00, Trend Millwork at $576,400.00, Wally Kosorski & Co at $615,810.00 and Division 6 at $714,000.00. Three options are applied to Mica-Tec's bid as deductions of $24,180.00, $41,314.00 and $6,586.00, bringing it to $442,920.00. The options are described in the tabulation headers as removing millwork at the classroom island, changing the reception desk work surface to plastic laminate in lieu of Corian, and installing carpet at the circle windows, with a note that Option 1 adds metal stud and drywall to replace millwork at $12,345.00 and Option 2 adds carpet at $8,340. In prefabricated casework, ASG's $219,650.00 base bid was well below Farnell Contracting at $314,000.00, Strata Design at $323,565.00, Detroit Technical Equipment at $326,000.00 and Trend Millwork at $478,000.00.

This is the third attempt at these categories. Casework was one of three categories held back from the March 2018 award of bid 9855 for lack of acceptable bids; it was held back again from the September Bid Pack 2 award when the bids were not opened due to low bidder turnout; and it clears here only after the design was value-engineered to fit the budget.

**Business 8.B: Bid Pack #23 — Schroeder, Troy Union, Smith, IAE and Troy High.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids covering mechanical and electrical upgrades and window and door replacements at Schroeder and Troy Union Elementary Schools and Smith Middle School; renovation of the kitchen at Smith Middle School; kitchen equipment for Barnard, Bemis and Hamilton Elementary Schools; renovation work to the Troy High auto and wood shop classrooms; conversion of the closed swimming pool area into classrooms at International Academy East; and bathroom renovation and construction of a new office suite for the TCT Program at the International Academy building. Bid responses were reviewed by the TSD Operations Department, TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow.

Christa Amalio of Barton Malow reports that one apparent low bidder was passed over for missing scope and the second low bidder is included in the recommendations; post-bid interviews are complete; and bid pricing received including selected alternates is within the bond budgets assigned for each building. The recommended contracts are: 040000 masonry, BNE Masonry (Alternate 2), $349,100.00; 050000 steel, Men of Steel, $48,000.00; 060000 general trades, Advanced Building Group (Alternates 1, 2, 3), $394,319.00; 070000 roofing, JD Candler, $20,310.00; 080000 exterior doors and windows, Hewett Company, $434,249.00; 096000 flooring, Continental Contracting, $209,500.00; 099000 painting, Seven Brothers Painting, $49,584.00; 114000 food service equipment, Great Lakes Hotel Supply, $266,495.00; 230000 mechanical, CSM Mechanical for IAE and Smith, $881,133.00; 230000 mechanical, Contrast Mechanical for Troy Union and Schroeder, $990,000.00; 230900 temperature controls, MCMI, $598,050.00; 260000 electrical, Great Lakes Power & Lighting (Alternates 1 and 4), $767,000.00; and 320000 sitework and concrete, Brencal Contracting, $306,200.00 — total awards $5,313,940.00.

The bond award value is $2,979,173.00, the sinking fund award value is $1,725,961.00, and the Smith kitchen award value is $608,806.00. The resolution accordingly approves $2,979,173.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, $1,725,961.00 as an expenditure of the Sinking Fund, $608,806.00 as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund, and $504,744.50 as contingency for the project to be paid from the appropriate fund as determined by the Business Office.

The tabulation breaks the awards down by building. International Academy East takes $1,637,249.00 — the largest single share, reflecting the pool-area conversion — with Brencal's entire $306,200.00 of sitework, BNE's $272,000.00 of masonry, Advanced Building Group's $249,205.00 of general trades, Contrast Mechanical's $470,000.00 and Continental's $154,500.00 of flooring all falling there. Smith takes $1,172,149.00 plus the separately funded $608,806.00 kitchen, including Hewett's $245,628.00 of doors and windows, Great Lakes Power's $326,000.00 of electrical, MCMI's $197,700.00 of controls and CSM's $248,759.00 of mechanical. Troy Union takes $949,852.00, Schroeder $757,171.00, Troy High $88,712.00 for the auto and wood shop work, and the three elementary kitchens $32,878.00 at Bemis, $31,367.00 at Barnard and $35,756.00 at Hamilton. The four alternates carried in the pricing are Troy Union ceilings, Smith overhead doors, and Smith roller shades.

The tabulation also carries the estimates the awards are measured against: $1,495,179.00 for IAE, $1,037,140.00 for Schroeder, $2,997,755.00 for Smith, $682,000.00 for the Smith kitchen, $270,750.00 for Troy High and $1,177,950.00 for Troy Union, with bond and sinking fund budget lines of $1,223,353.00, $782,728.00 and $1,284,439.00, and differences from original of $62,635.00 and $54,500.00. Smith and Troy High came in well under estimate; IAE came in above its estimate but within its assigned budget.

This single bid pack delivers most of the 2019 program set out in the August bond and sinking fund update: BP #23's Schroeder, Troy Union and Smith work, the Smith kitchen renovation from food service funds, the Troy High auto and woodshop renovations, and the IAE pool area conversion. The $2,000,000 IAE line that dominated the four-year BSSF projection appears here as $1,637,249.00 of awarded work.

**Business 8.C: wireless audio systems and installation.** Invitations were sent to eight potential bidders to provide closed sealed pricing for the required audio auditorium equipment at Athens and Troy High Schools, with three responses received. Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, reviewed the proposals with Gino Minchella, Theatre Manager, and recommends the low bidder to specification: Advanced Lighting & Sound, Inc. at $91,106.00, funded from the Facility Rental Fund. The resolution awards the wireless audio auditorium equipment for Athens and Troy High to Advanced Lighting & Sound, Inc. in the amount of $91,106.00 as an expenditure of the Facility Rental Fund — one of the few awards in the year drawn on that fund, which is fed by outside groups renting district facilities.

**Other 10.A: naming the Early Childhood Center.** In December 2017 the Board passed a resolution to proceed with the construction of an early childhood center facility, and while construction is ongoing it is appropriate to formally name the facility. The resolution recites that the district's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; that the Board has adopted the district's strategic plan focusing its work on four characteristics of world class; that one of the four characteristics is to Invest in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten Students through increasing access to a high quality, literacy-rich preschool experience; that to increase access for a rich preschool experience the Board approved the construction of a new Early Childhood Learning Center in December of 2017; and that the building is scheduled to open in the fall of 2019 and Board Policy 6000.09 states the selection of future school names will be left to the discretion of the Board. It resolves that the Board hereby names the new building the Troy School District Preschool.

The choice is notable for what it declines to do. Board Policy 6000.09 gives the Board complete discretion, and the district had spent the year selling land, borrowing $11 million without a public vote and awarding contracts on a building that had gone from resolution to nearly finished in twelve months; the name it settles on carries no person's name and no donor's, only the district's and the function's.

**Other 10.B: 2019 MASB Board of Directors nomination.** Seven seats on the MASB Board of Directors are up for election. The MASB Board of Directors is comprised of 19 members: 16 directors elected from the eight regions, two from each, and one director each from Groups V, VI and VII; directors are elected by active member school boards, with several seats up each year. As approved by the 2018 Delegate Assembly, beginning in 2019 and in each subsequent year the MASB President will nominate a member to serve as an at-large director subject to Board approval, and beginning in 2021 the Board of Directors will consist of 22 members including three at-large directors. Article VIII, Section 7 of the MASB Bylaws provides that a board's nomination of candidates must be forwarded to the MASB Executive Director by Wednesday, January 9, 2019. The resolution nominates Steve Gottlieb, who has agreed to be a candidate and meets the qualifications as approved by the 2018 Delegate Assembly, to run for a seat on the 2019 MASB Board of Directors, certified by Gary N. Hauff as adopted at the meeting of Tuesday, December 18, 2018.

Gottlieb's candidacy carries forward into the following February's packet, where the Troy Board casts its ballot in a Region 8 race in which he is one of seven candidates.

Read as a whole, the December 2018 packet closes a year that reshaped the district's physical plant and its balance sheet. The preschool it authorized in December 2017 has a name, a director, a completed construction award and — after three tries — its casework. Bid Pack 23 commits another $5,313,940.00 across five buildings. The operating millage the Headlee Amendment had eroded is restored at 18 mills by the voters and by an amended L-4029. And a twelve-year trustee leaves, one meeting after asking the superintendent to put a succession plan in writing.

PERSONNEL (6.A.). Recommendation to appoint Mr. Joseph Duda as Principal, Larson Middle School. CURRICULUM (7.A.). Report on the Social Studies Grades 6-12 Textbook Adoption, presented by Anne Mull, Director of Instruction and Assessment. Work began August 31, 2011 with survey needs assessment and data results, an overview of Common Core literacy standards, and selection of social studies teachers. Timeline: November 3, 2011 presentations by four vendors; November 3 - February 22, 2012 continued evaluation; February 23, 2012 presentations by three vendors; teachers then selected materials. Current and proposed course sequences run from grade 6 geography through grade 12 World History and Geography 2, with grade 7 Ancient Civilizations, grade 8 Integrated U.S. History through Reconstruction, grade 9 Government/World History and Geo. 1, grade 10 American History, and grade 11 Economics and Government or Economics and World His. & Geo 1. Evaluation criteria included reading level, alignment to standards, differentiation, NIMAS compliance for special education, test bank quality, SmartBoard and internet resources, and practice activities in digital and hard copy. Instructional frameworks cited include Understanding by Design (Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe), Nonlinguistic Representation (Robert Marzano), Multiple Intelligences (Howard Gardner), Cooperative Interaction (Elizabeth Cohen), and Spiral Curriculum (Jerome Bruner). Featured materials include chapter-level videos, podcasts for essential questions, downloadable eReader files, Essential Question Journals, Economics and You, How the Economy Works, Visual Glossary, Action Graphs, Quick Study Guides, a Personal Finance handbook, and American Government on the Go audio and video.

CURRICULUM (7.B.). Report on English Language Arts Material Adoption, Grades K-5, also presented by Anne Mull. Prior purchases were Houghton Mifflin Harcourt (HMH) Literature for grades 9-12 in July 2010 and grades 6-8 in July 2011; the recommendation is purchase of HMH materials for grades K-5 in July 2012. New materials will supplement, not supplant, existing resources and align to all strands of the English Common Core Standards - reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing, language (grammar), and technology. Rollout begins in spring with professional development in word study; author and researcher Shane Templeton will spend a half-day with all elementary teachers in May, and teachers receive the HMH Word Study Teacher Guide referencing HMH Journeys mentor text. In fall of 2012, with approval, each teacher receives a set of 15 mentor texts and online access. On August 29, 2012 teachers receive professional development in using the materials in the workshop model; in September of 2012 each elementary teacher receives training in the workshop model and differentiation including for English language learners; at least two additional half-days are scheduled during the 2012-2013 school year. Components listed include the Comprehensive Language and Literacy Guide: A Readers Workshop Approach, Word Study Guide, Decodable Readers, Big Books, Online Leveled Readers, Student eBook, Language Support Cards for English Language Learners, Interactive Smart Board Lessons, Focus Wall Posters, online Comprehensive Screening/Diagnostic Assessment for grades 2-5, Vocabulary Readers, Write-In Readers for Intervention, WriteSmart CD-ROM, ExamView Assessment on CD-ROM, Teacher One-Stop Planner CD-ROM, and Interactive Simulations by Destination Reading (2013-2014). Guided reading support is based on Irene Fountas principles. A Troy Balanced Literacy diagram lays out Reader's Workshop, Word Study, and Writer's Workshop, with Big Books for grades K-1, Decodable Readers for grades K-2, and Trade Novels for grades 3-6.

OTHER (10.A.). Consideration of a resolution to schedule a Special Board of Education Meeting on Tuesday, May 15, 2012, at the Administrative Building prior to the Board Workshop, for Business items and adoption of the Oakland Schools Biennial Election resolution.

OTHER (10.B.). First reading of revisions to Board Policies B-1302 Agendas for Regular Meetings, G-1401 Political Activities, K-1303 Commercial Advertising, K-1401 Solicitations on School Property, and new Board Policies C-1501 E-mail Retention and J-2012 Anti-Bullying, all reviewed by the Board's attorney for compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act, and the Revised School Code; each Board member reads a policy round-robin. B-1302 (series B-1300) provides that the agenda is prepared by the superintendent and Board president, delivered to members five calendar days preceding the meeting, posted at the Administrative Center four calendar days preceding the meeting with the agenda and board packet made available on the district website the day of but prior to the meeting, delivered at least twenty-four hours before special meetings, and that adding or deleting an item requires a motion seconded and approved by a vote of at least four members; revised January 16, 1979, March 17, 1998, and June 19, 2007. G-1401 Political Activities (series G-1400) recognizes employees' right to campaign and hold office while barring campaigning during school hours, use of district supplies or equipment, involvement of students, and display of political material on district property except on personal vehicles parked there; it requires complete neutrality by all school personnel including contracted personnel and restricts use of District resources, technology including District e-mail, and student/parent contact information absent written consent of the superintendent or designee; adopted January 16, 1979, April 21, 1998. K-1303 Political and/or Commercial Advertising by District Employees (series K-1300) carries parallel prohibitions plus a commercial-purpose restriction; adopted May 3, 1976, revised January 16, 1979, April 21, 1998, and April 20, 2010. K-1401 Solicitations (series K-1400) prohibits solicitations on school property, including product, article, service or political solicitations, unless approved by the superintendent or designee or involving an isolated, private, person-to-person legal transaction; adopted April 19, 1976, revised January 16, 1979, April 21, 1998, and March 23, 2012. New policy C-1501 E-mail Retention (series C-1500) applies to all users except students, defining User to include employees, officers, temporary employees, interns, vendors, consultants, contractors, authorized agents and volunteers; it requires mailbox management under Technology Resource Center (TRC) size limits, automatic deletion by TRC of e-mail and note items more than one year in age unless retained pursuant to law, court order, direction of the Superintendent, the Board's records policy K-1002, or the Records Retention and Disposal Schedule of Michigan Public Schools (Educational Bulletin #522); backups of the District e-mail system are kept only two business days; litigation holds suspend destruction until TRC is directed otherwise by the Superintendent's Office; electronic calendars and task items are available for two years; and beginning July 1, 2012 the District e-mail system will use an archive system retaining user messages for one year, with automatic destruction of archived messages more than one year old except when quarantined for litigation. New policy J-2012 Anti-Bullying (series J-2000) prohibits bullying at school, defines bullying as any written, verbal, or physical act or electronic communication intended or reasonably known to be likely to harm students by substantially interfering with educational opportunities, placing a student in reasonable fear of physical harm or causing substantial emotional distress, having a substantial detrimental effect on physical or mental health, or causing substantial disruption; prohibits retaliation and false accusation; requires prompt reporting to the principal or designee, prompt and thorough investigation by the building principal or designee, notification to the parent/guardian of both victim and perpetrator, and at least annual reporting of verified incidents and consequences to the Board of Education; designates the superintendent as Responsible School Official; requires annual circulation, conspicuous posting, annual discussion with students, and inclusion in handbooks; and defines "at school" and adopts the definitions of "Telecommunications Access Device" and "Telecommunications Service Provider" from Section 219a of the Michigan Penal Code, 1931 PA 328, MCL 750.219a.

OTHER (10.C.). Second reading and consideration of revisions to Board Policy B-1209 Board Member Abstention from Voting and K-1301 Distribution of Materials to Students, first read at the April 17, 2012 meeting. B-1209 (series B-1200) as revised provides that a member shall abstain from voting affirmatively or negatively if a direct or indirect financial conflict of interest exists, if there is an appearance of a direct or indirect conflict of interest, or if abstention is explicitly required by the Board's by-laws or applicable law, with the nature of the conflict recorded in the minutes and abstention for any other reason not permitted; adopted April 8, 1975, revised June 7, 1977 and January 16, 1979. K-1301 requires individuals or organizations not representing students, teachers, administrators, or school-sponsored organizations to obtain prior approval of the superintendent or designee before distributing handwritten, duplicated or printed materials or lapel pins, stickers, tags or similar items to students or to parents through students, while preserving advertising in student publications published by student organizations; adopted April 19, 1976, revised January 16, 1979 and April 21, 1998.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of June 6, 2017 at Athens High School. The night is built around student recognition — 69 lettered items covering the winter All-State athletes, the 2016-2017 senior scholar athletes and a Youth Recognition deck spanning every academic and arts competition the district entered. The business is thin by comparison: a consent agenda carrying four sets of minutes and the second reading of five board policies, a resolution setting the 2017-2018 budget public hearing for June 20, 2017, and a bond update reporting Series 1 construction 98% complete against a $125.7 M program.

**Meeting**

Agenda: Pledge of Allegiance; Recognition (items A through OOO); Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (agenda items); General – Consent Agenda; Personnel; Curriculum; Business; Public Communication (non-agenda items); Other; Adjournment.

**Recognition**
Mike Jolly reads the two athletics items. 2.A names the All-State Athletes for Winter 2017 — twenty-three students, overwhelmingly Troy High synchronized swimmers, plus bowling, gymnastics and boys swim. 2.B lists the Senior Scholar Athletes for 2016-2017 who carried a 3.5 grade point average, an extended roster across both high schools. Minutes of the May 2 workshop, the May 16 meeting, and the May 23 special and closed sessions, plus second reading and adoption of five board policies: 2000.04 School District Clubs & Other Activities, 4000.01 Personnel – Labor Negotiation Team, 5000.03 Purchasing – Competitive Bidding & Micro-Purchases, 6000.02 Safety & Security – Firearms & Other Weapons, and 8000.09 General Policies – Web Accessibility. **What the attached minutes record**

Public comment that night ran heavily against two land questions — the preservation of Parcel 11 and Section 1 property, and the proposed Early Childhood Center on Parcel 16 — with residents from Abington, Terova, Paragon Drive, Bracken Drive and Highbury Drive speaking, including a TSD student. Item 8.A sets a public hearing on the proposed 2017-2018 budget for June 20, 2017 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building, with the proposed budget available for inspection at the Administration Building from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., June 14 through June 20, and notice published at least six days ahead carrying, in 11-point bold faced type, the statement that the property tax millage rate proposed to be levied will be a subject of the hearing.

**Item 10.A - First Reading: Board Policy G-1009, Teacher and Administrator Evaluation**

Members of the Board Policy Committee met to review Board Policy G-1009, Teacher and Administrator Evaluation; the new policy was reviewed by the Board of Education's attorney to confirm compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act, and the Revised School Code. The recommended action is that one Board member conduct the first reading. The policy text, filed under GENERAL SECTION G-1000 as "G-1009 Performance Evaluation Systems for Teachers and Administrators," states that the Troy School District is responsible for the employment and supervision of all personnel and shall comply with Section 1249 of the Revised School Code, which mandates certain components within the District's performance evaluation systems. The District shall adopt and implement for all teachers and school administrators a rigorous, transparent, and fair performance evaluation system; evaluate job performance and provide timely and constructive feedback; and establish clear approaches to measuring student growth and provide relevant data on student growth. The Board and Superintendent, or designees, will examine the recommendation of the Michigan Council on Educator Effectiveness and may revise the policy accordingly. Decisions regarding the development, content, standards, procedures, adoption and implementation of performance evaluation systems, and the impact of such decisions on the individual employee or the applicable bargaining unit, shall not be the subject of any terms and conditions within a collective bargaining agreement between the District and a collective bargaining representative of such teachers. With the exception of the Superintendent's performance evaluation, the Board delegates to the Superintendent or designee(s) responsibility for adopting and implementing that system in compliance with Section 1249, including developing administrative guidelines as needed. References cited: MCL 380.1249, MCL 38.83a; MCL 38.93, as amended by Public Acts 100, 101 and 102, effective July 19, 2011. Adopted: [Date TBD].

**Item 10.B - First Reading: Board Policy G-1010, Performance-Based Compensation**

Members of the Board Policy Committee met to review Board Policy G-1010, Performance-Based Compensation, a new policy also reviewed by the Board's attorney for compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act, and the Revised School Code, with one Board member to conduct the first reading. The policy text, filed under GENERAL SECTION G-1000 as "G-1010 Performance-Based Compensation for Teachers and Administrators," provides that the District shall implement and maintain a method of compensation for its teachers and school administrators that includes job performance and job accomplishments as a significant factor in determining compensation and additional compensation. The assessment of job performance shall incorporate a rigorous, transparent, and fair evaluation system that evaluates a teacher's or school administrator's performance at least in part based upon data on student growth as measured by assessments and other objective criteria. Decisions about the development, content, standards, procedures, adoption and implementation of the method of compensation required under section 1250 of the Michigan Revised School Code, about how an employee performance evaluation system is used to determine performance-based compensation under section 1250, and concerning the performance-based compensation of an individual employee or the impact of those decisions on an individual employee or the bargaining unit, are within the sole authority of the public school employer and shall not be the subject of any terms and conditions within a collective bargaining agreement. With the exception of performance-based compensation for the Superintendent, the Board delegates to the Superintendent or designee(s) responsibility for implementing and maintaining such a method of compensation in accordance with Section 1250. References cited: MCL 380.1250, effective July 19, 2011; MCL 423.215. Adopted: [Date TBD].

**Item 11.A - Closed Session: Negotiations and Superintendent Evaluation**

The Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss negotiations and superintendent evaluation; following passage, the Board will go into closed session, and no additional business will take place after that time other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The suggested resolution provides that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss negotiations and superintendent evaluation. A roll call vote is required, with the roster printed as Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood, Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Miletti.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, August 21, 2018, 7:00 PM, Administration Building, 4400 Livernois.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the July 17, 2018 meeting, the June 2018 Treasurer's Report, and the IA-East Schools of Choice resolution.

**What the July 17 minutes record**
A short meeting (7:05 to 8:00 p.m.) that did a great deal of contractual work, all 7-0 unless noted. Two-year probationary administrative contracts to Christine Foren as Supervisor, Special Education and Jessica Carrier as Director, Special Education, both effective July 1, 2018. **The Superintendent's contract extended July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2021.** The four assistant and deputy superintendents — Mark Dziatczak, Rick West, Kris Griffor and Jordan Harris — extended through June 30, 2020. Twenty-nine other administrators' contracts extended through June 30, 2020; **Mr. Gottlieb excused himself from voting on this item for reasons of a personal nature** — the list includes Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity & Accountability — so it carried 6-0 with one abstention.

Troy High also joined Athens, Avondale and Berkley in a cooperative boys' and girls' skiing team for 2018-19 and 2019-20. And the Board certified ballot language for a **replacement operating millage** — restoring and replacing the authority to levy 18 mills on non-homestead property, approved by voters in 2015 and since rolled back by the Headlee Amendment, with headroom against future rollbacks — for the November 6, 2018 general school election, the wording due to the Oakland County Clerk no later than August 14, 2018.

**Treasurer's Report — June 2018**
June is the fiscal year's closing month and the numbers show it. Total check disbursements are **$17,527,051.55**, of which the General Fund group is $12,632,198.69 and the General Fund (101) itself $11,582,952.38. Adding $2,373,385.53 of wire transfers, $209,641.78 of P-Card purchases and $31,230.57 of ACH debits, less $35,280.06 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are **$20,106,029.37**. Two lines show the capital program running at full speed: Building & Site Funds $3,271,337.13 and the Early Childhood Center Fund $724,608.21.

**Curriculum — 85 seats at IA East**
The Board adopts a Section 105c resolution accepting applications for **85 non-resident 9th grade students** who reside outside Oakland County, where that ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries, for the purpose of attending the International Academy East program located in the Troy School District. Unlike the elementary and middle school Schools of Choice resolutions adopted each February, this one is 105c only — IA East draws from beyond the county by design.

**Personnel — the August hiring class**
Probationary contracts for roughly sixty teachers for 2018-2019, heavily weighted toward the elementary grades and to special services. Hamilton alone takes six (Takouhy Kinzer and David Anderson in 3rd grade, Shalyn Fortuna in 1st, Ewa Dabrowski in 2nd, Christina Connolly in the resource room, Gabriella Mancini in the kindergarten resource room, plus Rebecca McNally in 3rd); Wattles takes five; Bemis four. The list includes six speech and language pathologists, three school social workers, a school psychologist, four resource room teachers and several early childhood program teachers at the Niles Center.

**Business — the custodial contract**
The Board authorizes administration to finalize an addendum to the Custodial, Grounds and Warehouse Services Contract with D.M. Burr Facilities Management, Inc. "to reflect the increased wages necessary to compete in the current labor market" — raising the aggregate contract price to reflect a **minimum wage of $12.00 per hour for custodians**, with the base contract increase not to exceed **$364,000** from the General Fund.

**Other — bond and sinking fund update**
Completed 2017 projects include Athens mechanical upgrades phase 2, mechanical and electrical upgrades at Barnard, Bemis and Wass, Administration Building mechanical upgrades, Athens and Troy High door replacements, the IA East kitchen renovation on MDE funds, the Troy High chiller replacement and roof replacements at six buildings. In process for 2018: mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Morse and Martell; hydronic piping replacements at Barnard, Bemis and Wass; an Athens vestibule for a special education entrance; an ADA-accessible ramp for the Troy Union stage; Bemis offices converted to a classroom; the Boulan old office renovation; and roofs at six more buildings.

The four-year Building Site and Sinking Fund projection is where the constraint shows. Against **$3,900,000 of projected revenue each year**, planned spending is $1,365,000 in 2018, **$6,160,000 in 2019**, $3,470,000 in 2020 and $3,345,000 in 2021 — the 2019 spike funded by carrying $2,535,000 forward from 2018 and drawing the balance down to $275,000, recovering to $705,000 and $1,260,000 thereafter. The 2019 bulge is mostly three items in the TSD approved projects line: **IAE at $2,000,000**, the Troy High pool at $250,000 and high school woods and autos at $250,000, plus a $150,000 board office.

A tennis court decision is put to the Board for Larson, Smith and International Academy/Baker: remove and replace four regulation courts at $55-$60K per court, $220-$240k per site, **$660-$720K total**, expected to last 7-8 years before requiring maintenance — or remove and restore with seed rather than sod at $30-$35K per site, **$90-$105K total**.

President Schmidt moved public communication for non-agenda items up on the agenda since one community member had asked to address the Board: Kristina Gerami, a Leonard parent, spoke regarding her concerns about specific information in her son's school records.

Resolution 18-062 approved the consent agenda 7-0: minutes of the June 5, 2018 meeting, the June 12, 2018 special meeting and closed session, the June 12, 2018 workshop and the June 19, 2018 meeting, plus the Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2018/2019.

Resolution 18-063 issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Christine Foren as Supervisor, Special Education, effective July 1, 2018, carried 7-0. Resolution 18-064 issued the same form of contract to Ms. Jessica Carrier as Director, Special Education, effective July 1, 2018, carried 7-0.

Resolution 18-065 extended the contract of the Superintendent of Schools, in effect from July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2021, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to the provisions of the written agreement, carried 7-0.

Resolution 18-069 certified the ballot language for an operating millage proposal. It recites that the Board has determined it is necessary for the continuing operation of the School District to restore and replace the authority to levy 18 mills for operating purposes on non-homestead property, which was previously approved by the voters in 2015 and has been rolled back by application of the Headlee Amendment to the Michigan Constitution, and to increase the prior authority in the event of future rollbacks, as described in the Replacement Operating Millage Proposal attached as Exhibit A; that it is necessary and desirable to submit the proposal to the district's electors at the general school election to be held on November 6, 2018; and that in order to do so the Board must certify the ballot wording to the Clerk of the County of Oakland, the School District Election Coordinator, as required by Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended, not later than August 14, 2018. **Consent item 5.C: Schools of Choice, Section 105c, 9th grade for 2019-2020.** In accordance with Michigan state law, school districts shall pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. It is anticipated that seats will be available for the 2019-2020 school year for grade 9 at the International Academy East, and the item proposes a Section 105c resolution for 85 non-resident 9th grade students who reside outside of Oakland County, if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

The resolution accordingly provides that the Board of Education of the Troy School District, exercising the option permitted by Section 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept applications for a Schools of Choice program for the 2019-2020 school year for 85 non-resident 9th grade students who reside outside Oakland County, if that Intermediate School District is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries, for the purposes of attending the International Academy East program located in the Troy School District. Unlike the paired 105/105c resolutions the Board adopts each February for elementary and middle school seats, this one is 105c only and an order of magnitude larger — 85 seats against the 40 kindergarten, 3 first grade and 14 middle school seats set six months earlier — because the International Academy is a consortium program drawing from beyond the county by design. It is also adopted more than a year ahead of the school year it governs.

The four-year BSSF projection sets planned spending against a flat revenue line. Site improvements: paving at the IAE south entrance $75,000 in 2018, Hamilton $175,000 in 2019, IAE $600,000 in 2020 and Hill $250,000 in 2021, with district-wide paving repairs of $15,000 in 2018 and $250,000 in each following year; district-wide elementary hard play at $50,000 in 2019 and $100,000 in 2020 and 2021; district-wide fencing $75,000 then $100,000 annually; district-wide concrete $250,000 in 2018 and $150,000 thereafter; and playground improvements at Barnard, Hill and Wass ($250,000 in 2019), Martell, Morse and Schroeder ($250,000 in 2020) and Costello, Leonard and Troy Union ($250,000 in 2021) — totalling $415,000, $975,000, $1,450,000 and $1,100,000 across the four years.

Flooring and refinishing: the district-wide bid at $650,000 plus $50,000 of asbestos in 2018; in 2019 Morse $230,000, Schroeder $260,000, Troy Union $275,000, Smith $460,000, the Wattles café $60,000 and gym refinishing $100,000; in 2020 Wattles $185,000, Hill $260,000, Leonard $185,000, Larson and Boulan band rooms $40,000, an Athens allowance of $250,000 and $50,000 of gym refinishing; and in 2021 Barnard $250,000, Bemis $225,000, Martell $245,000, Costello $225,000, a district-wide allowance of $200,000 and $50,000 of gym refinishing — totalling $700,000, $1,385,000, $970,000 and $1,195,000. Windows and doors carry a district-wide budget of $100,000 in 2019 and $150,000 in each of 2020 and 2021; casework $200,000 annually from 2019; roofing $250,000 annually from 2019; and mechanical and electrical $250,000 for Smith unit ventilators plus $150,000 for Smith lights in 2019, then $250,000 annually.

TSD approved projects are the swing item: $15,000 for data processing, $30,000 for the Niles roof and ductwork and $5,000 for Athens MC in 2018, totalling $50,000; then in 2019 the Troy High pool at $250,000, high school woods and autos at $250,000, IAE at $2,000,000 and the board office at $150,000, totalling $2,650,000; and nothing in 2020 or 2021.

The totals are $1,165,000 in 2018, $5,960,000 in 2019, $3,270,000 in 2020 and $3,145,000 in 2021, plus $200,000 of soft costs each year, for $1,365,000, $6,160,000, $3,470,000 and $3,345,000. Projected revenue is $3,900,000 in each of the four years. Carry-over runs from nil in 2018 to $2,535,000 available in 2019, $275,000 in 2020 and $705,000 in 2021, with the closing balances $2,535,000, $275,000, $705,000 and $1,260,000. In other words, the fund underspends in 2018 to bank the money for a 2019 program that runs well over a single year's revenue, and the IAE line alone consumes more than half of that year's excess.

A final decision is put to the Board on tennis courts at Larson Middle School, Smith Middle School and International Academy/Baker. Remove and replace four regulation courts would cost $55-$60K per court, or $220-$240k per site, for a $660-$720K total, with an expectation of 7-8 years before the courts require maintenance. Remove and restore, seeding rather than sodding, would cost $30-$35K per site, or $90-$105K total. The presentation ends there, on a question rather than a recommendation.

Read as a whole, the August 2018 packet is the district's start-of-year meeting: roughly sixty new teachers hired at once, 85 out-of-county seats opened at IA East for the following year, a labor-market wage increase pushed through the custodial contract at up to $364,000, and a capital plan that has banked $2,535,000 to spend a year's revenue and a half in 2019. Behind all of it sits the millage the Board had put on the November 6 ballot the month before — a replacement of the same 18 non-homestead mills the district had been levying since 2015, eroded by Headlee.

**Consent agenda minutes.** The December 6, 2011 meeting opened at 7:00 p.m. under President Philippart with Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Malven, Miletti and Underwood present, Superintendent Fowler, administrators Keeling, Machesky, Rajter and Witt, and approximately 45 audience members. Resolution 11-104 certifies at least four of five best practices for the $100 per pupil one-time grant due by June 1, 2012 under MCL 388.1622f, citing a service consolidation resolution sent to the Michigan Department of Education on September 13, 2011, annual status reports by February 1, competitive bids on non-instructional services, and a home-page link to the MI School Data Portal; Rajter said the state would make payments in January and prorate them over eleven remaining payments. Resolution 11-105 approved Ms. Philippart's attendance at the National School Boards Association Annual Federal Relations Network Conference in Washington, D.C., February 5-7, 2012. Troy High physics teacher John Morrison's club was one of 15 high school teams nationally awarded $10,000 by Lemelson-MIT InvenTeam for a mechanical-assist stair climber. On kindergarten, Dr. Fowler stated the district would see over $3 million loss in revenue from the state if it continued a half-day program, in contrast to approximately $1.6 million to implement a full-day program; Jan Keeling said seven teachers would be needed, that Schroeder and Costello have space, and that training would run three hours; Dr. Joan Lessen-Firestone of Oakland Schools presented. Closed session under the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c) ran 8:45 p.m. to 9:38 p.m., with adjournment at 9:40 p.m.; minutes signed by Secretary Paula Fleming. **Items 10.B and 10.C – policy first readings.** B-0102, Board Members' Term of Office, sets a term of six (6) years commencing with the general school election in November of 2016 and on the November general election date in even years thereafter (adopted January 15, 2008). B-1202, Place of Meeting, locates meetings at the District Administrative Centers unless otherwise announced at least twenty-four hours in advance with notice posted per law (adopted April 8, 1975; revised March 15, 1977, January 16, 1979, April 15, 2003). B-1204, Quorum, provides that four members of the Board constitute a quorum, permits remote participation with the presiding chair's permission but without voting, and yields to the Open Meetings Act, MCL 15.261 et seq. (adopted January 16, 1979; revised July 10, 2012). B-1211, Public Participation in Board of Education Meetings, replaces 30 minutes of agenda-item comment at the beginning and 30 minutes of non-agenda comment at the end with public participation limited to 60 minutes per Board meeting, opening comment generally reserved for items posted as "Consideration." Speaker Request Forms are available 30 minutes prior to the start; recognized speakers get up to three (3) minutes (revised April 1988, March 17, 1998, July 10, 2007, March 17, 2009, April 20, 2010).

**Item 5.D, Oakland ISD budget.** Under Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended, the intermediate school board must submit its proposed budget no later than May 1 each year, and each constituent board must, not later than June 1, adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval and submit objections and proposed changes. The Troy Board resolved that it had reviewed the proposed Oakland ISD budget and expressed its support, adding that "it is the responsibility of the Intermediate School District to be responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget" and that its support "is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624 of the Revised School Code." FOOD SERVICE EQUIPMENT UPDATE. Troy began investigating a temperature monitoring system in November 2012 and installed a Smart Temps pilot unit at Larson in May 2014; as of February 2015 the system has been very dependable. It would monitor walk-ins, reach-ins and hot holding units and document food temperatures during preparation and serving, mandatory under HACCP and currently done manually. Listed Smart Temps clients include University of Michigan (most recent), Central Michigan, Ball State University, Notre Dame, Stanford, Saline Schools, Walled Lake Schools, West Bloomfield Schools, Jefferson County, Kentucky (largest district), and Michigan City Schools, Indiana; districts installed in 2008 were still operating strong in 2014, life expectancy could be 10 years or more, and technology changes about every 5 years. Annual monitoring provides unlimited Command Center logins, phone support, onsite training, loading of food and serving menus, automatic updates, monthly data logs, data archiving for 7 years, and alerts by SMS, e-mail and phone. Alternate vendor Great Lakes Hotel gave no response on monitoring costs; its reference School City of Hammond, Indiana (Dr. Julie Boettger) uses E-Control for walk-in coolers/freezers and dish machines only across 22 schools and is piloting Smart Temps, while Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, North Carolina (Cindy Hobbs) and Charlotte County Public Schools (Don Buck) had not responded as of 2/4/15.

POLICY REVIEW. The packet includes a page of the August 2013 Troy School District Board Policy table of contents (B-1206 Rules of Order through B-4001 Cable-casting of Board Meetings, plus Chapter C items C-1001 through C-1103) and full policy texts. B-1703 Suspension permits temporary suspension by a vote of four members (adopted April 8, 1975; revised January 16, 1979). B-1704 Notification requires first and second readings (adopted April 8, 1975; revised January 16, 1979 and July 10, 2007). B-1801 Policy Drafting reserves drafting to the Board and requires legal counsel review. B-1901 gives the superintendent power to act absent policy. B-2001 requires prior approval by resolution for out-of-state meetings (adopted June 21, 1976; revised March 17, 1998). B-2002 sets board member compensation at $100 per annum (adopted January 16, 1979; revised March 17, 1998 and April 15, 2003). B-2101 bars member conflicts of interest and hiring of immediate family during a member's term (adopted June 21, 1976). B-3001 provides that the first applicant receiving four votes is appointed and vacancies filled within thirty (30) days (adopted March 17, 1998; revised September 2003). B-4001 requires unedited cablecast except where comments violate Regulation 9130, the Open Meetings Act or FERPA (adopted March 17, 1998).
