CONSENT AGENDA - ORGANIZATIONAL MEETING MINUTES, JANUARY 17, 2012. President Philippart called the organizational meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building. Present in addition to Ms. Philippart were Board members Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Schmidt and Underwood, along with Superintendent Fowler; administrators Birmingham, Cottone, Jolly, Keeling, Machesky, Rajter, Witt and Wood; and approximately 65 members of the audience. Resolution 12-001 made Ms. Philippart acting chairperson (Ayes 7, Nays 0), and Judy Holmes was appointed temporary secretary. Roll-call votes carried 7-0 elected Ms. Philippart president (12-002), Mrs. Edmunds vice president (12-003), and Mr. Miletti secretary (12-004), each serving until December 31, 2012. Resolution 12-005 appointed Mark S. Rajter, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for January through December 2012. Resolution 12-006 adopted the Fund Depositories and Investments resolution for the same period, directing Treasurer Rajter to deposit all public monies, including tax monies, in Bank of America, Bank of New York, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Citizen's Bank, Comerica Bank, Fifth Third Bank, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Withdrawals may be made by checks bearing the facsimile signature of Treasurer Mark S. Rajter, with the handwritten signature of Rajter or Superintendent Barbara A. Fowler permitted in emergencies on the General Fund and Payroll accounts at Bank of America. PNC Bank accounts established for paying Troy Career Center expenses are drawn on the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager or Program Coordinators. Checks over $10,000 drawn on the Bank of America account for remaining health care claims require the additional handwritten signature of Jasen Witt, Assistant Superintendent for Human Resources, or Monica Papasian, Finance Director. The Comerica Bank account for health care and dependent care flexible spending claims may be drawn by ACH debit to Next Generation Enrollment, Inc. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy D-1103 and combined across funds under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code, with authorized institutions Ambassador Capital Management, Bank of America, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Charter One Bank, Citizens Bank, Comerica Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF, Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and The Private Bank; the certification is signed by Paula Fleming, Secretary, on the 17th day of January 2012. Resolution 12-007 continued designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board; 12-008 designated Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, to post notices of meetings; 12-009 adopted the 2012 calendar-year meeting schedule. The organizational meeting adjourned at 7:12 p.m., submitted by Judy Holmes, Acting Secretary, and Todd Miletti, Secretary.

REGULAR BOARD MEETING MINUTES, JANUARY 17, 2012. Called to order at 7:12 p.m. with the same members, administrators and roughly 65 audience members. The Board recognized 104 senior scholar athletes from fall sports who maintained a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while competing, among them Joshua Allen (Football), Arianna Armin (Girls' Swim & Dive), Ujwal Bharath (Boys Tennis), Taylor Bommarito (Volleyball), Sameer Desai (Boys Tennis), Christofer Hatzis (Boys Water Polo), Emma Kollman (Volleyball), Tingxi Liu (Swimming), Marisa Oleski (Girls Golf), Mayara Sanches (Cheerleading), Edgar Wang (Boys Water Polo) and Kevin Zywicki (Boys Tennis). Fall all-state athletes recognized were Zachary Doepke (Boys Soccer), Kelly Feng (Girls Golf), Matthew Kuntzman (Boys Tennis), Jason Leslie (Boys Soccer), Kento Mizusaki (Boys Tennis), Sanath Shettigar (Boys Soccer), Matt Smolinski (Boys Soccer), William Yau (Cross Country) and Richard Zhang (Boys Tennis). Three Troy High School students - seniors Edgar Wang and Justin Yuan and junior Wayne Shu - were recognized as 2011 Siemens Competition winners who will share $50,000 in scholarship money after placing second in early December in a national field of 20 finalists at George Washington University in Washington D.C. For National School Board Recognition month, Ms. Birmingham showed a video, Board members received an original canvas artwork created by Troy art teacher Heather Kelly, and Dr. Machesky and Mrs. Keeling reported a donation made in the Board's honor to the Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence. Resolution 12-010 approved the consent agenda: minutes of the December 6, 2011 meeting, minutes of the December 13, 2011 workshop, and the Treasurer's Report for November and December 2011 (7-0). Resolution 12-011 appointed Jasen Witt chief spokesperson with Mark Rajter and Sara Konieczka as team members for negotiations with TESPA/MEA/NEA, whose contract expires June 30, 2012 (7-0). Resolution 12-012 approved new hires Molly Brehm and Erin Hill (7-0). Dr. Machesky presented on OCALP, the Oakland Community Accelerated Learning Program hosted by Oakland Community College, in which Troy was one of five surrounding districts participating. Physical education teacher Jamie Grant presented the new T.R.O.Y. (Teachers Recognizing Outstanding Youth) Fitness Program for grades K-5, replacing the traditional Presidential Physical Fitness Award. Resolutions 12-013 through 12-016, each 7-0, adopted limited Schools of Choice programs for 2012-2013 under Sections 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996: nonresident kindergarten and first grade students from within Oakland County, the same from contiguous intermediate school districts, and grades 6-8 at Baker Middle School under both sections. Dr. Fowler gave the third of four updates on the 2011-2012 Superintendent's Goals, addressing Visibility, Facilities Study, Data Processing Cost Analysis, Strategies for Student Success and Community Outreach. Student representative Maggie Steele of Troy High reported on the Gala Concert on Saturday, February 4th and a Snowcoming Dance with Spirit Week; Jonny Dowdall of Athens High reported a student council can drive collecting over 5,000 cans and over 400 pairs of socks, and awards at the University of Michigan Model UN conference in Ann Arbor for Ramis Wadood, Promit Ghosh, Mukund Mohan and Misha Rahman. Ms. Underwood welcomed Karl Schmidt to the Board. Resolution 12-017 moved the Board into closed session on negotiations under the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), by 7-0 roll call; closed session began at 8:37 p.m., the meeting reconvened at 9:28 p.m. and adjourned at 9:29 p.m.

B-1401 requires minutes to record the time, date and place of the meeting, members present and absent, topics discussed and decisions made, the purpose of any closed session, and all roll call votes, resolutions, movers and seconders and vote counts, with roll call votes required for non-unanimous or statutorily required votes; proposed minutes must be available for public inspection within eight business days after a meeting and approved minutes within five business days after approval; records are released under the Michigan Freedom of Information Act, Act No. 442, PA 1976; official minutes are bound and kept in the vault at the administrative office. B-1401 was adopted April 8, 1975 and revised March 15, 1977, January 16, 1979, March 17, 1998 and June 19, 2007. New policy I-1701 states the district may occasionally show video of speeches, presentations and enrichment activities outside the district curriculum that are not produced by the district; parents/guardians wishing to opt out must notify the child's building principal or classroom teacher, will be informed of the right as part of the district's annual notices, and reasonable provisions will be made for students removed from classrooms during video presentations.

**Item 7.A, Accountability Update Fall 2013.** Anne Mull, Director of Instruction and Assessment. In August 2013 the Michigan Department of Education released the Michigan School Accountability Scorecards, the Top to Bottom ranking and the Reward, Focus and Priority lists under NCLB flexibility from the U.S. Department of Education; Adequate Yearly Progress will no longer be reported. Annual Measureable Objectives run from the 2011-2012 proficiency rate toward an end proficiency rate of 85% by 2021-2022 in a five color system. Statewide green districts include 38 single school entities, 23 new districts and 15 small districts with fewer than 30 students tested; green schools include 73 new schools and 22 small schools; county examples are Novi Adult Ed (approximately 6 students assessed), Oxford Virtual Academy and the Kennedy Center in Pontiac. Focus schools turn on the gap between average scale scores of the top 30% and bottom 30%; Reward schools sit in the top 5%. From 2012-2013 to 2013-2014 Troy High moved from Continuous Improvement to Focus and Costello from Reward to Continuous Improvement, while Barnard, Bemis, Boulan Park, Hamilton, Larson, Leonard and Wattles moved to Reward but remain Focus on the 4 year cohort; Baker, Morse, Smith and Troy Union remained Focus; Hill, Schroeder and Wass remained Reward; Martell and Niles remained Continuous Improvement. The bottom 30% subgroup shows 0% proficient until overall proficiency exceeds 70%, and an AMO of 33% translates into 80% overall; Michigan schools with 2013-14 AMOs below 70% are 58% reading, 89% writing, 95% math, 98% social studies, 99.8% science.

Purposes: remodeling and equipping buildings to enhance security, technology equipment and infrastructure, additions, site improvements and school buses. Bonds are dated as of delivery in denominations of $5,000 or multiples, maturing the first day of May, interest payable May 1 and November 1 with record dates April 15 and October 15, CUSIP 897404, registered to Cede & Co. as nominee of the Depository Trust Company. Taxes may be levied without limitation as to rate or amount under Article IX, Sections 6 and 16, into a 2014 School Building and Site Bonds Debt Retirement Fund. The negotiated sale names Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated as senior managing underwriter, Clark Hill PLC as bond counsel and Stauder, Barch & Associates, Inc. as financial advisor, with ratings possible from Moody's Investors Service, Fitch Ratings and/or Standard & Poor's. Exhibit A, the bond form under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976 and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, is signed by Nancy Philippart, President, and countersigned by Paula Fleming, Secretary. Exhibit C, the Continuing Disclosure Agreement under SEC Rule 15c2-12, requires the annual report by the 180th day after fiscal year end beginning with the year ending June 30, 2014, filed to EMMA, plus notice of any of 14 listed events within ten business days. Form 3451 commits the District to certify and levy its debt millage annually and file an Annual Loan Activity Statement.

**Minimum Fund Balance**
A minimum fund balance of 12% is defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 fiscal year total expenditures per each June 30 audit. Any shortfall measured at November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 is the "Deficiency"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Contribution," an equal-percentage off-schedule reduction of base salaries. A balance above 17% yields a "Surplus"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Bonus," paid in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Capital asset sale proceeds over $2 million are excluded.

**COVID-19 policy (item 4.A)**
Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, with the first reading waived under policy 1000.03. Employees testing positive or showing principal symptoms (fever, atypical cough, atypical shortness of breath) may not enter district property until three days after symptoms resolve and seven days after they first appear or since swabbing, or upon a negative test; close contact within approximately six feet requires 14 days. Executive Order 2020-36 bars retaliation. FFCRA emergency paid sick leave provides up to 80 hours capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for an employee's own quarantine, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for care of others. Emergency FMLA expansion gives up to 12 weeks for care of a child under 18, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. The policy expires December 31, 2020.

ITEM 3.A — TEA CONTRACT RATIFICATION (dated 04.14.20). Board representatives and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA reached a tentative agreement March 27, 2020; TEA membership ratified it April 2, 2020. The redlined Table of Contents places Article 37 Ancillary Teachers at page 62, Article 38 Minimum Fund Balance at page 78 and Article 39 Duration of Agreement at page 80, which directs both teams to meet on or before October 15, 2020 to discuss negotiations.

SALARY SETTLEMENT (Article 11.1). As of May 1st, eligible teachers on Steps 2 through 13, and those who moved to Step 13.5 during 2019-2020, receive a lump sum equal to half their current step increment and move a half step. As of May 15th, eligible teachers who began 2019-2020 on Longevity 1, 2 or 3 receive $500.00, added to the 2020-2021 Schedule A longevity steps, and all teachers receive a $200.00 ratification bonus. As of July 1, 2020 all eligible teachers move one salary step and each cell of Schedule A (Steps 1 through 14) increases by $500.00; a $500.00 off-schedule payment is made in the first pay period of 2020-2021. Teachers elect 21 or 26 equal payments. Six paid holidays are observed: Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, New Year's Day, Good Friday and Memorial Day.

SCHEDULE A, 2020-2021. Eleven lanes are printed — BA, BA20, MA, MA30/EDS/ESL Endorsement, PHD/EDD, and grandfathered BA25, MA5, MA10, MA15, MA20 and MA25. Step 1 pays 41,800 (BA), 45,500 (MA), 48,700 (MA30/EDS) and 52,000 (PHD/EDD); Step 14 pays 73,500, 85,000, 93,400 and 96,700, topping out at 91,750 in MA25. Longevity increments run 2,682 / 4,564 / 6,445 in the BA lane and 3,269 / 5,734 / 8,204 in PHD/EDD, paid for service beyond 15, 20 and 25 years in Troy Schools. Teachers were barred from BA+15, BA+25, MA+5, MA+15 and MA+25 after 1996-97 and from MA+10 and MA+20 after 2009-10; only teachers hired on or before December 14, 1971 may advance to BA+30.

EXTRA-DUTY SCHEDULES. Schedules B and C pay a percentage of $64,000, raised from $60,467. Varsity football and basketball pay 11.60% ($7,424.00); assistant varsity and junior varsity 7.50% ($4,800.00); varsity gymnastics, wrestling, swimming and competitive cheer 9.00% ($5,760.00); varsity baseball, track, soccer, volleyball, lacrosse and hockey 8.00% ($5,120.00); varsity tennis, golf and cross country 6.00% ($3,840.00). Schedule C spans 7.50% ($4,800) for K-12 arts coordinators and the high school band director down to 1.00% ($640) club sponsorships. Schedule D pays $30.00 per hour for curriculum development, teaching in place of a substitute and TEAM/SAT meetings, $35.00 per hour plus a $60.00 annual prep fee for instructional trainers, and $20.00 per hour for web design, with mileage at the prevailing IRS maximum rate.

CLASS SIZE, STIPENDS AND SEVERANCE. Elementary maximums are 26 in kindergarten (27), 28 in first and second grade (30) and 29 in third through fifth (30), with $80 per marking period per student over the cap paid to the TEA Education Fund. Secondary base maximum is 30, with Advanced Placement at 25 (30), Progressive Learning Support at 21 (23), physical education at 33 in middle school and 36 in high school, and counselor caseload at 400 with $500 per semester if caseload exceeds 25 after count day; exceeding a maximum by one pupil in an emergency costs $1,000.00 per occurrence. Other stipends include $500 per year for secondary teachers traveling between schools, $350 per semester for early/late building assignments and $500 per mentee. Severance pays tenure teachers with ten or more years half the per diem rate for unused sick days to a maximum of 60 days plus 30 days at the substitute rate, and those with less than ten years the substitute rate to a maximum of 90 days; payments of $5,000.00 or more go into a District 403(b). Retirement severance pays $1,000.00 at 10-14 years, $1,500.00 at 15-19 years and $100.00 per year at 20 or more.

INSURANCE AND EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATORS. Article 26 maintains compliance with the Publicly Funded Health Insurance Contribution Act (PA 152 of 2011), the Board paying the annual maximum allowable and teachers the difference over 21 pays. MESSA PAK A bundles medical, Delta Dental, VSP III vision, life and long-term disability; life is two times salary, except $50,000 AD/D for teachers hired on or after June 4, 1991. Long-term disability begins after 60 calendar days and pays up to two-thirds of salary to age 70. Plan B pays $1,000 annually, or $2,500 if 45 or more teachers decline district medical coverage. New Article 36 covers early childhood educators in the Board's tuition-based preschool program under Michigan's Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), with a salary schedule of $28,008, $29,564, $31,120, $32,676 and $34,232 for Steps 1 through 5, a $1,000 annual master's stipend, a $3,000 cafeteria plan in lieu of medical coverage, a $50,000 term life policy and disability capped at $3,000 per month. Appendix 5 lists BCBSM plans CB 2, CB 3, CB 4 and Simply Blue effective 1/1/2020 with in-network deductibles of $100, $250, $500 and $1,400, and dental under Group #9941.

MINIMUM FUND BALANCE. The article sets a minimum fund balance of 12%, defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 school/fiscal year total expenditures determined by each June 30 audit. If that balance falls below 12%, the amount needed to restore it is calculated as of November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 as the "Deficiency"; the Deficiency multiplied by 55.6% is the "Contribution," achieved by reducing base salaries of all actively employed bargaining unit members by an equal percentage through an off-schedule reduction beginning with the first payroll period in January 2018, accounting for retirement and FICA, unless another method is agreed before December 31, 2018 and/or December 31, 2019. Where the balance exceeds 17%, the excess measured on the same dates is the "Surplus"; the Surplus multiplied by 55.6% is the "Bonus," paid as an equal-percentage off-schedule lump sum in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Costs of new programs in excess of $2 million should not increase total year-over-year budgetary expenditures unless federally or state mandated, and one-time revenues from capital asset sales in excess of $2 million are excluded. Article 25.2 entitles the TEA to monthly financial reports.

CALENDARS AND APPENDICES. The 2020/2021 calendar totals 186 teacher days and 181 student days, with 6-12 marking periods ending November 5, January 21, March 25 and June 16. The payroll schedule runs from 8/21/2020 through 8/20/2021. A Letter of Agreement on Schoology grading amends Sections 14.14 and 14.15 of the 2017-2020 agreement through June 16, 2020. Appendix 1 is the grievance report form (rev/10-96), Appendix 2 the mentoring log, Appendix 3 board policies 4000.03 and 4000.04, and Appendix 4 the Child Care Supervisor Evaluation.

ITEM 4.A — COVID-19 BOARD POLICY. The Board considered a policy on COVID-19 Mitigation, Self-Reporting, Leave of Absence, noting that policy 1000.03 Adoption or Amendment of Bylaws and Policies permits waiver of a first reading. Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, it bars employees and contractors who test positive or display principal symptoms from entering district property until three days have passed since symptoms resolved and seven days since symptoms first appeared or since swabbing, or until a negative test; close contact requires 14 days. Principal symptoms are fever, atypical cough or atypical shortness of breath; close contact is being within approximately six feet of an individual for a prolonged period. Executive Order 2020-36 prohibits retaliation for staying home. Employees must maintain at least six feet of distance and follow Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance; health information is protected under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 and the Family Education Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, with exposure reporting under Board Policy 5502. Under the FFCRA Emergency Paid Sick Leave Act, full-time employees receive up to 80 hours and part-time employees hours equal to their 2-week average, capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for the employee's own quarantine or symptoms, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for caring for others. The Emergency Family and Medical Leave Expansion Act provides up to 12 weeks to care for a child under 18 whose school or child care is closed, for employees with at least 30 calendar days of service, the first 10 days unpaid and later days at not less than two-thirds of pay, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. Legal references are PL 116-127 § 5101 et seq. and § 3101 et seq., 134 Stat. 177, and Executive Orders 2020-35 and 2020-36. The policy expires December 31, 2020 unless state or federal law extends the date.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, June 20, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Business — A. Public Hearing: 2017/2018 Proposed Budget; 3. Recognition — A. 2016-2017 School Year in Review, B. Mission Moment: Athens AP Capstone & Seminar Students; 4. Additions & Deletions; 5. Public Communication (agenda items); 6. General – Consent Agenda — A. Treasurer's Report – April & May 2017; 7. Personnel — A. Report: World Language Materials, B. Consideration: World Language Materials Adoption, C. Report: ELD Materials, D. Consideration: ELD Materials Adoption; 9. Business — A. Consideration: 2016/2017 Budget Amendment, B. Consideration: 2017/2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution, C. Consideration: Section 11 Purchase Agreement, D. The agenda's ordering is itself notable: business comes before recognition, because item 2.A is the statutory public hearing on the proposed budget, which must precede adoption later in the same meeting.

**Business 2.A: public hearing on the preliminary 2017-2018 budget.** The item attaches a PowerPoint presentation and a draft of the 2017-18 budget book, to be finalized following board adoption of the budget.

**Recognition 3.A: 2016-2017 School Year in Review.** Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, introduces the video.

**Recognition 3.B: Athens AP Capstone and Seminar students.** Athens AP Seminar teachers Brenda Rice and Sue Syme, along with AP Research teacher Rachel Webb, present a brief overview of the AP Capstone Program. The overview is followed by a question and answer session in which Board members put questions to the students themselves, who answer about their experiences and the unique learning opportunity the program provides. The item records that the students were chosen for the event based on their success in the program and their ability to express themselves well. Athens Principal Lara Dixon introduces the teachers, who in turn introduce their students; the AP Seminar students named include Rija Awan, Nathan Babcock, Saihaj Deol and Rishita Gudeti. Gudeti would appear again eighteen months later among the district's 54 National Merit Scholarship semifinalists.

**Consent agenda 6.A.** The Treasurer's Report for April and May 2017 — two months presented together, as the June meeting is the last of the fiscal year.

**Personnel 7.A: TEA contract ratification.** A tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached on June 9, 2017. The TEA membership voted to ratify the agreement on June 16, 2017. The tentative agreement is a contract for the period of July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020, and its specifics are attached, signed by Mr. Tony Lucchi, President of the TEA, and Mr. Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, on June 9, 2017. The resolution ratifies and adopts that agreement.

The timing is tight and deliberate. The Board appointed its negotiating team on February 28, 2017 — Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass — against a contract expiring June 30. The tentative agreement came on June 9, membership ratification on June 16, and Board ratification on June 20, ten days before expiry. The term chosen is unusual: rather than a clean three-year deal ending June 30, 2020, the contract runs to January 31, 2020, placing the next expiration mid-school-year.

**Personnel 7.B: Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School.** The recommendation is Mr. David Recker. He started his career in education following graduation from college in 2012, teaching language arts and journalism at the Dayton Early College Academy in Dayton, Ohio. He moved to the Troy area in 2014 and accepted a language arts teaching position at Troy High School. During his time in Dayton and at Troy High he fulfilled many additional responsibilities including implementing the International Society for Technology in Education's standards, leading the Continuous Improvement Committee to increase use of best practices, and serving as coordinator for several extracurricular clubs and committees. He holds a bachelor's degree in adolescent to young adult education from the University of Dayton and a Master of Arts in K-12 education administration from Michigan State University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, effective July 1, 2017. The packet attaches his Oakland Human Resources Consortium online application, submitted May 10, 2017.

**Curriculum 8.A and 8.B: secondary world language materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, and Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended world language materials for grades 6-12 for the upcoming school year. The consideration item records that Dziatczak and Gottlieb, along with members of the Teaching and Learning team, provided information on the recommended Chinese, French, German, Japanese and Spanish world language materials for grades 6-12, and that Board members had an opportunity to review textbooks, ask questions and discuss the recommendation at the June 13 Board Workshop. The total cost of these materials is $419,606.82, and the resolution approves them for the 2017-2018 school year in that amount.

**Curriculum 8.C and 8.D: ELD materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak and Christin Silagy, Director of ELD, Federal Grants and State Assessments, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended ELD materials for grades 6-12. The consideration item records the same June 13 workshop review, gives the total cost of the materials as $171,735.32, and the resolution approves them on the same terms.

The two adoptions together commit close to six hundred thousand dollars of instructional materials in a single meeting, both for grades 6-12, and both reviewed by the Board in person the week before — the packet is careful to record that trustees handled the textbooks themselves.

**Business 9.A: 2016-17 budget amendment resolution.** The amendment covers the General Fund, Debt Service Funds, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Adult Education and Community Service Fund, Facility Rentals Fund, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. The amended fund totals include General Fund $146,020,168; Food Service Fund $4,032,399; Troy Career Center Fund $2,215,068; Capital Projects Fund $16,288,758; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,885,000. This is the year's final true-up, following the Budget Amendment #2 adopted in March.

**Business 9.B: 2017-2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution.** The appropriations resolution covers the General Fund, Special Revenue Funds, Debt Service Funds, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund as required by the Department of Education. The resolution approves the general appropriations and budget and millage rates for fiscal year 2017-18 as attached and made part of the official minutes of the June 20, 2017 regular meeting: General Fund $147,430,144; Special Revenue Funds $9,516,614; Debt Service Funds $18,778,792; 2014 Capital Projects Funds $21,615,000; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,270,000.

The millage rates approved are, by tax base and purpose: non-homestead general operating, 18.0000 mills; commercial personal property general operating, 11.6320 mills; homestead general operating, 5.6320 mills; and all properties debt retirement, 4.7000 mills.

On the revenue side, the General Fund is budgeted at local $37,990,138, state $97,760,866, federal $3,506,988 and incoming transfers and other $8,200,393, for total revenues and incoming transfers of $147,458,385. The estimated fund balance at July 1, 2017 is $22,335,432, all of it available to appropriate, giving total available to appropriate of $169,793,817. Of that, $147,430,144 is appropriated: instruction takes $101,335,630, comprising basic programs $83,230,516, added needs $17,245,604 and adult and continuing education $859,510; support services begin with pupil services at $10,678,738.

The 18 non-homestead mills approved here are the same levy that would be eroded by Headlee and restored by the November 2018 replacement election.

**Business 9.C: Section 11 purchase agreement.** The School District issued a Request For Proposals To Purchase Real Property to obtain proposals to purchase certain surplus vacant real property located in Section 11, and received twelve proposals, examined in conjunction with legal counsel Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. The recommendation is that the Board authorize the sale of the property to Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. in the amount of $4,225,000.00.

The resolution describes the property as 18 +/- acres of vacant land located north of Long Lake, east of Rochester Road and west of Allison Street in Troy, Michigan, Sidwell Numbers 20-11-328-003 and 20-11-401-001. It recites the proposal from Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. to purchase the property for a purchase price of Four Million Two Hundred Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($4,225,000.00) Dollars; that the district is desirous of authorizing the sale on the terms generally described and substantially similar to those contained in the Purchaser's response and clarifications to the RFP; and that it wishes to authorize Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate the terms and conditions of a final Offer To Purchase on terms acceptable to him after consultation with legal counsel, and to execute the negotiated Offer To Purchase and any documents necessary and incidental to the sale.

This is the sale the March 2017 district-owned property resolution authorized marketing, and it is the largest of the district's land transactions in these packets. The structure is the same one used for Section 23 in January — the Board authorizes a negotiation rather than approving a signed agreement — but unlike the January item, this resolution names the buyer and states the price. Mondrian Properties had first appeared in these packets as one of two bidders discussed at the January 10, 2017 workshop on Section 23; it takes Section 11 here, and would go on to buy Section 16 and the Section 1 front parcel in 2018. Twelve proposals for this parcel is the largest field the district drew for any of its properties.

**Business 9.D through 9.F: service contract renewals.** Rick West's June 8, 2017 memorandum to the Board, copied to Dr. Machesky, explains that the initial terms for three service contracts expire on June 30, 2017 and that the district has been negotiating renewal terms for each.

First Student provides bus transportation services. The initial term was the three-year period commencing July 1, 2014 and ending June 30, 2017, with an option to extend for up to two additional years. West writes that the district currently has a very competitive contract based on per-route pricing and believes it can negotiate a better deal for a two-year renewal than by rebidding the services. His recommendation is candid about the pressure: "Given our competitive per route cost, the starting wage for bus drivers is low relative to neighboring districts. This is causing difficulty in staffing; therefore, we will be recommending a renewal contract that will increase the per route cost by 5% - 8% for the first year and 3% - 5% for the second year." He cites comparative per-route data from other county districts and the nationwide bus driver shortage, and notes the increase will be reflected in the 2017-18 proposed budget. The resolution authorizes administration to finalize the renewal for the 2017/2018 and 2018/2019 school years.

Safe Ed provides professional security consultation solutions at Troy Athens, Troy High School and Troy Career and College High School, under an initial three-year term commencing July 1, 2014. West records that Safe Ed has been a quality partner in providing security services since 2011 and recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020. The current base contract cost is $300,500, and the recommended base contract for the three years is $305,000, $310,000 and $315,000 respectively. The resolution authorizes finalizing the renewal for 2017/2018, 2018/2019 and 2019/2020.

Clean Ed employs six facility maintenance technicians responsible for providing supplemental support to the district's skilled trades staff. The initial term was one year commencing July 1, 2016. West recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020, noting there will be no additional cost for these services as Clean Ed charges a flat fee per employee to handle the human resource functions of employment for these positions.

**Business 9.G: worker's compensation insurance.** The district solicited a worker's compensation insurance proposal from MASB-SEG. It is currently self-insured through the State of Michigan with York Risk Management serving as third-party administrator and Midwest Casualty handling excess insurance claims.

West's June 8, 2017 memorandum explains the trade: "Our claims history has been excellent over the past few years which keeps the cost of our workers compensation low; however, we do continually have $400,000 exposure per employee injury." SET SEG, the district's current property casualty insurance carrier, provides full coverage workers compensation insurance, and given the claims history the district has an opportunity to switch to very affordable full coverage. He recommends making the change, which "will provide us a more predictable budget number for workers compensation and eliminates the $400,000 exposure per employee injury," and notes it would be discussed at the June 13 workshop with the SET SEG proposal attached for review.

The resolution authorizes administration to accept the proposal from MASB-SEG for full coverage worker's compensation insurance effective July 1, 2017 for an amount not to exceed $98,968.00. The item is a clean illustration of what a district buys with insurance: not a lower expected cost — self-insurance with good claims experience is cheap — but the removal of a tail risk and a number the budget can rely on.

**Business 9.H: renewal of food services contract.** On June 21, 2016 the Board approved a resolution allowing administration to enter into a contract with Sodexo Management, Inc. to continue providing the food service operation for the district. The renewal must be approved by the Michigan Department of Education and the Troy Board of Education annually, and the item records that MDE has approved this renewal. The resolution authorizes administration to approve the contract renewal with Sodexo for the 2017/2018 school year.

**Other 11.A: 2017 Sinking Fund Community Input Survey.** The final report, commissioned by the Troy Board of Education and dated June 13, 2017, is organized as introduction, perceptions of district performance, projected sinking fund voting patterns and prevalent public attitudes.

The background section states the problem without hedging. Because of persistent funding gaps from the State, the district continues to seek other ways to fund quality education. In 2013 voters overwhelmingly supported a $125 million bond to help cover many expenses over the bond's 10-year lifespan; the district structured that bond so as not to raise property tax rates, but keeping the bond tax-neutral "also meant it wouldn't cover everything the District knew it needed." The Board hoped state funding would increase sufficiently when the economy improved, "but that hasn't happened." As a result the district continues to struggle to pay for things like preventative maintenance on its buildings. Recent legislative adjustments to appropriate uses for a sinking fund have made it a potential avenue for covering significant district costs such as maintenance, facility improvements and construction, safety and security measures, and technology.

Consequently the Board is considering whether to place a sinking fund proposal on the November ballot. Because the district recently retired some debt, it could structure a new 1-mill sinking fund so that the total school millage rate in Troy would stay where it is, with no property tax increase from what homeowners pay today. That 1 mill would provide the district with $3.6 million per year for the next ten years, to be used to fill current holes in preventative maintenance, update classrooms and technology in a timelier manner, and cover debt payments on new or existing buildings. The report notes the strategic tension: given ongoing needs it would be appropriate to ask for more than 1 mill, "especially because a school district can only pursue one sinking fund every ten years."

Methodology: a phone survey fielded by Epic MRA, a Lansing-based market research company and the firm that completed the 2013 TSD bond survey, averaging 18 minutes in length and fielded April 20 to 24, 2017. To keep district costs as low as possible, a Board member with market research expertise drafted and analyzed the survey following standard research industry practices. The sample was 400 Troy residents living within the Troy School District area, registered voters who indicate they are at least "seldom" voters in local school related elections, with age distribution consistent with voting patterns from the 2011 and 2013 Troy elections. Twenty percent of interviews were completed with cell-only households, and the cooperation rate was extremely high — 80% of those who answered and qualified completed the survey. Full sample results are accurate to within +/- 5% at the 95 percent confidence level. The sample profile is 53% women and 47% men, with an age distribution of 5% aged 18 to 29, 7% aged 30 to 39, 17% aged 40 to 49, 35% aged 50 to 64, 34% aged 65 or older, and 2% declining to say.

The headline finding: the 1-mill sinking fund proposal enjoyed wide support, driven most by a sense of necessity and general educational commitment. On the vote question, 61% said Yes, 7% leaning Yes, 4% leaning No, 16% No and 12% not sure. Reasons given for Yes were maintenance and upkeep important (21%), pro-education or always vote yes (18%), more funding needed (16%), no tax increase (15%), educational quality (5%) and property values (4%).

The report's conclusion is stated three separate times across its slides, in identical words: no tax increase is what earns the endorsement from the community — and raising it collapses support. On the segment analysis, "maybe" voters are characterized as more pragmatic than supporters and less pessimistic than non-supporters, with a conversation around new technology and investment protection identified as the productive line of argument for them.

Read against the strategic tension the background sets out — that a district gets one sinking fund per decade and therefore has reason to ask for more than a mill — the survey's answer is unambiguous: the support is real but it is contingent entirely on tax neutrality, and the district's own polling told it not to reach.

Read as a whole, the June 2017 packet closes the fiscal year and sets up the next several. It ratifies a teacher contract running into 2020, adopts a $147,430,144 General Fund at 18 non-homestead mills, sells eighteen acres for $4,225,000.00 to the developer who would buy two more parcels from the district, locks in four service contracts through 2020, trades a $400,000 per-injury exposure for a $98,968.00 premium, buys nearly six hundred thousand dollars of secondary language materials, and receives the polling that would shape the November ballot question.

Item 8.A, Bid #9729 Server Expansion. Bids were sent to eighteen potential bidders for expansion of the existing UCS infrastructure to support 1250 additional virtual desktop users; three vendors responded, none of them a no bid, and the award is based on total cumulative price. Base bids: Data Strategy $161,305.35; Information Systems Intelligence $121,463.58; Netech $146,828.37. For furnishing and installing 10 B200 M3 servers the quoted amounts were Data Strategy $166,430.78, Information Systems Intelligence $150,714.74 and Netech $145,544.83. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agenda packet for the organizational and regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, January 15, 2019, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Election of Acting Chairperson; 3. Appointment of Temporary Secretary; 4. Annual Organizational Meeting of the Board of Education — A. Nomination and Election of Officers (President, Vice President, Secretary), B. Appointment of Treasurer, C. Establish Fund Depositories and Investment Resolution for 2018/19 and 2019/20, D. Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel, E. Designation of Superintendent to be Deputy Secretary, F. Designation of a Person for Posting Notices of Meetings, G. Meeting Schedule for 2019 Calendar Year; 5. Recognition — A. Mission Moment: Baker Middle School Food Drive, B. Board Recognition Month; 6. Additions & Deletions; 7. Public Communication (agenda items); 8. General – Consent Agenda; 9. Personnel; 10. Curriculum; 11. Business; 12. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 13. Other; 14. Adjournment.

**The agenda memo.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board setting out the organizational sequence. The first order of business is to elect an acting chairperson who will conduct the meeting until a president has been elected. Each officer election follows the same procedure: the chair declares nominations in order, a nomination is made and seconded, and a motion and support are made to close nominations; the memo states plainly that four votes are required for election. After the president is elected, the newly elected president declares nominations in order for vice president, then for secretary, following the same procedures. On the treasurer, the memo records that by Board Policy the treasurer is appointed annually by the Board as a nonvoting officer, that the assistant superintendent of business services has served as treasurer of the Board, and that the superintendent recommends this procedure continue.

**Organizational items.** Item 2 resolves that a named member serve as acting chairperson to officiate the meeting until the election of a president has been completed. Item 3 suggests the acting chairperson appoint Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the secretary of the Troy Board of Education has been elected. Item 4.A.1 provides the nomination form for president — one member nominating another to serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2019 — followed by the close of nominations and a suggested resolution, with the same structure repeated for vice president and secretary. Item 4.B appoints the treasurer. Item 4.C establishes fund depositories and the investment resolution for both 2018/19 and 2019/20. Item 4.D designates board and district legal counsel; 4.E designates the superintendent to be deputy secretary of the Board; 4.F designates a person responsible for posting notices of meetings; and 4.G adopts the meeting schedule for the 2019 calendar year.

**Recognition.** Item 5.A is a Mission Moment on the Baker Middle School food drive; item 5.B recognizes Board Recognition Month.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the December 4, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the December 18, 2018 Board of Education Meeting; C. Treasurer's Report for November 2018; D. Budget Adjustment #1. The budget item is a 2018-19 Budget Amendment Resolution which resolves that the total revenues and unappropriated fund balance estimated to be available are as set out in the attached schedules, made part of the official minutes. The bulk of the packet's middle sections is the November 2018 check register run by fund, together with listings of ACH debits, wire transfers and P-Card purchases.

**Personnel.** Item 9.A is a consideration of elementary and secondary personnel recommendations.

**Business 11.A: Boulan and Larson locker replacement.** The resolution awards the bid for locker replacement at Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools in the amount of $152,065.00.

**Business 11.B: 2019 roof replacement project.** The resolution awards the roof replacement bid as set out in the attached schedule, as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The schedule covers elementary schools, Smith Middle School and the Operations Building, and names Quality Roofing for Athens High School at $197,421.00, with a contingency of $78,212.10, for a total of $860,333.10.

**Business 11.C: Troy High School pool renovation.** The resolution awards the pool renovation as set out in the attached schedule, as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund and the Sinking Fund: B & B Pools for pool upgrades at $209,090.00, Shoreview Electric for electrical work at $123,400.00, Paint Plus for painting at $149,300.00, and a contingency of $48,179.00, for a total of $529,969.00.

**Business 11.D: 2019 flooring replacement program.** The resolution awards flooring replacement work as set out in the attached schedule, as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Fund: Conventional Carpet, Inc. at $829,598.03, Kuhn Specialty Flooring at $112,500.00, additional and emergency flooring at $15,000.00, and a contingency of $11,250.00, for a total of $968,348.03.

**Business 11.E: Early Childhood Center signage.** The resolution awards the bid for signage for the Early Childhood Center to ASI Sign in the amount of $30,827.94.

Taken together the five business items commit well over two million dollars of capital work in a single January meeting — the flooring and roofing programs alone account for $968,348.03 and $860,333.10 — drawn across the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, the Building Site and Sinking Fund and the Early Childhood Center accounts, and set against a backdrop in which the district was simultaneously completing the new preschool and preparing the third series of its 2013 bond.

**Other.** Item 13.A adopts the 2019 Board committee assignments. Item 13.B is a first reading of revisions to board policies, which return for second reading and adoption at the following meeting.

**Meeting**

**Agenda**
1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Public Communication; 3. Board Candidate Selection (packet page 3); 4. Other; 5. Closed Session — Consideration: Negotiations (packet page 54); 6. Adjournment. Items need not be taken in the order shown; consent agenda items are acted on at one time unless removed.

**The vacancy and the process**
Item 3.A, Board Member Nominations and Appointment, recites that due to the resignation of Mrs. Paula Fleming on January 21, 2020 the Board must appoint an individual to serve through the end of Mrs. Fleming's term of office, ending December 31, 2020. The Board president accepts nominations from Board members, and individual Board members may not nominate more than one candidate. Blank nomination lines are provided for a first, second and third nominee; the president then asks for further nominations, pauses, and closes nominations. Roll-call sheets with YES and NO lines follow for each nominee, with the member order rotating across Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Gottlieb. A suggested resolution with Moved by / Supported by lines reads: "Be It Therefore Resolved that ____ be appointed to fill the vacancy on the Board of Education for the term expiring December 31, 2020," voted by roll call beginning with Schmidt. No results, nominators or appointee are recorded in the document.

**Candidate materials**

| Candidate | Packet page | Snapshot from the questionnaire |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emina Alic | 6 | Divider page only; no extracted text in the source |
| Vital Anne | 12 | Vice-President of Software Integrity and Testing at Altair; in Troy 16 years |
| Tim Burns | 21 | Criminal defense attorney; Oakland County Commissioner 2007-2011 |
| Russell Reynolds | 26 | Billing and accounting analyst at Shift Digital, Birmingham |
| Tony Sarna | 32 | Troy High graduate; co-owner of three technology businesses |
| Srinivas Simhan | 39 | Software developer at Blue Cross Blue Shield; FRC Team 226 mentor |
| Barrington Wilkins | 43 | Attorney, U.S. Attorney's Office in Detroit |
| Lisa Zheng | 47 | Stanford MS EE and Wharton MBA; investment and consulting background |

## Resolution 13-077 — School Improvement Bond Proposition
The proposition (Exhibit A) goes to a Special School Election on November 5, 2013, certified to the Election Coordinator on or before August 27, 2013, not less than seventy (70) days prior, under the Michigan Election Law, Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954. Ballot terms: borrow not to exceed One Hundred Twenty Five Million ($125,000,000) Dollars in general obligation unlimited tax bonds to remodel, equip, re-equip, furnish and re-furnish buildings to enhance security; acquire and install technology equipment and technology infrastructure; construct additions; and improve sites plus purchase school buses. Maximum term not more than fifteen (15) years exclusive of refunding; estimated millage in the first year 1.84 mills ($1.84 per $1,000 of taxable value); estimated simple average annual millage to retire the bonds 2.93 mills ($2.93 per $1,000 of taxable value). The bonds would be guaranteed under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program, against $93,605,000 of qualified bonds outstanding and $0 of qualified loans; proceeds cannot be used for salaries, repair or maintenance costs or other operating expenses. Adopted Yes 7 / No 0, certified by Paula Fleming under the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Members discussed Detroit's recent bankruptcy filing and its possible effect on surrounding districts and bond sales.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 26, 2019 at the Services Building. It sets the district's enrollment posture for 2019-2020 — closing Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park and both high schools to open enrollment except for up to 25 incoming ninth graders transferring to Athens, while opening a limited Schools of Choice program for 50 kindergarten, one first grade and 20 middle school seats — and awards the two largest remaining pieces of the new preschool: $702,576.00 of playground construction to Rolar, Inc. and $482,495.76 of furnishings. It also carries the December 2018 Treasurer's Report with total disbursements in period of $8,420,287.20.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Regular meeting, February 26, 2019, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Three items: the Fall 2018 All-State Athletes; a Mission Moment on elementary student artwork created for the new TSD Preschool; and Principal Appreciation Month.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the January 8 workshop and the January 15 organizational and regular meeting, the December 2018 Treasurer's Report, and second reading and adoption of new and revised board policies reviewed by the Board Policy Committee for compliance with the Revised School Code.

**Treasurer's Report — December 2018**
General Fund check disbursements total $4,103,654.39 and total disbursements in period are $8,420,287.20. At December 31, 2018 the General Fund balance stands at $18,641,192, consolidated Debt Service at $8,096,255 and consolidated Special Revenue at $2,454,680.

**Curriculum — who may enroll in 2019-2020**
Dr. Machesky presents enrollment projections for 2019-2020 and beyond, built on an analysis of the district's enrollment history prepared by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants.

On the strength of those projections, administration recommends closing several buildings to open enrollment. Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park are closed on total enrollment and physical space constraints. Athens and Troy High have been closed for several years as the district works to maximize each building's enrollment, and both are closed again — with one exception: **not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students who live in the Troy High attendance area but wish to attend Athens**, with applications accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March. Students with siblings already at Athens or Troy High in grades 9 through 11 may open enroll to remain for the year.

Separately, and in the opposite direction, the Board adopts the annual Schools of Choice resolution required by state law. Under Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, the district will accept applications for a limited program for 2019-2020 covering **50 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 20 total 6th-8th grade nonresident students** at Baker, Larson and Smith middle schools, open to students from districts within or outside Oakland County where that intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD boundaries.

**Business — finishing the preschool**
RFP 9873, Bid Pack 5 of the Early Childcare Center project, sought competitive bids for playground area construction — site construction, playground equipment and site amenities for the new building. Five bidders responded, and Rob Carson and Barton Malow recommend Rolar, Inc. on low bid for its category, including four alternates, at $702,576.00 from the Early Childcare Center Fund.

Furnishings for the preschool were sourced and priced through cooperative bid contracts and reviewed by Rob Carson, Kris Griffor, Erin Keyser and TMP Architecture, awarded at $482,495.76 from the Early Childhood Center Fund with the resolution made part of the official minutes.

**Other**
The Board casts its ballot in the 2019 MASB Board of Directors' election for Region 8, a three-year term with one seat. The candidates are Joshua Denzler (Lake Shore Public Schools, Macomb County), **Steve Gottlieb (Troy School District, Oakland County)**, Birgit McQuiston (Lake Orion Community Schools), Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. (Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County), Angie Smith (Farmington Public Schools), Michael Swiecki (Wyandotte Public Schools, Wayne County) and Regina Williams (Harper Woods School District, Wayne County).

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, February 26, 2019, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. All-State Athletes Fall 2018, B. Mission Moment: Elementary Student Artwork for TSD Preschool, C. Principal Appreciation Month; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the January 8, 2019 workshop, B. Minutes of the January 15, 2019 organizational and regular meeting, C. Treasurer's Report – December 2018, D. Second Reading and Adoption of New/Revised Board Policies; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: Enrollment Projections, B. Consideration: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment, C. Report: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C, D. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C; 8. Business — A. TSD Preschool Playground, B. TSD Preschool Furniture; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. 2019 MASB Board of Directors' Election; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition.** The evening opens with recognition of the All-State Athletes for Fall 2018, a Mission Moment featuring elementary student artwork created for the new Troy School District Preschool, and Principal Appreciation Month.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the January 8, 2019 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 15, 2019 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for December 2018; and second reading and adoption of new and revised board policies. The policy item records that members of the Board Policy Committee reviewed the listed policies against the Revised School Code and that the first reading of the revised and additional policies was conducted at the prior meeting.

**Treasurer's Report, December 2018.** General Fund check disbursements total $4,103,654.39, and total disbursements in period — check disbursements together with ACH debits, outgoing wire transfers, P-Card purchases and prior period void disbursements — come to $8,420,287.20. The summary revenue and expense budget reports for the period ending December 31, 2018 give a General Fund balance of $18,641,192, a consolidated Debt Service Funds balance of $8,096,255 and a consolidated Special Revenue Funds balance of $2,454,680. The middle sections of the packet carry the December check register run by fund.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents to the Board on enrollment projections for the 2019-2020 school year and beyond. The analysis of the district's enrollment history and projections was provided by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2019-2020.** Administration reports having reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park schools be closed to open enrollment. It notes that the district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years, and that based on current projections for 2019-2020 both should be closed again — with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Applications for those twenty-five spots at Athens will be accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March.

The resolution closes Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2019-2020 school year, with that twenty-five-student exception, and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High who are currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2019-2020 school year.

**Curriculum 7.C and 7.D: Schools of Choice under Sections 105 and 105c.** A report precedes the resolution. In accordance with Michigan state law, school districts must pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. The item anticipates that a limited number of seats will be available for 2019-2020 for kindergarten, first grade, and grades six through eight at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools, and proposes a resolution for fifty kindergarten, one first grade, and twenty total sixth through eighth grade nonresident students who attend a school district within or outside of Oakland County, provided that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

The resolution accordingly provides that the Board of Education, exercising the option permitted by Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2019-2020 school year for fifty kindergarten, one first grade and twenty total sixth through eighth grade nonresident students on those terms. Read alongside item 7.B, the two resolutions set the district's enrollment posture from both directions in a single meeting: closing the buildings under space pressure while opening a bounded number of seats where capacity exists.

**Business 8.A: preschool playground.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on playground area construction as part of the Troy School District Preschool project, with responses reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and Barton Malow Company. Rob Carson's February 21, 2019 memorandum to Rick West, covering RFP 9873, Bid Pack 5 of the ECC Building Project, records that the RFP produced five bidders and that the scope of work is site construction, playground equipment and site amenities for the new Early Childcare Center building, with an attached bid summary detailing four alternates he recommends as part of the RFP. He recommends, on low bid for the category, category 116000 Playground Equipment to Rolar, Inc. including alternates A1, A2, A3 and A4 at $702,576.00. The resolution awards the playground area construction to Rolar, Inc. in the amount of $702,576.00 as an expenditure of the Early Childcare Center Fund.

**Business 8.B: preschool furnishings.** Quotations were received for competitive pricing on furnishings for the Troy School District Preschool. The recommended items were sourced and priced through cooperative bid contracts and reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations; Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction; Erin Keyser, Director of Early Childhood Programs; and TMP Architecture. The resolution awards the furnishings as attached in the amount of $482,495.76 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund, with the resolution made a part of the official minutes of the February 26, 2019 regular meeting; the attached award schedule assigns vendors by category on low bid.

**Other 10.A: 2019 MASB Board of Directors' election.** Biographical data for the candidates is attached for the Board's review. The Region 8 seat is a three-year term with one seat, and the candidates are Joshua Denzler of Lake Shore Public Schools in Macomb County; Steve Gottlieb of the Troy School District, Oakland County; Birgit McQuiston of Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County; Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. of Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County; Angie Smith of Farmington Public Schools, Oakland County; Michael Swiecki of Wyandotte Public Schools, Wayne County; and Regina Williams of Harper Woods School District, Wayne County. The resolution casts the Troy Board of Education's ballot for one candidate to serve on the 2019 Michigan Association of School Boards' Board of Directors for the Region 8 three-year term — an election in which one of the district's own trustees, Steve Gottlieb, is a candidate.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, October 16, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois — ending in closed session on attorney-client privilege.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment invites Athens parents and district teachers Dawn and Mark Hayes to tell the story of how their special-needs daughter Allie was asked to be this year's Grand Marshall of the Athens Homecoming Parade.

The Board then commends **54 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists**. More than a million students from some 22,000 high schools entered the program nationwide and only 16,000 seniors are selected; semifinalists score in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT and earn comparable SAT scores. The packet prints the roster with phonetic pronunciation guides beside most names, for reading aloud. Copies of the resolution go to the students at an October 30 reception.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the September 4 workshop and the September 18 meeting, the August 2018 Treasurer's Report, the Sex Education Advisory Board membership, the revised Code of Conduct and the Oakland Schools PAC representative.

The Sex Education Advisory Board is co-chaired by Kristy Pierce and Nicole Jenkins; by statute at least half its members must be parents and one parent must co-chair. Janet Grieme and Toina Wilson serve as Troy's parent representatives to the Oakland Schools special education Parent Advisory Committee, which participates in developing and reviewing the county plan for delivery of special education programs and services.

**What the September 18 minutes record**
Hammond and Miletti were absent, so everything carried 5-0. Twelve spring all-state athletes were recognized, all in girls' sports. The Mission Moment honored Troy Center for Transition students who spent the summer at the Technology Resource Center: TRC collected every district-owned iPad and **replaced 5,000 at the elementary level, handling almost 15,000 iPads in all**, and the TCT students uncased, cleaned, de-stickered and re-cased them at a rate the TRC team struggled to keep up with. The district also received ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the CAFR for fiscal year ended June 30, 2017, and three MASB awards: Karl Schmidt's Master Board Member Award (a minimum of 368 education credits), Elizabeth Hammond's Level One Certification, and Gary Hauff's 20 Years of Service.

Mark Dziatczak's enrollment update as of September 12, 2018: **elementary down 61, middle school up 91, high school down 26 — the district up 4 students overall** against the same point the prior year.

And resolution 18-075 sold the Section 1 front parcel: 5.95 +/- acres plus up to an additional 1.74 +/- acres for a detention pond, to **Mondrian Properties for $1,974,000.00 plus an additional $40,000.00 for each unit over 24 approved by the City of Troy**, with a $25,000.00 earnest money deposit — the same buyer that took the Section 16 land in March, and the second half of the Section 1 plan adopted 4-2 that same month. The remaining land, including 11.28 +/- acres at Sidwell 20-01-451-001, is designated the Conservation Property.

**Treasurer's Report — August 2018**
Total check disbursements are $9,488,186.13, the General Fund group $4,846,208.08 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,614,275.55. With $1,612,398.21 of wire transfers, $205,054.03 of P-Card purchases and $16,089.81 of ACH debits, less $10,486.00 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,311,242.18.

**Curriculum — the gap analysis**
Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor report on 3rd grade reading and gap analysis. On combined grades 3-8 M-STEP for 2017-18, Troy is at **73% ELA, 48% math, 55% science and 44% social studies**, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 51%, 36%, 33% and 27% and Michigan at 44%, 33%, 24% and 27% respectively. By grade, Troy's ELA runs 73%, 73%, 77%, 73%, 73% and 68% across grades 3 through 8. On the 2017-18 PSAT and SAT, Troy posts 84% on PSAT ELA grade 9, 80% on grade 10 and 79% on SAT ELA 11, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 70%, 69% and 67%. Ranked across the 28 Oakland LEAs, Troy sits at or within two places of the top on every measure shown.

**Business — the audit**
David Youngstrom, audit partner at Yeo & Yeo, reports an **unmodified opinion**, the highest level of assurance, on the June 30, 2018 financial statements, with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies and no material noncompliance — and unmodified opinions on both federal major programs, the Child Nutrition Cluster and the Special Education Cluster.

General Fund revenue for the year: state $101,977,419 (67%), local $38,844,065 (26%), interdistrict sources $7,537,593 (5%) and federal $3,333,254 (2%). Expenditures: salaries $73,741,957 (49%), employee benefits $48,780,644 (32%), purchased services $19,695,836 (13%), supplies and materials $6,053,649 (4%) and other $1,980,625 (1%) — or by function, instruction $104,214,738 (69%) and supporting services $46,452,918 (31%), holding at 69% instructional for the third straight year against an Oakland County average of 64%.

Per-pupil General Fund revenue has risen from $10,641 in 2013 to $11,596 in 2018, with expenses at $11,516 — revenue exceeding expense in each of the last several years by a narrowing margin. The unassigned General Fund balance is between 14.74% and 16.52% of expenditures across 2014-2018. Enrollment over ten years runs 12,177 (2009) down to 12,032 and back up to **13,089 in 2018**.

Management comments carry federal procedures forward from the prior year as in progress, note time and effort record keeping as corrected, and raise federal procedures and athletic receipt procedures for the current year. Future challenges named: the state economic and political condition, rising fringe benefit costs, the retirement rate increase, **a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M**.

**Consent minutes: the September 18, 2018 regular meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff and Philippart were present; Mrs. Hammond and Mr. Miletti were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky, administrators Carrier, Gottlieb, Fulcher, Griffor, Dziatczak, Harris, Soggs and West, and approximately 60 additional members of the audience. Every vote carried 5-0 with two absences.

Mr. Fulcher and the Board recognized the 2018 spring all-state athletes: Angela Anderanin (girls tennis), Paige Anderson (girls track), Tahra Brodbine (girls soccer), Jenna Doyle (girls track), Lauren Fulcher (girls track), Grace Johnson (girls track), Morgan MacDonald (girls lacrosse), Lauren Miller (girls soccer), Hanna Palomino (girls track), Sahaja Pinnu (girls tennis), Hailey Stewart (girls soccer) and Megan Worrel (girls track).

The Mission Moment recognized Troy Center for Transition students for their summer work at the Technology Resource Center. TRC collected all district-owned iPads over the summer and replaced 5,000 iPads at the elementary level, a project that required TRC staff to handle almost 15,000 iPads. Beth Soggs described how students from the Troy Center for Transition played an enormous part in the successful completion of the project, volunteering for weeks on end to help with uncasing iPads, cleaning the devices, removing stickers, putting new cases on, sorting charging bricks and cables, and "providing us daily with great company and an abundant supply of smiles." The minutes record that the students displayed amazing work ethic, showed up each day ready to work, and plowed through iPads at a rate that was difficult for the TRC team to keep up with a steady supply for them to case; the TRC team felt extremely fortunate to have established the relationship and looked forward to partnering again. Recognized were Emily Bernacki, Charley Mapes, Erin O'Donovan, Jared Weinberg, Phil Chu, Johnathan Kim, Alec Watson and Megan Daley.

The Association of School Business Officials International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the district for excellence in the preparation and issuance of a high quality Comprehensive Annual Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2017; Rick West and his staff were recognized. Three Michigan Association of School Boards awards were also presented: Board President Karl Schmidt achieved the MASB Master Board Member Award, which requires a minimum of 368 education credits; Trustee Elizabeth Hammond received Level One Certification for completing the CBA Program requirements; and Board Secretary Gary Hauff was recognized for 20 Years of Dedicated Service on the Board. The minutes note that these honors place the Troy Board among a handful of Michigan school district governing bodies that have demonstrated a true commitment to student achievement and exemplary leadership.

President Schmidt introduced the 2018-2019 high school student representatives, the first of them Lauryn Collins of International Academy East, a junior active in the Black Student Association, Interact Program, Poetry Club, Symphony Orchestra and the Athens girls swim and dive team, whose stated goals are swimming in the Olympics and a career as a pediatric surgeon.
