The middle sections of the packet are the September check register run by fund.

**Consent item 5.E: Consumers Energy Company easement, Boulan Park Middle School.** Consumers Energy Company has requested an easement on the Boulan Park Middle School property. The resolution recites that Consumers Energy desires to construct, operate, maintain, inspect, survey, replace, reconstruct, improve, remove, relocate, change the size of, enlarge and protect a pipeline or pipelines in, on, under, over, across and through a portion of the parcel owned by the Troy School District, the County of Oakland and the State of Michigan, commonly known as Boulan Park Middle School; that in order to obtain access for those purposes the district desires to grant Consumers Energy a permanent easement on terms substantially similar to those in the attached Easement Agreement; and that the district wishes to authorize Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., to execute it. The operative resolution so authorizes him.

The attached agreement is captioned Easement for Pipelines, Coolidge & Golf View Scada Pressure Monitor, SAP# 32537548, Master Tract# TRN000916037635, Agreement# MI00000038782, with the owner identified as The School District of the City of Troy, of 4400 Livernois. The naming — a SCADA pressure monitor at Coolidge and Golf View — indicates the easement is for utility monitoring equipment rather than a transmission line crossing.

**Personnel 6.A: Assistant Principal, Smith Middle School.** The recommendation is Ms. Kimberly Cornelissen. She started her education career as a fourth grade teacher at Wass Elementary and also served as a Summer Success Academy teacher from June 2014 through July 2016. During her professional career she has been a member of the Wass Elementary Leadership Team, attended the Aspiring Principals' Leadership Academy at Oakland Schools as a Troy School District representative, and acted as a Continuous School Improvement Team member for Wass Elementary. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Special Education from Michigan State University and a Master of Arts in K-12 Educational Administration from Michigan State University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, with duties beginning Monday, December 3, 2018.

Unusually, the packet publishes the full selection funnel. There were 148 applications submitted. Of those 148 applicants, seventeen were granted first round interviews: Jessica Blumer, Kimberly Cornelissen, Shannon Feliciano, Scott Germansky, Patrick Griffin, LaDonna Hunter, Megan Koslowski, Zack MacIntosh, Kristin Martin, Matt Provost, Taylor Richey, Steve Robinson, Catherine Sovone, Laura Schlitt, Kelly Smith, Andrea Steaban and Mike Woodberg. Of the seventeen, two moved to the final round — Kimberly Cornelissen and Laura Schlitt — with Cornelissen the final selection. Several of the seventeen are the district's own people: Jessica Blumer had been hired as an elementary resource room teacher at Bemis in the August 2018 class, and Zack MacIntosh was among the 36 Outstanding Teacher nominees recognized in April.

This is the vacancy created by the chain of moves in May: Tim Fulcher left the Smith principalship for the athletics directorship, Christian Mueller came from Utica to fill it, and the assistant principalship it left behind is filled here.

**Business 8.A: Troy High School sign refurbishment.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Troy High School, reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations. Carson's November 8, 2018 memorandum on RFP 9866 records that the scope of work is to provide labor and materials to replace the electronic message center, school logos and aluminum skirting on the school sign at the Long Lake entrance as detailed in the bid specifications; that on October 30 five bids were opened, which resulted in Signarama of Troy being identified as the low qualified bidder; and that having reviewed Signarama's bid he recommends they be awarded the work. He requests a total project cost of $21,739.30, consisting of the base bid of $19,763.00 and a 10% contingency of $1,976.30, funded from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The resolution awards the Troy High School sign refurbishment to Signarama of Troy in the amount of $21,739.30 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business 8.B: purchase agreement, Boyd Street property.** The resolution recites that the School District desires to sell a parcel described as the easterly 6.00 feet of Lot 27, "Beaver Run Subdivision," a part of the southwest quarter of Section 23, Town 2 North, Range 11 East, City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, as recorded in Liber 46 of plats on page 27, Oakland County Records; that the district has received an Offer To Purchase from Delmar Homes at a purchase price of Ten Thousand and 00/100 ($10,000.00) Dollars; and that the district has reviewed the Offer and is desirous of accepting it. The resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to the Offer and authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to execute it.

The certification block beneath the resolution recites a regular meeting "held on the 16th day of October, 2018" and the Exhibit A cover sheet names Madhu Babu Jampala — both carried over unrevised from the previous month's Wattles Road item. The resolution text itself is unambiguous: the Boyd Street strip, Delmar Homes, $10,000.00.

This is the district's fourth land transaction of 2018 and by far the smallest. Section 16 went to Mondrian Properties in March; the Section 1 front parcel went to the same buyer with a per-unit escalator in September; the Wattles Road parcel went to an individual in October; and here a six-foot-wide strip of frontage goes to a homebuilder for $10,000.00 — a lot-line adjustment rather than a development sale, and the tail end of a year in which the district systematically cleared its surplus real estate.

Read as a whole, the November 2018 packet is a short meeting between two long ones. Its one substantive personnel action fills the last vacancy in the spring's chain of administrative moves, and its two business items — a $21,739.30 sign and a $10,000.00 strip of land — are the smallest dollar figures the Board acted on all year, in a year whose other resolutions ran to millions of dollars of construction and borrowing.

**Item 7.A, Enrollment Projections.** Dr. Machesky presents analysis by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D., of STANFRED Consultants. Head counts exclude 235 students in ECP, SCSE and GROW, and all projections assume 100 SOC kindergarten and 50 SOC first grade students. Schools of Choice enrollment ran 287 in Fall 2009/10, 416 in 2010/11, 590 in 2011/12, 700 in 2012/13, 821 in 2013/14 and 907 in 2014/15. K-5 moved from 5,230 in 1997/98 to 4,964 in 2004/05 and back to 5,398 in 2014/15, with 2019/20 outcomes of 5,468 high, 5,130 most likely and 4,798 low. Grades 6-8 stood at 2,811, projected to 3,193, 3,070 or 2,950; grades 9-12 stood at 4,100, projected to 4,441, 4,187 or 3,935. K-12 head count was 11,841 in 2000/01 and 11,955 in 2009/10, reaching 12,309 in 2014/15, projected to 13,102, 12,387 or 11,674 by 2019/20. Projected totals excluding SCSE/ECP/GROW run 12,227, 12,142, 12,055, 12,003 and 12,031 across 2015/16 to 2019/20, or 12,462, 12,377, 12,290, 12,238 and 12,226 including the 235. Comparisons show 2013/14 projected 12,494 against actual 12,573, and 2014/15 projected 12,653 against actual 12,556.

**Items 7.B and 7.C, curriculum reports.** Mrs. Haezebrouck reports on the three-year pilot of Reading Recovery, Kinder-Core and Teaching and Learning Leaders begun in 2013-2014. Reading Recovery teacher representatives are Natalie Haezebrouck, Heidi Palaj, Joni Gabriel and Trudy Motzenbecker; Teaching and Learning Leaders are Carol Machak, Kaity ORiordan and Shari Pawlus. Training of two Reading Recovery teachers serving Leonard and Wattles moves from weekly and year-long with four half days of Kinder-Core PD to monthly with LLI in kindergarten and two half days; the teacher lab expands to all third grade teachers, and a typical day serves four first graders. Other initiatives include Hamilton reading instruction for grades K-3 and work with 34 teachers bridging sixth grade general and special education math support. District Science Coordinator Jessica Ashley with biology teachers Andrea Bolterstein and Jennifer Sprague present "Biotechnology in OneTroy 2014-2015" on Technology Bond equipment including autoclaves, centrifuges, digital micropipettes, spectrophotometer, microscopes and MiniOne Systems, involving Richard Chan from The MiniOne System and roughly 1,000 freshmen biology students in pipetting, gel loading and PTC gene labs aligned to NGSS.

**Item 8.A, Smith Middle School and Niles School remodeling.** Bids were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance and Operations, 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083, 248.823.4050; Doug Madden of Barton Malow; and Michelle Kerns, Owners Representative. RFP Bid 9804 was issued February 16, 2015 for Smith gymnasium and locker room bleachers, electrical and lighting upgrades and painted finishes, and Niles restroom fixture and lighting replacement. Low bids awarded from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund are category 061000 General Trades to Advanced Building Group at $154,000.00, category 096400 Wood Flooring to Foster Specialty Floors at $41,940.00, category 126600 Telescopic Stands to Interkal at $22,546.00, category 230000 Mechanical to Contrast Mechanical at $21,700.00 and category 260000 Electrical to Metro Electric at $68,300.00, totaling $308,486.00. Competing bids included E&L Construction Group at $194,700.00, Heritage at $199,500.00, Construction Solutions at $211,700.00, Kiefer Specialty Flooring at $42,555.00 and Irwin Seating Company at $24,859.00; Advanced Building Group's alternate to paint locker interiors adds $16,300.00.

**Item 8.B, Data Storage and Backup Solution.** Kris Young, Director of Technology, John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners and Rick West recommend awarding the contract to EMC/Presidio for $469,750.00 from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund. The April 1, 2015 letter from Convergent Technology Partners, 801 S. Saginaw Suite 505, Flint, MI 48502, signed by John C. Foster, RCDD, President and Kristie Young, notes five years of maintenance and configuration for 5% growth over each of the next five years. The existing EMC system, purchased three years ago, carries approximately $345,000 due this year rising roughly 15% annually; the new system starts at approximately $50,000 per year in year six. VMAXe five-year cost totals $1,956,185 against XtremIO at $399,750 after a $150,000 trade-in on $549,750, a total cost of ownership of $1,556,435; backup maintenance totals $154,292 estimated against $90,000 proposed, a TCO of $64,292. Storage at $399,750.00 plus backup at $90,000.00 gives $489,750.00 less a $20,000.00 bundle discount. WSCA pricing on a $907,195.00 list gives $657,716.38 at 27.5% and $399,750.00 at a total 55% discount. XtremIO offers 20.00TB raw and 17.00TB useable capacity and up to 150,000 IOPS; the backup appliance is 24 TB with Data Domain DD Boost.

**Item 10.A, Bond Projects Update.** Barton Malow and TMP report on the 2013 Bond Program Series 1: Troy High School classroom and storage additions and Boulan Park and Larson office additions completing around December 2015, and the Athens LGI and multi-use classroom renovation in spring 2015. BP #8 Athens mechanical and electrical upgrades and BP #11 International Academy East pool-to-LGI conversion go out for bids August 2015; BP #9 Larson and Boulan mechanical, electrical and site paving bids were due April 7, 2015; BP #13 Smith and Niles contracts are awarded April 14, 2015.

**Items 10.B through 10.E, board policies.** First readings cover B-1210 Closed Session, which requires five affirmative roll call votes except for purposes 1, 2 and 3, lists seven permitted purposes, cites Section 10, 11 or 13 of Act No. 267, Public Acts 1976, destroys closed session minutes one year and one day after approval, and was adopted April 8, 1975 and revised March 15, 1977, March 17, 1998 and April 15, 2003; B-1301 Agenda Format, revised April 20, 2010; and B-1401 Minutes, requiring proposed minutes within eight business days and approved minutes within five, compliance with the Michigan Freedom of Information Act, Act No. 442, PA 1976, and official minutes bound in the vault at the administrative office, revised April 17, 2012. A separate first reading amends J-2012 Anti-Bullying Policy, adopted June 5, 2012 and revised May 6, 2014, for cyberbullying under Michigan Public Act 478 Revised School Code, referencing Section 219a of the Michigan Penal Code, 1931 PA 328, MCL 750.219a. Second readings and adoption cover B-0102 Board Members' Term of Office, setting six-year terms beginning with the November 2016 general school election and even years thereafter, adopted January 15, 2008; B-1202 Place of Meeting, adding twenty-four hours advance notice; B-1204 Quorum, setting four members as a quorum and permitting non-voting remote participation subject to the Open Meetings Act, MCL 15.261 et seq., revised July 10, 2012; and B-1211 Public Participation, limiting participation to 60 minutes per Board meeting in place of two 30-minute segments, requiring Speaker Request Forms available 30 minutes prior to the meeting, and allowing up to three minutes per speaker with no transfer of time.

Actions, all Yes 7, No 0: 16-044 approved the May 3 and May 17, 2016 minutes; 16-045 ratified the tentative agreement reached May 25, 2016 with the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA for July 1, 2016 through June 30, 2017; 16-046 approved new hires Stephanie Pilarski, Michael Thomas, Alyssa Kay, Elizabeth Twentyman, Kathryn Starn and Duane Goulbourne; 16-047 appointed Dan Mills assistant principal at Athens High School and 16-048 appointed Mike Cottone principal at Troy Union Elementary School, each on a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure beginning July 1, 2016; 16-049 set the public hearing on the proposed 2016-2017 budget for June 21, 2016 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, with notice at least six days beforehand carrying in 11-point bold faced type the statement that the property tax millage rate proposed to be levied to support the proposed budget will be a subject of the hearing, and Exhibit A making copies available at the Administration Building from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. June 15 through June 21, 2016, signed by Secretary Paula Fleming; and 16-050 accepted the MASB-SEG Property/Casualty Pool proposal effective July 1, 2016, not to exceed $276,715.00. Dr. Machesky reported 112 Troy graduates at the International Academy graduation. Adjourned 9:09 p.m.

## June 14, 2016
The special meeting opened at 5:02 p.m. in the Administration Building with Schmidt absent. Resolution 16-051 awarded sidewalk and concrete replacement to Luigi Ferdinandi & Son, not to exceed the annual budgeted amount, from the 2014 Capital Projects Fund; 16-052 awarded interior painting to Paint Plus, Inc. in the amount of $65,000 inclusive of contingency, plus future work at bid hourly rates, from the 2014 Capital Maintenance Fund; both Yes 6, No 0. 16-053 moved a closed session on superintendent evaluation at 5:15 p.m.; adjourned 6:45 p.m. The board workshop followed at 6:50 p.m. with consultant Bill Bowman of Great Northern, covering the Section 1 property, the May cash position and budget report, the 2015/2016 final budget amendment and proposed 2016/2017 budget, summer learning, ELD, MHSAA eligibility and early childhood; adjourned 10:45 p.m.

## June 21, 2016
The special meeting convened at the Services Building at 5:45 p.m. with attorney Gary Collins of Collins & Blaha; closed session 5:46 p.m., adjourned 6:40 p.m. The regular meeting opened with the public hearing on the proposed 2016-2017 budget at 7:00 p.m.; Rick West presented tax values, homestead and non-homestead forecasts, the foundation allowance, the increase in student enrollment, and general fund revenues and expenditures. No audience member spoke; the hearing closed at 7:18 p.m. Approximately 60 people attended. Recognitions covered retiring School Life Troy photographer Ed Morykwas, with publisher Raad Alawan presenting a certificate; a School Year in Review video from Kerry Birmingham, Director of Communications and Strategic Initiatives; Mina Mori of the Wayne State University Center for Peace and Conflict Studies, whose "Discovering Japan in the 21st Century" program guided seven teachers and two board members for ten days in Japan, with a certificate presented by Brenda Carter, President-Elect of the Michigan Association of School Boards; fourth-year Spirit of Diversity Awards from the Troy Diversity & Inclusion Council; and Dr. Machesky's selection as a National School Public Relations Association 2016 "Superintendent to Watch," recognizing fewer than 25 superintendents nationally.

Actions: 16-054 approved the Treasurer's Report for April 2016; 16-055 approved new hires Brittany Beylerian, Julia Alder, Katherine Eve, Katherine Kolber, Laura Ferris and Lauren Brown; 16-056 extended the Superintendent's contract from July 1, 2016 through June 30, 2018 without tenure; 16-057 extended contracts through June 30, 2018 without tenure for Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent for Teaching and Learning, Rick West, Assistant Superintendent Business Services, Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent Elementary Instruction, and Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent Employee Services. Christin Silagy updated the board on the ELD program, WIDA alignment and the EL Handbook.

Resolution 16-058 amended the 2015/2016 general appropriations: General Fund $142,161,937; Food Service Fund $3,182,130; Troy Career Center Fund $2,103,221; Adult Education/Community Service Fund $5,239,522; Facility Rental Fund $1,300; Debt Service Funds $16,635,088; Capital Projects Fund $19,540,000; Capital Maintenance Fund $300,000. **Meeting**
Regular meeting, March 19, 2019, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment honors a Prudential Spirit of Community Award recipient, and the Board recognizes Wass Elementary School as a State School of Character.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the February 5 workshop and February 26 meeting, the January 2019 Treasurer's Report, and an ancillary funds budget amendment.

**Treasurer's Report — January 2019**
General Fund check disbursements total $4,980,973.78 and total disbursements in period are $10,412,414.95. At January 31, 2019 the General Fund balance stands at $22,442,908, consolidated Debt Service at $11,713,241 and consolidated Special Revenue at $2,630,135.

**The 2018-19 budget amendment**
The resolution amends the general appropriations and budget for fiscal 2018-19 across ten funds, each a first amendment: Food Service, Troy Career Center, Adult Education and Community Service, Troy School District Preschool, Facilities Rental, Capital Maintenance, the 2014 Capital Projects Fund, the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, the Early Childhood Learning Center Capital Projects Fund and the Sinking Fund Capital Projects Fund. The Food Service Fund is amended to $4,244,139. The packet notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes.

**8.C — the third bond series**
The $125,000,000 bond issue was approved by voters on November 5, 2013, and the district now proceeds with the third series, not to exceed $27,000,000, designated the "2019 School Building and Site Bonds" (unlimited tax general obligation). Dr. Richard Machesky and Rick West are the individuals authorized to accept a purchase offer on the bonds. The attached authorizing resolution recites that the 2013 proposal permitted issuance in one or more series for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings and other facilities to enhance security; acquiring and installing technology equipment and infrastructure; constructing additions; preparing, developing and improving sites; and purchasing school buses — and that under Section 6 and Section 16 of Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount.

**Remaining business**
Districtwide site work projects are awarded to Asphalt Specialists, Inc. at $822,140.00 from the Building and Site Sinking Fund, with a bid tabulation attached. Asbestos abatement is awarded to Trust Thermal Abatement at $288,420.00, supported by a bid tabulation and a NOVA Environmental contractor award recommendation listing bids by building. Cabling infrastructure for the Troy School District Preschool is awarded to Complete Interactive Technologies at $59,905.31, and aquatic sports timing equipment for Athens rounds out the business items. A personnel item covers elementary and secondary appointments.

**Treasurer's Report, January 2019.** Rick West transmits the check register including current period voids, together with listings of ACH debits, wire transfers and P-Card purchases, certifying that the disbursements were payments made for obligations of the Troy School District and that all materials or services listed on the invoices have been received or performed. The summary revenue and expense budget reports for the period ending January 31, 2019 give a General Fund balance of $22,442,908, a consolidated Debt Service Funds balance of $11,713,241 and a consolidated Special Revenue Funds balance of $2,630,135. The bulk of the packet's middle sections is the January check register itself, run by fund.

**Consent item: 2018-19 budget amendment resolution.** The attached Budget Amendment Resolution for the 2018-19 fiscal year covers ten funds, each receiving its first amendment of the year: the Food Service Fund, the Troy Career Center Fund, the Adult Education and Community Service Fund, the Troy School District Preschool Fund, the Facilities Rental Fund, the Capital Maintenance Fund, the 2014 Capital Projects Fund, the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, the Early Childhood Learning Center Capital Projects Fund and the Sinking Fund Capital Projects Fund. The item notes that the resolution does not have to be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. The resolution resolves that the general appropriations and budget of the Troy School District for fiscal year 2018-19 for those funds be amended and approved as attached and made part of the official minutes of the March 19, 2019 regular meeting; the Food Service Fund figure is 4,244,139.

**Personnel.** Item 6.A is a consideration of elementary and secondary personnel recommendations.

**Business 8.A: districtwide site work projects.** The resolution awards the bid for site work projects to Asphalt Specialists, Inc. in the amount of $822,140.00 as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund, with a bid tabulation attached listing bid packages, companies and total costs for competing vendors.

**Business 8.B: districtwide asbestos abatement.** The resolution awards the bid for asbestos abatement to Trust Thermal Abatement in the amount of $288,420.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund and the Building and Site Sinking Fund. The supporting material includes an asbestos abatement bid tabulation organized by bid number, buildings, contractor and bid amount, and a NOVA Environmental contractor award recommendation.

**Business 8.C: the 2019 School Building and Site Bonds.** The item records that the $125,000,000 bond issue was passed by the voters on November 5, 2013, that the district wishes to proceed with issuing the third series of bonds in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000, and that Dr. Richard Machesky and Rick West will be the individuals authorized to accept a purchase offer on the bonds. The resolution authorizes the issuance of bonds designated the "2019 School Building and Site Bonds" in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000, with the attached resolution in its entirety made a part of the official minutes of the March 19, 2019 regular meeting.

The attached authorizing resolution is captioned Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, Resolution Authorizing 2019 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), and is framed for adoption at the regular meeting held March 19, 2019 at 7:00 p.m. local time. It recites that on November 5, 2013 the qualified electors of the School District approved a proposal authorizing the issuance of bonds in an aggregate amount of not to exceed $125,000,000, to be issued in one or more series, for the purpose of remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings and other facilities to enhance security and for other purposes; acquiring and installing technology equipment and technology infrastructure in school buildings and other facilities; constructing additions to school buildings; preparing, developing and improving sites at school buildings and other facilities; and the purchase of school buses — referred to as the 2013 Bond Proposal. It further recites that under the provisions of Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for bonds authorized pursuant to the 2013 Bond Proposal shall be without limitation as to rate or amount, and that the bonds will be issued in one or more series based on the type of bonds issued, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed the authorized figure.

**Business 8.D: preschool technology cabling.** The resolution awards the bid for cabling infrastructure for the Troy School District Preschool to Complete Interactive Technologies in the amount of $59,905.31 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund, following an earlier bid update brought to the March 5 workshop.

**Business 8.E: aquatic sports timing equipment for Athens.** The final business item covers the purchase and installation of aquatic sports timing equipment for Athens High School.

The outcomes of these items are recorded in the March 19, 2019 minutes carried in the following month's packet: site work to Asphalt Specialists at $822,140.00 (resolution 19-029), asbestos abatement to Trust Thermal Abatement at $288,420.00 (19-030), the $27,000,000 bond authorization (19-031), preschool cabling to Complete Interactive Technologies at $59,905.31 (19-032) and aquatic sports timing equipment to Riegle Timing Consultants LLC at $65,008.00 (19-033), each adopted 7-0.

**Item 6.A - District Health Insurance Update**, by Jasen Witt, Assistant Superintendent of Human Resources. 2011 Public Act 54, signed June 8, 2011, amends PERA at MCL 423.215b, barring employer cost increases after contract expiration, step increases, lane changes and retroactive pay increases, and requiring employees to absorb insurance cost increases by wage deduction. 2011 PA 152, the Publicly Funded Health Insurance Contribution Act, MCL 15.561 et seq., signed September 27, 2011, applies to coverage years beginning on or after January 1, 2012 and caps employer payments at $5,500 per employee with single coverage, $11,000 for employee plus spouse and $15,000 for family, adjusted annually by the Medical Care Component of the CPI; its elective 80/20 option requires a two-thirds board resolution, contracts in effect on or before September 15, 2011 are grandfathered but extensions are not, and non-compliance costs 10% of State Aid. BCBSM plans for non-rep, administrators and TESPA are CB 4 PPO ($500/$1,000 deductible, 80% coinsurance, $1,500/$3,000 out-of-pocket maximum), CB 3 PPO ($250/$500, 80%, $1,000/$2,000) and CB 2 PPO ($100/$200, 90%, $500/$1,000), all with $50 emergency room copay and $10/$40 prescription drug. Teachers and secretaries are on MESSA with $500/$1,000 deductible, 100% coinsurance, $20 office visit, $25 urgent care, $50 emergency room and Saver Rx; Pak A monthly rates for 7/1/11-6/30/12 include single rates of $657.17, $698.60 and $663.55 and family rates of $1,622.19, $1,663.62 and $1,613.50, with six-month trended rates for 7/1/12-12/31/12 reaching family $1,737.78 at 5% and single $756.44, two-person $1,583.13 and family $1,808.93 at 10% for teachers hired before 6/4/91. Trend citations: Segal 2012 medical/Rx PPO 9.5%, dental 3.8%, vision 3.8%; BCBS Michigan facility 10.19%, physician 11.56%, prescription drugs 12.98%, combined 11.28%; health care trend 9%-12% and prescription drugs 13%-14% with specialty drugs at +21%. HSA-eligible high deductible plans require minimum deductibles of $1,200 single and $2,400 family and cover preventive services at 100%. Next steps involve TESA secretaries and TEA teachers, both under contracts through June 30, 2013.

**Item 7.A - District Goals Overview**, by Dr. Rich Machesky, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction. Goals include 100% of fourth grade teachers observing other classrooms four times by the end of 2012-2013 and 100% of fifth grade teachers by the end of 2013-2014, full K-12 balanced literacy materials by the end of 2012-2013, alignment of the secondary math sequence to the common core with materials selected for 2013-2014, data-interpretation training and claim-evidence-reasoning writing in grades 6-11, and expansion of MI CLASS/HI CLASS literacy training from 12 middle school social studies teachers to 24 teachers in grades 6-12, under a Vision 2013 framework using Atlas Rubicon, TEAM evaluation and NCA external review.

**Item 7.B - District MEAP Results**, by Anne Mull, Director of Instruction and Assessment, covering grades 3 through 9 in math, reading, science and social studies with old and new cut-score series from 2005-06 through 2011-12. MEAP writing proficiency was 78 in 2010-11 and 74 in 2011-12 for grade 4 and 71 then 69 for grade 7, with the note that a new writing test appeared in Fall 2010 and no new cut scores were established for writing. Comparison charts plot Troy against Oakland County districts and percent economically disadvantaged. Planned work includes K-5 word study professional development, a Carol Jago literacy presentation on June 18, preparation for Common Core assessments in 2015, and a Quality Assurance Review in Fall 2013.

**Item 10.A - First Reading.** Revisions to Board Policy B-1209, Abstention from Voting, adopted April 8, 1975 and revised June 7, 1977 and January 16, 1979, would permit abstention only for a direct or indirect financial conflict of interest, an appearance of conflict, or an explicit statutory or bylaw prohibition. Revisions to K-1301, Distribution of Materials to Students, adopted April 19, 1976 and revised January 16 1979 and April 21, 1998, require prior approval of the superintendent or designee for outside distribution. The board's attorney reviewed both for compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act and the Revised School Code.

**Item 10.B - Second Reading and Consideration.** Revisions to Board Policy B-1401, Minutes, adopted April 8, 1975 and revised March 15, 1977, January 16, 1979, March 17, 1998 and June 19, 2007, require proposed minutes to be available for public inspection within eight business days after a meeting and approved minutes within five business days after approval, with records available under the Michigan Freedom of Information Act, Act No. 442, PA 1976. New Board Policy I-1701, Opting Out of Video Presentations, lets parents notify the building principal or classroom teacher to opt a child out of non-district-produced videos; first reading of both occurred at the February 7, 2012 board meeting.

**Item 11.A - Closed Session.** Consideration of negotiations, entered by resolution as permitted by the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), with a roll call listing Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood, Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff and Miletti.

Over four months, Board members and administration worked with Kevin Sutton of Lusk Albertson to update the Bylaws and Policies; a first reading was held at the December 6, 2016 Board Workshop. The manual, copyrighted to Lusk Albertson PLC, runs 0000 Introduction through 8000 General Policies. Governance: seven members on six-year terms elected at the November general election in even-numbered years; officers elected annually in January for one-year terms; the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services appointed Treasurer annually as a nonvoting officer; compensation of $100.00 per annum. Chapter 5000 Business requires a budget adopted prior to July 1 each year, prepared in conformity with GASB 54, an endeavor to maintain a minimum year-end general fund balance of fifteen (15) percent, monthly financial reports, an annual independent audit presented at a public meeting, credit-card payment no later than 60 days from the initial statement date, and a fixed-asset threshold of $5,000. Other provisions include two epinephrine auto-injectors per building and transportation eligibility at one mile for elementary students and one and one-half miles otherwise.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, April 17, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment marks April as Autism Acceptance Month, presented by Barnard Elementary principal Melanie Morey under the banner "Light it Up with Kindness." The district runs autism support classrooms at Barnard (2), Costello and Leonard at the elementary level, Boulan Park at the middle level, Athens at the high school level, and the Troy Center for Transition post-secondary, with Morse and a new program to be determined. April activities include a "Light it Up Blue" day where students may have one fingernail painted blue with a take-home sheet explaining why — the point being to prompt questions from people outside school — sensitivity training for general education peers, a "Walk a Mile in our shoes" challenge for staff to spend time in an autism classroom, and an Autism Speaks bracelet fundraiser run by student council.

The Board then recognizes **39 individuals nominated for the Troy School District Outstanding Teacher Award**, noting more nominations submitted by former and current students than ever before. Thirty-six receive certificates; three were sent to Oakland Schools for the county-wide program: Katy Stanley (math and social studies, Larson) as TSD Middle School Teacher of the Year, Stacie Klumpp (math, Athens) as TSD High School Teacher of the Year, and **Ed Segovia (2nd grade, Morse) as both TSD Elementary Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year**.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the March 6 workshop, the March 20 regular meeting, the March 22 Board retreat and the March 27 special workshop, plus the February 2018 Treasurer's Report and Budget Amendment #2. (The agenda index labels the treasurer's item "March 2018"; the consent page and the register itself are February.)

**How the March 20 votes actually went**
The minutes carried here show a Board that split. Public communication ran heavily to the Section 1 property — Chris Bunch of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, former Troy trustee Ida Edmunds, and residents Harry Broomfield, Donald Drife, Elizabeth Borrow, Tina Catron and Royal Oak's Mary Bogush all spoke on preservation. Mr. Miletti was absent; President Schmidt relayed that Miletti had asked him to say he fully supported all three Section 1 resolutions. Dr. Philippart, Mrs. Fleming and Mr. Hauff said they would support them; Mrs. Hammond was **not in favor of deeding the land to a conservancy**; Mr. Gottlieb said the information received was inaccurate and **recommended tabling**.

**Budget Amendment #2**
The 2017-18 amendment covers the General Fund (Amendment 2), Food Service, Troy Career Center, Adult Education and Community Service, Capital Projects and Capital Maintenance (each Amendment 1), plus the budget adoption for the new Early Childhood Learning Center Fund. Amended appropriations: **General Fund $150,661,687**, Capital Projects $35,949,281, Capital Maintenance $6,345,557, Adult Education and Community Service $4,043,585, Food Service $3,696,036, Troy Career Center $2,520,823 and Early Childhood Learning Center $2,421,731.

General Fund revenue rises $1,775,565 to $151,448,471 — state up $557,801 to $101,615,237, federal up $547,224 to $3,997,995, incoming transfers and other up $474,540 to $7,955,485, local up $196,000 to $37,879,754 — against an unchanged July 1 fund balance of $24,205,391, for $175,653,862 total available to appropriate. On the spending side, instruction rises $1,252,192 to $103,891,055 and support services $758,656 to $46,592,740, with the largest single swing a **$1,314,235 reduction in general administration** to $1,028,661, offset by increases of $918,281 in instructional staff and $778,628 in central services.

**Curriculum — the attendance area review**
Dr. Machesky summarizes the Facilities Study Team – Attendance Area Review Committee report first given at the April 10 workshop. The committee's charge was to resolve double split learning pathways, examine enrollment across buildings to address inappropriate overcrowding and imbalances, and minimize changes to attendance areas. It met on Monday evenings from October 16, 2017 to March 12, 2018 — **15 hours of meeting time excluding site visits** to Smith, Larson, Barnard, Costello and Hill.

The pathway problem has three shapes: a **double switch**, where Troy Union students split between Smith and Larson and the Smith group splits again to Athens; a **single switch**, where Wattles and Morse students at Baker split between Troy High and Athens; and a **middle school switch**, where Hamilton students split between Smith and Boulan Park but reconverge at Troy High. Five concerns are named — the Emerald Lakes quadrant double split from Troy Union, overcrowding at Barnard, at Schroeder and Bemis, and at Boulan Park, and the Hamilton feeder path. The report's own verdict on the constraints — geography, distance limitations, residential development, pathway retention, middle and high school imbalances — is blunt: "No Elegant Solution!"

Next steps send multiple options to transportation for cost estimates while central office examines Schools of Choice draw-down at specific schools, actual fall 2018 enrollment, potential grandfathering based on past practice and additional "neighborhood adjacent" options, with **final recommendations to be considered for implementation in 2019-2020**.

**Recognition 2.A: oneTROY autism programming.** The Mission Moment highlights the district's autism programs, April being designated Autism Awareness Month. The introduction describes autism as a condition characterized by difficulty in communicating and forming relationships, with students challenged in their ability to recognize and understand the thoughts, beliefs, desires and intentions of other people in order to make sense of their behavior and predict what they are going to do. Melanie Morey, principal of Barnard Elementary School, presents; the item is for recognition only and no certificates are handed out.

The presentation is titled "Troy School District celebrates Autism Acceptance Month — Light it Up with Kindness!" Its facts slide describes Autism Spectrum Disorder as a neurobiological disorder that typically affects development within the first three years of life, characterized by impaired communication ability (which may be verbal, partially verbal or non-verbal); impaired social interaction; restricted and/or repetitive interests and behaviors, including repetitive actions and verbally repeating words, phrases or sentences; and sensory issues involving over- or under-stimulation.

Autism support classrooms in the district are listed as Barnard (2), Costello and Leonard at the elementary level, with Morse and a new program to be determined; Boulan Park at the middle school level; Athens at the high school level; and the Troy Center for Transition post-secondary.

During April, schools around the district celebrate autism, and the framing is deliberate: the district is celebrating Autism ACCEPTANCE, moving past awareness to promote a culture of acceptance within the school community. Activities for students include a "Light it Up Blue" day, on which students may have one fingernail painted blue and receive a small take-home sheet explaining the purpose — the idea being to get people outside the school asking about the painted fingernail so students can talk to them about autism acceptance — encouragement to wear blue, "Light it Up with Kindness" lessons for teachers to share throughout the week, and sensitivity training for general education peers. For staff there is a "Walk a Mile in our shoes" challenge to spend time in an autism classroom to better understand how to support students with special needs in their own classrooms, a kickoff breakfast thanking staff for creating a culture of acceptance, and building-wide professional development on the spectrum of differentiation and universal supports for all students. For the community, student council sells autism awareness bracelets through the month with proceeds going toward the Autism Speaks walk that summer, which families and staff are encouraged to join. The closing slide notes that creating a culture of acceptance does not stop in April, and that the peer-to-peer programs continue to serve as a way for students to promote that culture throughout OneTroy.

**Curriculum 7.A: attendance area review summary.** Dr. Machesky provides a brief summary of the report shared with the Board at the April 10 Board Workshop. The presentation is from the Facilities Study Team – Attendance Area Review Committee, with Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor as administrative liaisons. Committee members named are Jeff Frederick, Courtney Spangler, Victoria King, Lori Bluhm, Lori Sisk, Emily Cremers, Laura Duzey, Veronica Pala and Delia Rodi-Barczys.

The committee's charge was to conduct a review of current Troy School District attendance area patterns according to specific criteria and present options to the Superintendent: resolve double split learning pathways in Troy; examine enrollment across buildings to address inappropriate overcrowding and inappropriate imbalances; and minimize changes to school attendance areas across Troy.

The timeline runs from calls to the community to serve on the committee in spring and August 2017, selection of team members in September 2017, an initial meeting on October 16, 2017 with identification of necessary resources and an initial request for reports, then meetings on various Monday evenings from 6:00 to 7:30 through March 12, 2018 — a total meeting time of 15 hours excluding visits — with visits to Smith, Larson, Barnard, Costello and Hill on November 16, 2017, and finalization of recommendations and considerations for presentation on March 12, 2018.

The attendance area problem is set out as three kinds of split. A double switch: Troy Union Elementary students split between Smith and Larson Middle Schools, and the Smith Middle School students split again to Athens High School. A single switch: Wattles and Morse Elementary students attending Baker Middle School are split between Troy High and Athens. And a middle school switch: Hamilton Elementary students split between Smith and Boulan Park Middle Schools and then both go to Troy High. The full pathway table is: Troy Union–Larson–Athens; Troy Union–Smith–Athens; Wass–Larson–Athens; Hill–Larson–Athens; Costello–Larson–Athens; Barnard–Baker–Athens; Morse–Baker–Athens; Morse–Baker–Troy; Wattles–Baker–Athens; Wattles–Baker–Troy; Martell–Smith–Troy; Leonard–Smith–Troy; Hamilton–Smith–Troy; Hamilton–Boulan–Troy; Schroeder–Boulan–Troy; and Bemis–Boulan–Troy.

The research inputs were current, historical and future enrollment; on-site visits; pre-school sites; the 2016 FST report; Schools of Choice and non-resident decisions; locker capacity; current capacity; room utilization; development; population density; open enrollment applications; and apartment pathways.

Five key attendance area concerns are identified: the Emerald Lakes quadrant, to eliminate the double split pathway from Troy Union; Barnard overcrowding, considering space at nearby schools to accommodate students; Schroeder and Bemis overcrowding, likewise; Boulan Park Middle School overcrowding, likewise; and the Hamilton feeder path, considering sending students to one middle school. The key conditions constraining any fix are middle school imbalances, high school imbalances, geography including distance limitations and neighboring options, residential development, and pathway retention — under a slide reading "No Elegant Solution!"

The committee describes its method as an iterative process: developing potential recommendations according to the charge criteria, requesting the data necessary to determine future impact on school enrollment, analyzing results against the charge criteria, and rejecting options that fail to satisfy them. Its summary is that it provided initial, potential options to the Superintendent that meet the charge criteria, considered the construction of the Early Childhood Center and program location changes, recognized new residential development in Troy, and recommended optimal solutions based on collaborative research and analysis.

Next steps: multiple options have been forwarded to the transportation department to develop initial potential costs, while the central office team looks more deeply into the impact of Schools of Choice draw-down at specific schools, actual enrollment in fall 2018, potential grandfathering procedures based on past practice, additional "neighborhood adjacent" options, and potential impact to Troy Schools beyond enrollment. An update will be provided at a future Board workshop, with final recommendations to be considered for implementation in the 2019-2020 school year.

Read together, the April 2018 packet is a pause between two heavy meetings: no business items at all, a budget amendment that adds $1,775,565 of revenue and stands up the Early Childhood Learning Center Fund at $2,421,731 for the first time, and a facilities report that names the district's structural attendance problems without yet proposing a fix — while the March minutes carried in the same packet record that the Board's 4-2 divisions over the Section 1 land and the early childhood project were not incidental but consistent.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Slide deck titled "Troy School District Capital Projects — Bond, BSSF and TLC Fund, Projects Update September 2020," presented as agenda item 8.B. at the Board of Education meeting of September 15, 2020. It inventories the 2020 building, site, roof, flooring and annual maintenance projects, displays completion matrices for the 2014 Bond at elementary and secondary buildings, and closes with Summer 2020 technology bond work. The technology section notes that the order of keyboard cases for all new iPads has been on backorder since July 15, with Apple then estimating the cases would ship by September 15.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Deck identity**
"Troy School District Capital Projects — Bond, BSSF and TLC Fund, Projects Update September 2020." Agenda item 8.B., Board of Education meeting September 15, 2020. A later section is headed "Technology Bond Projects — Summer 2020 — September 15, 2020 Board of Education Meeting." No dollar figures appear in the extracted text.

**2020 Bond/BSSF building improvement projects**
- Hill and Wattles Elementary Schools: mechanical upgrades (boilers, unit ventilators and HVAC units), electrical upgrades (panels and fire alarm systems), kiln room construction
- Athens High School: pool upgrades and art room renovation
- Costello, Martell and IAE: stage renovation with ADA accessible ramp and operable partitions
- Costello, Martell and Wattles: removal of in-wall cafe tables
- Boulan and Larson: window and door replacement
- Bemis: gym/cafe operable wall replacement
- Troy Union: ADA lift project in the kindergarten wing area
- Niles Relocation Project
- Building renovation of the new TSD Learning Center

**Site improvement projects**
IAE parking lot replacement/redesign including removal of tennis courts and new LED lighting; Athens student parking lot replacement/redesign with a new dedicated entry and exit; THS main entrance parking area improvement; Hill paved play and sidewalk replacements.

**Roof, flooring and maintenance**
Roof replacements at Athens (pool and main gym roofs), IAE (academic areas, main office and TCT) and Troy High (academic wings, counseling offices, auditorium seating and lobby areas). Flooring replacements at Hill and Wattles (classrooms and gym), IAE (cafeteria and stage), and polished concrete and terrazzo at Athens, Smith, Costello and Martell. Annual maintenance covers district-wide concrete replacement; asphalt patch, sealcoating and parking lot striping; fencing replacement and improvements; and brick/block repair and tuckpointing. Photo slides also show Hill Gym, Smith science room, Athens health room, Costello hallway, Larson Middle and the Martell kindergarten play area.

**2014 Bond matrices**
An elementary matrix lists Barnard, Bemis, Costello, Hamilton, Hill, Leonard, Martell, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass and Wattles against categories Safety & Security, Electrical, HVAC, Exterior Upgrades and Site Upgrades. A secondary matrix lists Baker, Boulan Park, Larson, Smith, Athens, Troy High, I.A. East and Niles, adding Individual Enhancement Projects. Legend entries: "Project Completed," "Cancelled," and "If cell has no color it was not included as part of scope."

**Technology Bond Projects, Summer 2020**
- Board Room AV upgrades: replaced control room hardware, cameras, cabling, projector, and side and podium displays
- District-wide PA system upgrade (in progress): replace 20-year-old paging hardware/software in all buildings; update cabling/amplifiers to bypass outdated classroom control panels
- Security camera hardware/software upgrades and additions (in progress): add 1 camera at main entrance; middle schools replace existing cameras and add cameras to improve coverage; IA East replace existing cameras and add cameras in the new addition; TLC install interior and exterior cameras
- Elementary and preschool iPads: ordered iPads to expand 1:1 in grades K, 1 and 2; iPads with keyboard cases to expand 1:1 in grades 11 and 12; iPads with keyboard cases for grades 3, 8 and 9; iPads with keyboard cases for teachers; keyboard cases ordered and installed on existing iPads for students in grades 4-7
- Note: keyboard cases for all new iPads on backorder since July 15; Apple estimate at the time was that cases would ship by September 15

2020 Bond/BSSF Building Improvement Projects. Hill and Wattles Elementary Schools receive mechanical upgrades covering boilers, unit ventilators and HVAC units, together with electrical upgrades covering panels and fire alarm systems, plus kiln room construction. Athens High School receives pool upgrades and an art room renovation. Costello, Martell and IAE receive stage renovation consisting of an ADA accessible ramp and operable partitions. Costello, Martell and Wattles have in-wall cafe tables removed. Boulan and Larson receive window and door replacement. Bemis receives gym/cafe operable wall replacement. Troy Union receives an ADA lift project in the kindergarten wing area. The list also includes the Niles Relocation Project and building renovation of the new TSD Learning Center.

Site Improvement Projects. IAE receives parking lot replacement and redesign, including removal of tennis courts and new LED lighting. Athens receives student parking lot replacement and redesign with a new dedicated entry and exit. THS receives main entrance parking area improvement. Hill receives paved play and sidewalk replacements.

Roof Replacement Projects. Athens (pool and main gym roofs); IAE (academic areas, main office and TCT); Troy High (academic wings, counseling offices, auditorium seating and lobby areas).

Flooring Replacement Projects. Hill and Wattles (classrooms and gym); IAE (cafeteria and stage); Athens, Smith, Costello and Martell (polished concrete and terrazzo).

Annual Maintenance Projects. District-wide concrete replacement; district-wide asphalt patch, sealcoating and parking lot striping; district-wide fencing replacement and improvements; district-wide brick/block repair and tuckpointing.

**Meeting**

Troy School District Board of Education, Tuesday, January 15, 2013. Organizational Meeting at 7:00 p.m., Regular Meeting at 7:15 p.m., Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. Superintendent Barbara A. Fowler, Ph.D. Trustees named in the roll-call sequences: Underwood, Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt.

**Organizational actions**

- Judy Holmes appointed temporary secretary; four votes required to elect an officer. President, Vice President and Secretary elected for terms until December 31, 2013.
- Mark S. Rajter, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, appointed Treasurer for January through December 2013 as a nonvoting officer.
- Depository and investment resolution for January through December 2013: depository banks (Bank of America, Bank of New York, JP Morgan Chase, Citizen's Bank, Comerica, Fifth Third, MILAF and PFM Securities through Fifth Third, PNC) and a list of investment institutions, investing under Board Policy D-1103 and Section 380.1223(1)(h) of the Revised School Code. Schools of Choice resolutions under Sections 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, cover 2013-2014: 100 nonresident kindergarten and 30 nonresident first-grade students, both for districts within Oakland County and for districts whose intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD, plus 25 nonresident sixth- through eighth-grade students at Baker Middle School under each section. Bids for the Morse Elementary UPS replacement went to four potential bidders with three responding, were reviewed by Kenneth Miller, Executive Director of Operations, and Richard Bracci, Senior Vice President, IDS, and the award goes to J. B. Electrical Company for $28,115.00 from the 2012-2013 General Fund. Ken Crawford, Interim Acting Director of Technology, and Mark Rajter recommend 22 Konica Minolta multi-function copiers for $250,796.00 with a five-year service agreement estimated at $44,250 annually; Merri Lynn Colligan identified the worst machines in fall 2012, Konica has indicated parts are no longer available, and the district used an existing Livingston Educational Service Agency pricing agreement with Konica Minolta that began in 2010 and is valid until 2/12/15. Purchase runs $25,000 less than a 36-month lease-to-own contract, and the .0039 cents-per-copy service rate covers maintenance, repairs and toner. **Superintendent's goals and bond preparation.** Dr. Fowler's 2012-2013 update centers on increasing the number of students college and career ready in literacy, mathematics, science and social studies. Five cohort groups of seven to eight fourth-grade teachers give 100 percent participation in coordinator-facilitated teacher labs, alongside work with Carol Jago, Frank Serafini and Lester Laminack and 24 volunteer high school teachers in Hi-Class content literacy. Mathematics covers Smarter Balanced alignment, an elementary committee piloting three programs for spring recommendation, and Big Ideas Mathematics in grades 6 and 7 with grade 8 next fall. Science introduced the claim-evidence-reasoning framework through Darin Stockdill on August 29th, with 30-minute sessions at all 12 elementary schools and PASCO training for physics teachers; social studies targets 24 teachers trained in grades 6-12; and a math support class adds three hours of instruction per week for middle school students. Bond preparation for a November 2013 election includes a completed TMP Architecture facility assessment of site, roofing, plumbing/HVAC and electrical, a district-wide technology assessment, a nine-year bus replacement schedule, site visits completed by January 18, 2013, a community survey run January 7-10 and completed January 10, 2013, results to be reviewed at the January 22nd workshop, and the bond amount to be presented February 5th. A cost analysis of the current finance and human resources software puts cost per student at $12 or more; the district intends to move to Oakland Schools' Tyler Munis solution along with 22 other Oakland County districts over the next four fiscal years, subsidized for the first five years and approximately $10 per student thereafter, with final commitment letters due late Fall 2013.

**Policy K-1303.** A first reading of revisions to Board Policy K-1303, Commercial Advertising, in the K-1300 series on advertising and distribution of materials in the schools, was reviewed by the Board's attorney for compliance with state law, the Open Meetings Act and the Revised School Code. The policy bars commercial material causing substantial and material interference with normal school activities from being displayed on district-owned property without written consent of the superintendent or designee, permits display on personal vehicles parked on school property, and restricts school and contracted personnel from using district resources, technology, e-mail and student or parent contact information for commercial purposes. Adopted May 3, 1976; revised January 16, 1979, April 21, 1998, April 20, 2010 and June 19, 2012.

**3.A. Personnel — International Academy Letter of Understanding**
Ratification of a successor Letter of Understanding with the teachers at the International Academy, a consortium high school program. The tentative agreement was reached March 9, 2017, concluded May 31, 2017, and ratified by the IA teachers June 8, 2017; the term is July 1, 2017 through June 30, 2022. Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent/Employee Services, and Ryan Brinks, Associate Principal/IA East, represented Troy on the bargaining team; Harris and Christine Barnett (Bloomfield Hills) signed as chief negotiators, with Grat Dalton signing as Executive Director. Signature pages are held in the Human Resources Office of Bloomfield Hills Schools.

Negotiated changes include a five-year term; IA administration rather than the Joint Steering Committee determining applicant qualifications; termination language now referencing the home district's policies and procedures and applicable law, reflecting 2011 changes to the Public Employment Relations Act that made discipline and discharge a prohibited subject of bargaining; a new tri-campus club committee for supplemental-activity categories; a new Department Chairs article; new teaching-schedule language on preparation periods; and a Standing Committee of up to five teacher and up to five administration representatives.

**Stipends and supplemental pay**

Supplemental pay rates are Category I $866, Category II $1190, Category III $1570, with department-chair remuneration for all campuses capped at $10,990 over the contract term. Enrichment and orientation activities, substituting for another Academy teacher, and out-of-day parent/teacher conferences pay $25 per hour; the further math class carries a $3500.00 annual stipend.

**Personnel: successor Letter of Understanding, International Academy teachers.** The Board is asked to ratify and adopt the tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the International Academy teachers for the period July 1, 2017 through June 30, 2022. The agreement was reached March 9, 2017 but not concluded until May 31, 2017, and the International Academy teachers ratified it June 8, 2017. Mr. Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent/Employee Services, and Mr. Ryan Brinks, Associate Principal/IA East, represented the Troy School District on the bargaining team. The signature page names Grat Dalton, Executive Director; Christine Barnett, Chief Negotiator; and Jordan Harris, Chief Negotiator, with actual signature pages on file in the Human Resources Office of Bloomfield Hills Schools.

The International Academy is a consortium of public school districts operating a grade nine through twelve school-of-choice program at several campuses. The participating districts are Avondale, Berkley, Birmingham, Bloomfield Hills, Clawson, Huron Valley, Lake Orion, Rochester, Royal Oak, Troy, Waterford and West Bloomfield. The administrative team representing the districts: Lynne Gibson (principal of the IA), Sarah Fairman (IB Coordinator), Christopher Smith (associate principal, IA Central), Ryan Brinks (associate principal, IA East), Ryan Parrott (associate principal, IA West), Jordan Harris (Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, Troy) and Christine Barnett (Assistant Superintendent for Human Resources and Labor Relations, Bloomfield Hills). The teacher team: Dave McGuire (IA-East), Jeff DeMoss (IA-East), Kayla McCabe (IA-Okma) and Kelly Paterson (IA-East). Teachers assigned to the Academy remain employees of their home district; tenure is with the home district.

Article-by-article changes described in the cover memo: Article 1 sets a five-year term. Article 2(b) clarifies that the IA administration, not the Joint Steering Committee, determines applicant qualifications. Article 2(d) replaces reference to the home district's collective bargaining agreement and the Michigan Teachers' Tenure Act with the "home district's policies and procedures and applicable law," because 2011 changes to the Public Employment Relations Act made decisions on discipline or discharge of teachers a prohibited subject of bargaining. Article 4 revises the process for approving paid clubs and organizations to include a tri-campus club committee of teachers and administrators, which recommends a category to Administration; the administration approves and designates the category within ten school days. Article 5 is new and names Department Chairs for literature, history, math, theory of knowledge, French/German, Spanish, chemistry, physics, biology, economics, art, music, physical education/health and counseling, paid at Category III. New Article 9(c) provides that every effort will be made to give preparation periods on C Day, Interdisciplinary Day and outside evaluation days, though not every teacher will have one. New Article 9(d) provides that non-music teachers assigned five or more preparations per semester will receive an extra planning period for at least one semester where possible, or compensation of 1/16 of salary for the additional instruction block. Article 11(g) changes Standing Committee representation from "representatives of the current negotiation team" to up to five teacher and up to five administration representatives, because not all current negotiators will be available across the five-year term.

**Wages, stipends and supplemental pay.** Teachers are paid for required days according to their home district's step and salary track. Appendix A replaces the previous two-tier stipend (fewer than five years of experience versus five or more) with one stipend per district beginning July 1, 2017, increasing $50.00 at each Base step: Avondale, Berkley, Clawson, Waterford and West Bloomfield $3,600.00 BASE rising to $3,800.00 at Base +4; Huron Valley $3,400.00 to $3,600.00; Birmingham $3,050.00 to $3,250.00; Lake Orion, Royal Oak and Troy $2,850.00 to $3,050.00; Rochester $2,700.00 to $2,900.00; Bloomfield Hills $2,350.00 to $2,550.00. All teachers begin at the BASE stipend in 2017-18; from 2018-19 each returning IA teacher moves to Base +1 and then to the next level annually until reaching Base +4. Part-time teachers are prorated by FTE. Teachers who had been in the 5+ year range under the 2014-2017 Letter of Understanding receive a one-time 2017-18 bonus of $150 less the increase in their stipend: $143.00 for Lake Orion, Royal Oak and Troy; $121.00 Huron Valley; $119.00 Birmingham; $117.00 Rochester; $115.00 Bloomfield Hills; and $97.00 for Avondale, Berkley, Clawson, Waterford and West Bloomfield. The memo's worked example is a Berkley 5+ year teacher whose current longer year and longer day stipend is $3547, against a new base of $3600, leaving $53 and a stipend bonus of $97.

The superseded Appendix A-1 table (fewer than five years) shows a $118.08 difference rate and a $1200.00 longer-day allocation, running from 182 days in the home district at $1180.80 and $2380.80 total additional compensation down to 192 days at $0.00 and $1200.00. The five-years-experience table shows a $175.90 rate and $1787.50 allocation, from $1759.00 and $3546.50 at 182 days to $0.00 and $1787.50 at 192 days; 182 days is the minimum used in the calculation.

Appendix B sets supplemental pay at Category I $866, Category II $1190 and Category III $1570. Category I covers class sponsors for 9th and 10th grades, the Mentor/Mentee Committee Chair and IA-mission-related clubs; Category II covers the 11th grade class sponsor, honor societies, coordinators (Passport, Product Team, buildOn, Theory of Knowledge, School Improvement, Student Leadership, Extended Essay), assistant coaches and the Honors Convocation counselor duty; Category III covers the 12th grade class sponsor, department chairs, the Extended Essay Coordinator, coaches for competitive teams, the Student Leadership Advisor, Yearbook Advisor, graduation planning and the Directors of Fine Arts. Total remuneration for department heads across all campuses is capped at $10,990 during the term of the contract. A club or organization requires a minimum of ten students and must meet the equivalent of at least eighty minutes per month.

Other compensation terms: enrichment and orientation activities pay $25 per hour, with a maximum of eight hours per day (a seven hour and fifty minute day is paid as eight), a maximum of forty hours per activity, and principal discretion to designate up to six activities per year compensated up to 64 hours; travel time is capped at four hours. Substituting for another Academy teacher pays $25 per hour, as do parent/teacher conferences held outside the regular school day. The teacher assigned to the further math class receives a stipend of $3500.00 per school year.

**Work year and schedule.** Teachers work 192 days including 190 student days, with 190 instructional days plus enrichment/orientation days. Each teacher receives one paid discretionary day, non-cumulative, scheduled first-come first-served with no more than ten percent of staff off on any one day and scheduling completed by April 15. The International Academy provides a minimum of 30 professional development hours: 24 specified in the calendars and 6 more scheduled by November 1 each year, all completed by June 1, with pay docked one hour for each hour missed. The normal daily teacher schedule is seven hours and fifty minutes with 270 minutes of instructional time; in an eight-block schedule over two days a full-time teacher has six instructional blocks, and over a two-week period the workweek averages 250 minutes of preparation time per week. Lunch is a daily thirty-minute duty-free period, and homeroom/passport is not intended to exceed an average of forty minutes bi-weekly. Music teachers teach a Block E course and are assigned five rather than six instructional blocks for the corresponding period, or are compensated 1/16 of salary.

**Grievance procedure.** A grievance must be presented in writing to the IA principal within fifteen working days of the occurrence or of the grievant becoming aware of it; the principal schedules a meeting within five work days and responds in writing within five work days. Step Two goes to the Joint Steering Committee's Grievance Committee within ten work days; that committee has three representatives from the constituent districts, one from the grievant's home district, meets within ten work days and responds within five. Step Three is binding arbitration, which only the Association may invoke, filed within twenty work days under American Arbitration Association rules, with the losing party paying the arbitrator's fees and expenses. The arbitrator has no authority to alter, amend, add to or subtract from the agreement.

**Business: furniture purchase for secondary math classrooms.** Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, led a project team with Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and building administrators and staff to evaluate the use and needs for furniture in secondary math classrooms. The suggested resolution approves the bid for furniture for secondary math classrooms in the amount of $681,737.50 through Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and the Oakland County America Saves Cooperative Purchase Program as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The attached "The Learning Environment" presentation, which opens with a Franklin D. Roosevelt quotation, states a Total Investment of $681,737.50, installation of $49,580.00 and an estimated rebate of $27,000 (4%), with pricing including professionally coordinated delivery and installation during normal business hours and project management. Building allocations are Troy High School $168,450.06, Athens High School $145,148.20, Baker Middle School $66,680.00, Boulan Middle School $70,558.46, Smith Middle School $59,067.80, Larson Middle School $68,773.68, IA East $30,621.00 and TCCHS $22,858.30. The package selection tables list Package A totalling 2 (Smith 1, Boulan 1); Package B totalling 18 (Smith 3, Larson 1, IA East 1, Boulan 5, Athens 3, Troy HS 5); Package C totalling 1 (Smith 1); Package D totalling 9 (Athens 1, Troy HS 8); Package E totalling 6 (Smith 1, Larson 3, Baker 2); Package F totalling 17 (Larson 1, IA East 2, Boulan 1, Athens 8, Baker 1, Troy HS 4); Package G totalling 4 (Smith 1, Athens 1, Baker 2); and Package H totalling 5 (Larson 1, Athens 2, Baker 2).

**Other: policy readings.** Under policy 1000.03, Adoption or Amendment of Bylaws and Policies, the Board may by majority vote waive a first reading and proceed to act on a revision or new policy. The packet carries two alternative versions of both the waiver and the adoption resolution: one naming policies 0000.02 Board of Education, 5000.03 Purchasing and 2000.07 Health and Safety, to be used if 0000.02 is changed to strike language stating that the Board approves the negotiating team; the other naming 4000.01 Administrative Staff and Organization, 5000.03 Purchasing and 2000.07 Health and Safety, to be used if 4000.01 is changed to strike language stating that the superintendent appoints the negotiating team. Revised policy 2000.07 Health and Safety includes new language to comply with Michigan law prohibiting seclusion and restraint, except for emergency seclusion and emergency physical restraint in the manner permitted by law.

**March 5, 2019 workshop minutes.** President Schmidt called the workshop to order at 6:15 p.m. at the Troy Center for Transition/IA-East, 1291 Torpey Drive, with Mrs. Fleming, Mr. Gottlieb, Mrs. Hammond, Mr. Hauff, Dr. Philippart and Dr. Wilson present. The agenda covered public communication; a Section 1 update; a Teaching and Learning update including the 1:1 high school pilot review; a Business Services update covering districtwide site work projects, districtwide asbestos abatement, the 2019 school building and site bonds, an ancillary funds budget amendment, the Troy Preschool technology cabling bid and aquatic sports timing equipment for Athens; and the June 18, 2019 board meeting. It adjourned at 9:30 p.m., Gary N. Hauff signing as Secretary.

**March 19, 2019 meeting minutes.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. at the Services Building with Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson present, Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Cross, Jansen, Brasington, Dixon, Roncone, Griffor, Harris and West in attendance, and approximately 100 members of the audience.

The Mission Moment recognized Amogh Gowda, a junior at Troy High School and a distinguished finalist for the Prudential Spirit of Community Award for developing an awareness program on organ donation; he is a certified volunteer for Gift of Life Michigan who speaks at venues and volunteers at community events to empower youth and promote the fact that one organ donor can save up to eight lives. The Board also honored Wass Elementary School as a 2019 State School of Character, an award given to a select few schools each year for implementing 11 core principles including promoting good character, culture and ethics, fostering student self-motivation, giving students opportunity for moral action, and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building; Wass was praised for high quality work in all 11 principle areas and its application was forwarded for consideration as a National School of Character. Wattles Elementary was commended as a 2019 Honorable Mention School of Character and Athens High School was recognized as Emerging. Lori Soifer, Character.org Coordinator for the State of Michigan, presented the official certificate to Matt Jansen, Principal of Wass Elementary.

In public communication, Pietro Sarcina, a Troy resident, addressed the Board regarding the removal of the tennis courts at all middle schools in the District. Resolution 19-027 approved the consent agenda: minutes of the February 5, 2019 workshop, minutes of the February 26, 2019 meeting, the Treasurer's Report for January 2019, and an ancillary funds budget amendment. Resolution 19-028 approved the personnel recommendation, new hire Erin Mullins. Under business, resolution 19-029 awarded districtwide site work projects to Asphalt Specialists, Inc. in the amount of $822,140.00 as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund; 19-030 awarded districtwide asbestos abatement to Trust Thermal Abatement in the amount of $288,420.00 from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund and the Building and Site Sinking Fund; and 19-031 authorized the issuance of bonds designated the "2019 School Building and Site Bonds" in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000, with the full resolution made part of the official minutes of the March 19, 2019 regular meeting. Resolution 19-032 awarded cabling infrastructure for the Troy School District Preschool to Complete Interactive Technologies in the amount of $59,905.31 from the Early Childhood Center Fund, and 19-033 awarded aquatic sports timing equipment and installation to Riegle Timing Consultants LLC in the amount of $65,008.00 from the General Fund and Activity Fund. Resolution 19-034 cancelled the June 18, 2019 Board of Education meeting.

Resolution 19-035 designated a school safety liaison and emergency contact. It recites that Public Act 435 of 2018 establishes the Office of School Safety within the Department of State Police, tasked with working with the Michigan Department of Education to create model practices for school safety and offering school safety trainings; that Public Act 538 of 2018 requires the Department of State Police to create a School Safety Commission to review model practices and make policy recommendations; that Public Act 549 of 2018 requires the Board to designate a district employee as liaison to both bodies, who must regularly and continuously work under contract for the district; that under the Student Safety Act, MCL 752.913(3), the Attorney General operates a hotline for reports regarding potential self-harm and potential harm or criminal acts directed at school students, employees or schools in Michigan; and that Public Act 670 of 2018 requires the governing body to provide the Department of State Police, at least biannually, with current emergency contact information for at least one school official able to receive hotline information. It directs the Superintendent to designate the liaison and notify the Department of State Police by March 28, 2019, and to provide the contact information of at least one school official to receive information from the Attorney General's hotline by the same date. Every vote that evening was 7 yes, 0 no. Gary N. Hauff certified the resolution and that notice was given under the Open Meetings Act, Act 267 of the Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

The hearing closed at 7:20 p.m. Present with Miletti were Edmunds, Fleming, and Hauff; Philippart, Schmidt, and Underwood were absent; administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Keeling, Machesky, Rajter, Washington, and Witt attended with approximately seven audience members. OTHER (Item 10). Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., presents his 90-Day Entry Plan, dated July 1, 2014, under the banner "One Team, One Plan, One Goal" and the district theme "All Means All!" The plan restates the district mission of ensuring learning for all members of the school community, the vision of an exemplary learning community, and goals that all students be on track to be college/career ready in literacy, mathematics, science, and social studies. Its stated purpose is a seamless transition from Assistant Superintendent to Superintendent using a "seek first to understand" practice, with immediate focus on Board relations, building on the district's "lighthouse" tradition, organizational capacity, public image, and fiscal stewardship including oversight of the 2013 Bond project. The anticipated outcome is an Executive Summary Report of findings, observations, and tentative timelines that will also direct the TSD Strategic Plan and the Superintendent's evaluation. Five goals are set out: Goal #1 Student Achievement (review achievement data and gaps, instructional improvement and intervention systems, alignment of standards, curriculum, assessment and professional development, and Central Office alignment); Goal #2 Board Governance; Goal #3 Organizational Alignment; Goal #4 Community and Public Relations; and Goal #5 Line Support Functions including Human Resources, Finance, Technology and Operations, which includes assessing readiness for collective bargaining scheduled for 2015 and reviewing long-range technology plans.
