**Meeting**
Regular meeting, April 18, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment is Smith Middle School's **"U-Knighted Hour."** Over the previous summer a group of Smith teachers met to develop a homeroom for all students, the building having recognized a need for a stronger bond between staff and students and among students across grade levels. The plan: a **7-period day once a month, with U-Knighted time during the 7th hour** — students arranged by grade level and divided among **41 teachers, about 17 students per group**. The committee meets before each session to write the lesson plan, focused on character development, diversity, motivation, community, goal setting "and FUN!!!" Assistant Principal Amy Buchanan, counselor Jen Hartenburg and social studies teacher Glen Rexer present.

The Board then recognizes **38 nominees** for the Outstanding Teacher Award, noting more nominations submitted by former and current students than ever before. Thirty-five receive certificates and plants; three were sent to Oakland Schools for the county-wide program: **Kimberly Phillips** (4th grade, Wattles) as Elementary Teacher of the Year, **Lindsey Becker** (7th grade math, Baker) as Middle School Teacher of the Year, and **Kristy Pierce** (social studies and economics, Athens, and Student Congress advisor) as High School Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the March 7 workshop, the March 21 meeting, and the March 23 special meeting, closed session and retreat, plus the February 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**What the March minutes record**
All seven members were present at the March 21 meeting and every resolution carried 7-0: Budget Amendment #2, Bid Pack 19 at $443,960.00, Bid Pack 20 at $1,044,052.90, the Brainard pool locker award, the General Painting award, and — as resolutions 17-033 and 17-034 — the district-owned property resolution that authorized investigating preservation of Section 1, marketing Section 11, developing the Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16, and appointing TMP Architecture.

On March 23 the Board met twice. A special meeting at 5:00 p.m. adopted resolution 17-035 going into closed session **to discuss district-owned properties** under Section 8(c) of the Open Meetings Act, on a unanimous roll call; the closed session ran from 5:05 to 6:16 p.m. with the superintendent and five administrators present and no other business conducted. The Board retreat followed at 6:26 p.m., covering a budget update on 2017-18 financial planning and cultural proficiency, adjourning at 9:05 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report — February 2017**
Total check disbursements are $6,087,180.55, the General Fund group $5,020,916.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,644,455.96. With $2,017,257.64 of wire transfers, $133,949.69 of P-Card purchases and $31,841.51 of ACH debits, less $7,991.67 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $8,262,237.72.

**Personnel**
A probationary contract for **Caitlin Bray**, 1.0 ASD program teacher at Boulan Park Middle School, holding a B.S. in special education from Central Michigan and an M.A. in applied behavior analysis and autism from Ball State expected July 2017, with prior experience at Metropolitan Nashville Public Schools and Huron Valley Schools.

**Business**

| Item | Award | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classroom A/V displays (RFP 9839) | VSC — $718,743.85 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Synchronized clock system (RFP 9840) | Sound Engineering — $406,473.00 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Container refuse collection | GFL Environmental USA, Inc. | 2017, 2018 and 2019 General Fund |
| Flooring replacement (RFP 9838) | Conventional Carpet, Inc. — $201,380.00 | Capital Maintenance |

**The A/V displays** drew three proposals opened March 10: Digital Age Technologies with Philips at $307,368.00 for middle schools only, VSC with SMART at $655,270.67 for high and middle schools, and Tierney Brothers with SMART and LG at $808,219.31. DAT is **not an authorized SMART reseller**, so it bid the middle schools alone. Convergent Technology Partners ran a technical demonstration with VSC on March 23 attended by the Technology Committee and all secondary principals.

The RFP had specified non-interactive flat panels in the middle schools and interactive panels in the high schools; the discussion that followed the demonstration turned on making them consistent across the secondary level, on individual departments' use of interactive displays to deepen learning, and on using an interactive display as a center or remediation station while other students work in groups — **"increasing the ability for a collaborative space not tied to the front of the room."** The recommended award therefore modifies VSC's base bid: **$655,270.67 base, plus $120,269.84 to upgrade the middle schools to interactive flat panels, less $56,796.66 of cabling — $718,743.85.** Completion is set for October 30.

**The clock system** drew four proposals: Sound Engineering with Sapling at $391,473.00, DAT with Carehawk at $403,787.00, I.COMM with Primex at $430,372.96 and Amcomm with Primex at $492,000.00. Sound Engineering, the low compliant bidder, confirmed the Sapling SBL31S4041R 4-digit digital clock; countdown functionality programmed **at no additional cost** for all secondary buildings at the principals' request; clocks showing hours and minutes normally, switching to minutes and seconds during countdown; hourly synchronization with the district time server; and integration with the existing PA system, correcting the PA clock daily at 2:00 A.M., also at no cost. Installation proceeds building by building, each cut over before the next begins, with completion by August 4.

Drawings for the transportation building were not available during the RFP, so no bidder priced it. The recommendation adds **an allowance of $15,000.00** to cover that building and any other clocks not discovered during the walk-through — $391,473.00 plus $15,000.00 for the $406,473.00 award.

**Flooring replacement** covers hallways, classrooms and music rooms at Athens, Troy High, IA East and Larson. Three bids were opened March 8; Conventional Carpet, Inc., which has done similar work for Troy and other Metro Detroit districts, was low qualified bidder, with a separate purchase order per site and completion by August 12, 2017.

**Other**
The Superintendent shares his **World Class by 2020** presentation from the previous week's workshop with the community.

**Recognition 2.A: Smith Middle School's "U-Knighted Hour."** The previous summer, a group of interested teachers from Smith Middle School met to develop a homeroom for all Smith students. As a building, Smith had recognized the need to develop a stronger bond between staff and students, and among students between grade levels. The plan was to implement a 7-period day once a month and hold "U-Knighted" time during the 7th hour. Students were arranged by grade level and then divided among 41 teachers, resulting in approximately 17 students in each group. The committee meets before each U-Knighted Hour and develops a lesson plan for the groups, with the focus on character development, diversity, motivation, community, goal setting, "and FUN!!!" The program has been well received by students and staff alike. Amy Buchanan, Assistant Principal at Smith, counselor Jen Hartenburg and social studies teacher Glen Rexer are invited up to share more.

**Recognition 2.B: Oakland County Outstanding Teacher of the Year awards.** The Board recognizes the accomplishments of 38 individuals nominated for the Troy School District Outstanding Teacher Award Program. The nominees represent exemplary educators at the elementary, middle and high school levels, nominated by their peers and by parents, and this year the district received more nominations than ever submitted by former and current students. The nomination letters each described how the professionals honored go above and beyond to ensure their students learn, grow and thrive.

Thirty-five nominees receive certificates and plants: Adam Burns, TV production, English and Innovations at Athens; Amanda Hazergian, 2nd grade, Schroeder; Anne Drogosch, English language arts, Smith; Betsy Kennedy, English language arts, Baker; Brandon Preblich, physics, Athens; Cindy Christiansen, English language arts, Larson; Colette Carlin, 2nd grade, Hill; Dawn Hayes, special education resource room, Athens; Emily Beski, mathematics, IA East; Erica Conklin, special education, Barnard; Giovanna Marulli, 2nd grade, Hamilton; Gwen Simon, 4th grade, Barnard; Harriet Clark, communications, debate and English, Troy High; Jackie Losh, 1st grade, Schroeder; Jackie Skinner, 2nd grade, Wass; Janet Schoon, 5th grade instrumental music, Costello; Janice Boyer, 2nd grade, Hamilton; Jennifer Deward, 4th grade, Leonard; Julie Dagenais, 1st grade, Costello; Julie Marjamaa, kindergarten, Costello; Katherine Grabowski, special education, Larson; Kristen Marcaccio, kindergarten, Costello; Laurie Bussell, physical education, Bemis and Martell; Lindsey Gerbe, kindergarten, Barnard; Melinda Kaspari, 1st grade, Hill; Melissa Geeraerts, kindergarten, Hamilton; Melven Moffett, 2nd grade, Leonard; Nadeen Brown, 1st grade, Leonard; Nicole Given, kindergarten, Martell; and Trevor Potts, mathematics and technology, Larson, among others.

Three district nominees were sent to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the county-wide outstanding teacher award program administered by Oakland Schools: Kimberly Phillips, 4th grade teacher at Wattles Elementary, Elementary Teacher of the Year; Lindsey Becker, 7th grade math teacher at Baker Middle School, Middle School Teacher of the Year; and Kristy Pierce, social studies and economics teacher and Student Congress advisor at Athens High School, High School Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year. The agenda was public communication, a budget update on 2017-18 financial planning, and cultural proficiency. It adjourned at 9:05 p.m.

Adding ACH debits of $31,841.51, outgoing wire transfers of $2,017,257.64 and P-Card purchases of $133,949.69, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $7,991.67, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $8,262,237.72. The middle sections of the packet are the February check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: elementary and secondary.** The Board is recommended to approve a probationary contract for the 2016-2017 school year for Caitlin Bray, 1.0 ASD teacher at Boulan Park Middle School. Her biographical sketch records a B.S. in special education with a minor in integrated science from Central Michigan University, July 2013, and an M.A. in applied behavior analysis and autism from Ball State University expected July 2017; her teaching experience is with Metropolitan Nashville Public Schools in Antioch, Tennessee, as a special education teacher from July 2013 to May 2015, and with Huron Valley Schools in Highland, Michigan.

**Business 8.A: classroom A/V displays.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on classroom A/V displays, reviewed by Convergent Technology Partners. John C. Foster's April 11, 2017 evaluation and recommendation on RFP #9839 records that bids and proposals for classroom displays in the secondary school buildings were received, opened and publicly read at 1:30 P.M. on March 10, 2017, and that several mandatory alternates were requested for alternate solutions.

Three proposals were received: Digital Age Technologies with Philips displays at a base bid of $307,368.00, middle school only; VSC with SMART displays at $655,270.67 for high and middle schools; and Tierney Brothers with SMART and LG displays at $808,219.31 for high and middle schools. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution and acceptance of terms and conditions; all bidders provided compliant proposals and any exceptions or clarifications were deemed acceptable. The reason DAT's bid covers only part of the scope is stated plainly: DAT is not an authorized SMART reseller, therefore it only included the middle school displays in its response.

Further information and clarification were requested from bidders, and a technical demonstration and bid interview were conducted with VSC on March 23, 2017. The Technology Committee and all secondary principals attended the demonstration and remained afterward to discuss the potential solutions and options.

The clarifications and discussions recorded are substantive rather than procedural. The bid responses included non-interactive flat panel displays in the middle schools and interactive flat panel displays in the high schools, per the RFP requirements. Consideration of consistent interactive flat panel displays was discussed for the secondary level. Deep discussions were had regarding individual department use of interactive displays and the benefit to deepen learning. Discussions were also had regarding the ability to use the interactive display as a center or remediation station while other students are in work groups — therefore increasing the ability for a collaborative space not tied to the front of the room. The project includes an interactive flat panel display for all secondary classrooms that do not currently have a wall-mounted permanent display solution. VSC confirmed a single point of contact, a project manager, and daily online project updates to ensure project success, and confirmed it will meet the project schedule outlined in the RFP, completion October 30.

After final review, Convergent proceeded with the low compliant bidder, VSC, with the following modifications to the base bid response: base bid $655,270.67; upgrade middle schools to interactive flat panels, $120,269.84; deduct cabling, $56,796.66 — for a recommended award total of $718,743.85. The resolution awards the bid for classroom A/V displays to VSC in the amount of $718,743.85 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The pedagogical argument in the memo — that an interactive panel lets a teacher run a small group at a station while others work independently, rather than anchoring instruction to the front of the room — is what justifies spending an additional $120,269.84 to upgrade the middle schools beyond what the RFP itself required.

**Business 8.B: synchronized clock system.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on a complete, district-wide synchronized clock system, reviewed by Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's April 11, 2017 evaluation on RFP #9840 records that bids for a complete, turn-key, district-wide synchronized clock system were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 P.M. on March 10, 2017, with no mandatory alternates requested.

Four proposals were received: Sound Engineering offering Sapling at a base bid of $391,473.00; Digital Age Technologies offering Carehawk at $403,787.00; I.COMM offering Primex at $430,372.96; and Amcomm offering Primex at $492,000.00. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution and acceptance of terms and conditions; all bidders provided compliant proposals and none took any exceptions. Further information and clarification were requested on March 16, 2017, and as all systems met the RFP requirements including the additional clarification, Convergent proceeded with the low compliant bidder, Sound Engineering.

The clarifications: the proposed digital clock is the Sapling model SBL31S4041R, a 4-digit model; countdown functionality is available and will be provided and programmed at no additional cost to the district for all secondary buildings as requested by the principals; digital clocks will show hours and minutes in normal mode, switch to minutes and seconds during countdown mode, then revert to normal mode after the countdown is complete; the clock system will synchronize with the district time server on an hourly basis; the clock system will integrate with the existing PA system and correct the PA system time once a day at 2:00 A.M., with PA system integration at no cost to the district; Sound Engineering confirmed a single point of contact, a project manager, and weekly online written status reports; and Sound Engineering confirmed it will meet the project schedule outlined in the RFP, completion August 4, with installation by building — once a building is complete it will be moved to the new system before implementation commences in the next building.

A note records a gap in the bid: drawings for the transportation building were not available during the RFP process and therefore pricing was not included in any proposal. Convergent requests an allowance of $15,000.00 to cover that building and any other clocks not discovered during the walk-through of district buildings. The recommendation is accordingly the base bid of $391,473.00 plus the $15,000.00 allowance, for a total of $406,473.00. The resolution awards the synchronized clock system to Sound Engineering in the amount of $406,473.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business 8.C: container refuse collection services.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on district-wide container refuse collection services, reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations. The resolution awards the bid to GFL Environmental USA, Inc. based on their bid response, approved as an expenditure of the 2017, 2018 and 2019 General Fund — the only award in the packet stated without a dollar figure in the resolution, and the only one spanning three fiscal years.

**Business 8.D: floor replacement.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on flooring replacement work at Athens and Troy High Schools, International Academy East and Larson Middle School, reviewed by Rob Carson. His March 29, 2017 memorandum on RFP 9838 records that the scope is to provide flooring removal, floor preparation, and materials and installation of new flooring to hallways, classrooms and music rooms as detailed in the bid specifications for each school; that on March 8 three bids were opened, which resulted in Conventional Carpet, Inc. being identified as the low qualified bidder; and that Conventional Carpet has performed similar work for the Troy School District and for other school districts in the Metro Detroit area. He requests a total project cost award of $201,380.00, with a separate purchase order created for each site project, and a completion date of August 12, 2017. The resolution awards the flooring replacement to Conventional Carpet, Inc. in the amount of $201,380.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.

**Other 10.A: World Class by 2020.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board on April 18, 2017 that the Superintendent will share his presentation on "World Class by 2020" from the previous week's workshop with the community at that evening's Board meeting. The report is the public version of the strategic framing that recurs throughout these packets — the district's journey to become a World Class School District by 2020, and the four characteristics of world class that would later be cited in the Early Childhood Center naming resolution.

Read as a whole, the April 2017 packet is the district equipping its buildings. The two technology awards together come to more than a million dollars from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, and both were shaped in the evaluation rather than in the bid: the display project grew by $120,269.84 because the principals and Technology Committee decided, after seeing a demonstration, that middle schools should get the same interactive panels as the high schools, and the clock project grew by $15,000.00 because nobody had drawings for the transportation building. Around those, the meeting hires one autism-program teacher, replaces flooring in four buildings, contracts three years of refuse collection, and honors 38 teachers and a middle school that decided its students needed a homeroom.

STATEMENTS
Question 1 asks what personal characteristics define an excellent administrator. Godfrey answers that an excellent leader is often the determining factor within an organization, and that when an effort or team is headed by the right individual, time, resources and skills are maximized and people are empowered, inspired and productive. He identifies humility, integrity and vision as the three most important personal characteristics. He writes that educational leadership requires humility and a keen focus on service toward improving outcomes for learners, that selflessness and appreciation for collaboration are essential, and that servant leadership causes educators and stakeholders to sense their value and contribute toward common goals, whereas ego-driven leadership breeds competitive and hostile environments in which individuals fight for their own agendas rather than a shared vision. On integrity, he states it signals alignment between a leader's core beliefs and daily practice, that educational organizations have an implicit mandate to care for and nurture learners in environments fostering curiosity and inquiry, and that integrity in an educational leader translates to strong cultural values within the organization. On vision, he argues a concise, clearly communicated vision gives stakeholders a roadmap for navigating the changing landscape of education and prevents individuals and organizations from becoming sidetracked and discouraged by the perception or reality of wasted effort.

Question 2 asks how important technology is in education and what technology-related skills the applicant can contribute. Godfrey writes that 21st century learners have more information at their disposal than any generation before them, and that the expanding digital database of the internet can present as both gift and curse: the gift is access to worlds of knowledge at the click of a mouse or tap of a screen, which levels the playing field between educational haves and have nots, while the curse is the difficulty of filtering fact from fiction and truth from lies. His stated contributions are a healthy sense of perspective and an emphasis on critical thinking. He argues technology must remain a supplement to human understanding and connection rather than a replacement, comparing the Information Age to the eras revolutionized by the pencil and the printing press, and notes that the available wealth of knowledge includes voices previously stifled by oppressive and marginalizing forces. He concludes that when technology supplements critical thinking, learners add depth to breadth and learn to hold varying ideas in tension while remaining grounded in empirical truths.

Meeting and Attendance
Troy Board of Education meeting, Troy, Michigan, November 17, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar with public notice posted to allow remote community participation. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present via Zoom in addition to Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience.

Recognition
TSD Mission Moment honoring Troy High School English teachers Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick and Valerie Valentino, recipients of a Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice and Equity (DIJE) professional development grant. Their reading program includes Black Appetite. White Food by Jamila Lyiscott; We Got This. by Cornelius Miner; The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook by Lorena German; Educating Activist Allies by Katy Swalwell; and Linguistic Justice by April Baker-Bell.

Public Communication
There were no additions or deletions. Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two Martell Elementary School students, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat. Actions
| No. | Item | Mover / Support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20-084 | Consent agenda items A, B, C | Hauff / Hammond | 7-0 |
| 20-085 | Building signage award, Johnson Sign Company, $92,000 | Anne / Philippart | 7-0 |
| 20-086 | Bus purchase, Hoekstra Transportation, $1,687,276.00 | Philippart / Anne | 7-0 |

Minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, Board Meeting of November 17, 2020, held via Zoom Webinar. The meeting was held remotely and a public notice was posted in order to allow community members to participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT
The Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice, and Equity (DIJE) subcommittee awarded Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick, and Valerie Valentino of Troy High School a DIJE professional development grant. The stated goal of the grant is to support Michigan English teachers across the state as they engage in professional development they design that privileges diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity work. The recipients created a program of reading and learning supporting their commitment to disrupting stock stories, stereotypes, and westernized narratives. Their selected texts are Black Appetite. White Food: Issues of Race, Voice and Justice Within and Beyond the Classroom, by Jamila Lyiscott; We Got This.: Equity, Access, and the Quest to Be Who Our Students Need Us to Be, by Cornelius Miner; The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook, by Lorena German; Educating Activist Allies: Social Justice Pedagogy with the Suburban and Urban Elite, by Katy Swalwell; and Linguistic Justice: Black Language, Literacy, Identity, and Pedagogy, by April Baker-Bell. Their intention is to use the concepts and practice presented in their readings to plan learning for their students to build community and engage in rich activist lives.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS
None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two students who attend Martell Elementary School, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA (Resolution 20-084)
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 6, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2020. On roll call vote, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PERSONNEL AND CURRICULUM
No items were recorded under Personnel or Curriculum.

BUSINESS - BUILDING SIGNAGE (Resolution 20-085)
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for signage for the refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Athens High School and new messaging signs at the Troy Preschool and Troy Learning Center be awarded to Johnson Sign Company in the amount of $92,000 (inclusive of 6% contingency), and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and/or the Sinking Fund. On roll call vote, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BUSINESS - BUS PURCHASE (Resolution 20-086)
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $1,687,276.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. There was discussion about the end of life cycle for buses and how much money the District could sell them for. There was also discussion about looking into grants for electric buses; however, Mr. West explained that it would be cost-prohibitive at this time. On roll call vote, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION - NON-AGENDA ITEMS
None.

OTHER - EXTENDED LEARNING PLAN
Dr. Machesky shared an update on the District's extended learning plan and provided PowerPoint slides showing the most recent numbers in COVID cases and how much they had been climbing in Michigan and in Oakland County. Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato also shared updates from their respective areas, and there was further discussion among Board members.

RECONFIRMATION OF COVID-19 PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE PLAN (Resolution 20-087)
The minutes recite that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall, and that under this order Michigan school districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved must post its Preparedness Plan on the district website home page for public access. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan. On roll call vote, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond No, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes. Yes: 6, No: 1.

OPEN MEETINGS ACT RESOLUTION (Resolution 20-088)
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. The whereas clauses state that Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the State's Open Meetings Act to restrict the reasons a member of a public body may attend a public meeting remotely beginning January 1, 2021; that advancing technology enabled school districts across the State to meet remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, to develop and implement plans to educate students safely and effectively, and to ensure safe and effective public participation; that the restrictions in Senate Bill 1108 allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty; that threats to public health and other disasters will not vanish on December 31, 2020, and that contagious diseases, flooding, tornadoes, acts of terrorism or other causes occurring after that date could make it unsafe or impossible for public bodies to meet in person or for some members to attend in person; that not allowing an immune-compromised member of a public body to participate remotely would be a clear violation of the Reasonable Accommodation clause of the Federal Americans with Disabilities Act; and that decisions about situations that may or may not merit remote attendance by members of a local public body are best determined by that body and the community it represents rather than the State Legislature.

The resolved clauses urge the Legislature to ideally amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to include a provision requiring local public bodies to set their own policies regarding remote meeting participation based on the needs and priorities of their own local communities rather than dictating universal policy to all public bodies in the State without regard to local control; urge the Legislature at a minimum to amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to extend indefinitely its provisions allowing remote attendance to accommodate absence due to a medical condition or a statewide or local state of emergency or state of disaster, in addition to military service, and to add accommodations for family emergencies and work obligations; and direct the Board Secretary to transmit copies of the resolution within five business days of adoption to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards. On roll call vote, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BOARD COMMENTS
Mrs. Hammond spoke about the events that happened during the last Board meeting, said how unfair it was presented, and stated that she will continue to advocate for what she believes in. Dr. Wilson thanked the teachers and administrators for their hard work in making things go as smoothly as possible. Dr. Philippart announced that the TFEE is holding a pandemic-safe fundraiser offering a raffle for $1,000 worth of gift cards, with tickets available for $5 each. Mr. Gottlieb thanked the TSD staff and fellow board members for all they are doing during these trying times. Mr. Hauff thanked veterans for their sacrifice and service, thanked the Central Office staff and hardworking teachers, and said oneTROY is the greatest school district in Michigan. Mrs. Anne thanked everyone for all they are doing during these difficult times.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES
Pranay Gupta, student representative from International Academy - East, reported on what is happening with students learning virtually in his school. Nathania Nartey, student representative from Athens High School, reported on what is happening with students now that they are 100% virtual. Sejal Patel, student representative from Troy High School, was not in attendance. Carleton Thomas, student representative from Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance.

ADJOURNMENT
Dr. Machesky thanked the Board for their continued efforts to support the District's work and for their help in supporting the LIVE program. He congratulated Bemis Elementary School for being recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School for the second time and wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving. Mr. Schmidt wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and announced that the next Board Workshop would be held on December 1st at 6:00 p.m. via Zoom. The meeting was adjourned at 8:45 p.m. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the preparation notation GH/jh.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, December 19, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
A Mission Moment on Wass Elementary's Armed Forces Student Lesson.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the November 14 workshop, the November 21 meeting and the November 28 special workshop, the October 2017 Treasurer's Report, and a resolution supporting the School Finance Research Collaborative. The November 14 workshop covered Diversity & Inclusion Part II with Dr. Jay Marks and previewed the bus purchase and PowerSchool contract.

**Treasurer's Report — October 2017**
Total check disbursements are $9,022,755.09, the General Fund group $4,685,631.59 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,313,774.74. Adding $2,010,787.36 of wire transfers, $211,824.56 of P-Card purchases and $16,774.75 of ACH debits, less $1,538.88 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,260,602.88.

**The School Finance Research Collaborative**
The item opens with a question and a blunt answer: "A very important question commonly asked among Michigan's public school leaders is 'How much does it cost to educate a child?' The answer is simple and straightforward — **we don't know.** The state of Michigan has never had a comprehensive school adequacy study conducted." Education experts and business leaders have formed the broad-based, bipartisan Collaborative; MASA and MASB support it and local boards are asked to endorse.

The resolution's recitals: Michigan ranks **32nd in student achievement nationwide**; the Governor's 21st Century Education Commission found "the urgency could not be greater regarding the falling K-12 performance," with Michiganders ranking **41st on fourth-grade reading**; efficient distribution requires a transparent calculation of what it costs to meet performance standards, and students with greater educational needs should receive additional resources to have an equal chance. It notes the 2016 statewide Adequacy Study produced valuable information but **used only one methodology** and did not fully examine special education costs, preschool, charter schools, career and technical education, the impact of high concentrations of special needs students, or geographically isolated and very small districts.

**Personnel**
The **Troy Educational Secretaries Association (TESA)**, MEA/NEA contract is extended **through June 30, 2021** — a two-year extension. This is the contract whose negotiation had taken the Board into closed session on December 5. (A month later the Board would extend TESPA, the support personnel association, through June 30, 2022 on the same pattern.)

**Business — roofing and abatement**
Roof replacement at five district buildings, reviewed by district roofing consultant WeatherTech with Michelle Kerns and Rob Carson: **J. D. Chandler $888,400.00, Royal West $473,500.00, 10% contingency $136,190.00 — $1,498,090.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

Asbestos abatement at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard, reviewed by Rob Carson, awarded to **NOVA Environmental, Inc. in the amount of "$82,700.00.00"** as printed. Both the contractor and the amount are defective: NOVA is the district's abatement *consultant*, not the abatement contractor, and the figure carries a doubled decimal. The Board would adopt a corrected resolution on January 16, 2018 substituting **Qualified Abatement** at $82,700.00, with President Schmidt explaining that "the name of the consulting firm was inadvertently put in the initial resolution."

**Business — the budget amendment**
General Fund Budget Amendment #1 for 2017-18 sets the fund at **$148,584,440**.

**Business 8.E — the Early Childhood Center**
The district "has been engaged in the process of designing an Early Childhood Center since August of 2016." The recitals restate the mission, the vision of becoming a World Class educational entity by 2020, and that **one of the four established pillars is Investing in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten students**; they recount the March 21, 2017 resolution appointing TMP Architecture at not more than $933,716 for phases 1 through 4, and note a comprehensive and collaborative design process involving many stakeholders since March 2017.

Seven resolved clauses:

1. Authorize **continued design development, preparation of construction documents, and bidding**.
2. Develop the center **on the vacant land located on the current Niles Continuing Education site**.
3. Authorize administration to **establish an Early Childhood Center Fund**.
4. Transfer **$4,700,000 from the Capital Maintenance Fund** into it, restricted to the project.
5. Direct that **revenue from any property sale between this resolution and June 30, 2020** be deposited into the fund and restricted to the project.
6. Appoint **Barton Malow Company** construction manager of record, consistent with its bond-work proposal, paid from the ECC Fund professional services budget.
7. **Supersede and replace any and all previous conflicting resolutions.**

Clause 2 is the substantive change. The March 2017 resolution had sited the center on "approximately 8 acres of Section 16" while preserving the balance; here the project moves to the Niles site — which is why Section 16 could later be sold whole, and why the preschool was built at 205 Square Lake Road. Clause 7 is what makes that stick. Clause 5 broadens the March rule: no longer only the three named parcels, but *any* property sale for two and a half years.

**Other**
Adoption of MASB's Board of Education Governance Standards, "intended to help support school boards in their efforts to govern responsibly and effectively on behalf of all students."

The agenda index places the Mission Moment heading under item 7 Curriculum through a layout error; it belongs to item 2.

**Recognition 2.A.** A TSD Mission Moment on Wass Elementary School's Armed Forces Student Lesson.

**Consent minutes: the November 14, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:03 p.m. with Mr. Schmidt absent. Present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Carson, Griffor, Harris, Soggs and West, plus three members of the audience. The agenda was public communication; board professional learning on Diversity & Inclusion, Part II with Dr. Jay Marks, Diversity & Equity Consultant; and a business services update covering the bus purchase discussion and the PowerSchool contract — both of which the Board acted on at the November 21 meeting the following week.

**Treasurer's Report, October 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $4,313,774.74, with Total General Fund of $4,685,631.59 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $9,022,755.09. Adding ACH debits of $16,774.75, outgoing wire transfers of $2,010,787.36 and P-Card purchases of $211,824.56, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $1,538.88, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,260,602.88. The middle sections of the packet are the October check register run by fund.

**Consent item 5.E: School Finance Research Collaborative.** The item begins with a question and an unusually direct answer: "A very important question commonly asked among Michigan's public school leaders is 'How much does it cost to educate a child?' The answer is simple and straightforward - we don't know. The state of Michigan has never had a comprehensive school adequacy study conducted, which is why education experts and business leaders from all over the state have formed the broad-based, bipartisan Michigan School Finance Research Collaborative. This group believes that it's time to change the way Michigan's schools are funded to ensure that every student gets the education needed to reach his or her full potential."

MASA and MASB support the Collaborative's work and would like to send a clear message to policymakers in Lansing that the work is critical if Michigan's public schools and the services they provide are going to be funded in the most effective and appropriate manner possible. Local school boards are asked to consider adopting a resolution in support of the Collaborative and the work it is doing to determine the true cost of educating Michigan's public school students.

The resolution's recitals build the case. The Michigan Constitution states that the legislature shall maintain and support a system of free public elementary and secondary schools as defined by law. Michigan ranks 32nd in student achievement nationwide according to recent research. The Governor's 21st Century Education Commission states that the urgency could not be greater regarding falling K-12 performance, further stating that Michiganders underperform their peers, ranking 41st on fourth-grade reading performance nationally. The Commission further stated that Michigan needs to efficiently distribute resources, that efficient distribution requires a transparent calculation of what it costs to meet performance standards, and that students with greater educational needs should be provided with additional resources where needed to have an equal chance of meeting those standards.

A further recital addresses the study the state did conduct: in 2016 the State of Michigan conducted a comprehensive statewide cost study, an Adequacy Study, that produced and provided valuable information but used only one methodology and did not fully examine special education costs due to data availability issues, did not examine preschool, charter schools, career and technical education, the impact of high concentrations of special needs students, or the cost challenges faced by geographically isolated schools and very small school districts. The recitals conclude that the way Michigan's public schools are funded is fundamentally in need of examination.

The item sits interestingly beside the rest of the packet. The same Board that here endorses a statewide finding that nobody knows what educating a child costs is, on the same agenda, transferring $4,700,000 of its own accumulated funds into a preschool it decided to build with money from selling land — an object lesson in a district financing what the state formula does not.

**Personnel 6.A: extension of the TESA contract.** The Board is recommended to approve the extension of the Troy Educational Secretaries Association (TESA), MEA/NEA contract through June 30, 2021 — an extension of two years to the current TESA Collective Bargaining Agreement. The resolution so approves, and the collective bargaining agreement between the Troy School District and the Troy Educational Secretaries Association/MEA/NEA is attached in full.

The attached agreement covers the ordinary ground of a support-staff contract: work performed within the TESA/MEA/NEA unit and the amount of supervision necessary; reporting lines to the immediate supervisor and to the TESA/MEA/NEA president; mileage when employees must use a personal vehicle; seniority dated from the most recent date of hire for a TESA/MEA/NEA position; and provisions applying specifically to employees hired into a TESA bargaining unit position after June 30, 2011.

The timing connects to the January 2018 packet: the December 5, 2017 closed session, whose minutes appear in the February 2018 packet, was held to discuss the TESA contract extension, and the January 9, 2018 closed session was held on TESPA — the Board extending its two support-staff agreements in successive months, TESA to June 30, 2021 and TESPA to June 30, 2022.

**Business 8.A: 2017-18 budget amendment resolution.** The Budget Amendment Resolution for fiscal year 2017-18 covers the General Fund. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes, and the resolution amends and approves the general appropriations and budget for the General Fund as attached and made part of the official minutes of the December 19, 2017 regular meeting. The amended General Fund total is $148,584,440. This is General Fund Budget Amendment #1 for the year; Amendment 2 would follow in April 2018.

**Business 8.B: roofing bid.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on roof replacement work at five district buildings. Bid responses were reviewed by WeatherTech, the district's roofing consultant, along with Michelle Kerns and Rob Carson. The resolution awards the roof replacement as follows, approved as expenditures of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund: J. D. Chandler $888,400.00; Royal West $473,500.00; and a 10% contingency of $136,190.00, for a total of $1,498,090.00.

The same two contractors had split the district's December 2016 roofing award, also with a 10% contingency, with their relative shares reversed this time.

**Business 8.C: asbestos abatement.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on asbestos abatement work at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard Elementary Schools, with bids reviewed by Mr. Rob Carson, Director of Operations. The resolution awards the bid for asbestos abatement at those four schools to NOVA Environmental, Inc. in the amount of "$82,700.00.00" and approves that amount as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

Both the contractor name and the figure are defective as printed. The amount carries a doubled decimal — "$82,700.00.00" — and NOVA Environmental is the district's asbestos *consultant*, the firm that prepares contractor award recommendations, not the abatement contractor. The error was caught within weeks: the January 16, 2018 packet carries a corrected resolution awarding the same work at the same four schools to **Qualified Abatement** at $82,700.00, reproducing this original with the contractor name struck through and the correct name substituted. The January 16 minutes record President Schmidt explaining to the Board that the corrected resolution "was just an error naming the company that was awarded the bid" and that "the name of the consulting firm was inadvertently put in the initial resolution," with the December 19 minutes also amended to reflect the correction.

The abatement is the companion to the mechanical and electrical work at the same four elementary schools awarded a month earlier under Bid Pack 21 — floor tile and insulation have to come out before mechanical systems go in.

**Business 8.D and 8.E: the Early Childhood Center.** Item 8.D is a report; 8.E is the resolution, and it is the most consequential item in the 2017 packets.

The item records that the district "has been engaged in the process of designing an Early Childhood Center since August of 2016" — placing the origin four months before the December 2016 workshop at which an "Early Childhood Timeline" first appears in these packets, and seven months before the March 2017 resolution that appointed the architect.

The recitals restate the framework: the Board's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; its vision is to become a World Class educational entity by 2020; one of the four established pillars in becoming World Class by 2020 is Investing in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten students; the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to service its pre-kindergarten students; the Board as part of a resolution approved on March 21, 2017 appointed TMP Architecture as architect of record and authorized it to commence the design process in accordance with its proposal dated March 10, 2017, at a cost not to exceed $933,716 to complete phases 1 through 4, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund; and the district has been engaged in a comprehensive and collaborative design process involving many stakeholders since March 2017.

The seven resolved clauses are:

1. The School District authorizes the continued design development, preparation of construction documents, and bidding of an Early Childhood Center.
2. The School District desires to develop the Early Childhood Center on the vacant land located on the current Niles Continuing Education site.
3. The School District authorizes Administration to establish an Early Childhood Center Fund.
4. The School District authorizes a transfer of $4,700,000 from the Capital Maintenance Fund into the Early Childhood Center Fund and the funds be restricted for the development of the Early Childhood Center.
5. The School District directs revenue generated from any sale of property between the date of this resolution through June 30, 2020 be deposited into the Early Childhood Fund and restricted for use in the development of the Early Childhood Center.
6. The School District appoints Barton Malow Company as the Construction Manager of Record and authorizes Administration to finalize a contract with Barton Malow consistent with their proposal submitted for the bond work, with their services approved as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund Professional Services Budget.
7. This resolution supersedes and replaces any and all previous resolutions in whole or in part that conflict with this resolution.

Clause 2 is the substantive change and the reason clause 7 exists. The March 21, 2017 resolution had provided that the district "desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16 and preserve the balance of the subject property." Nine months of design work later, the site moves to the vacant land at the Niles Continuing Education site — and the supersession clause quietly voids the Section 16 siting. That single change is what made the rest of the district's land program possible: with the preschool no longer needing eight acres of Section 16, the whole 19.43-acre parcel could be sold to Mondrian Properties in March 2018, and the preschool was ultimately built at 205 Square Lake Road, the address that appears on the 2018 bid tabulations.

Clause 5 also broadens the March rule materially. The March resolution restricted revenue from "these property sales" — the specific parcels it had named. This clause restricts revenue from *any* sale of property over a two-and-a-half-year window ending June 30, 2020, which captures the Section 16 sale, the Section 1 front parcel, the Wattles Road parcel and the Boyd Street strip, all of which were still ahead.

Clause 4's $4,700,000 transfer from Capital Maintenance is the first real money committed to the project, and clause 6 completes the professional team — TMP Architecture appointed in March as architect of record, Barton Malow appointed here as construction manager of record, both firms already working on the district's bond program.

Read against what followed, this resolution is the hinge. Three months later the Board would authorize bonds without a vote of the electors and award the construction contracts; the naming resolution of December 2018 would cite the same World Class pillar language used here. But the decision that shaped everything — where the building goes, what fund holds the money, and that every land sale for the next two and a half years belongs to the preschool — is made in these seven clauses.

**Other 10.A: Board Governance Standards.** MASB's Board of Education Governance Standards are intended to help support school boards in their efforts to govern responsibly and effectively on behalf of all students. By adopting the Governance Standards, boards take an important step toward demonstrating their commitment to governing effectively on behalf of students and promoting greater self-awareness of their role.

Read as a whole, the December 2017 packet closes the year by committing the district's future. It endorses a statewide finding that Michigan does not know what educating a child costs, extends its secretaries' contract to 2021, spends $1,498,090.00 on roofs and $82,700.00 on abatement — the latter on a resolution naming the wrong company for the wrong amount, corrected four weeks later — and then, in seven clauses, decides where the preschool will be built, creates the fund that will pay for it, and assigns to that fund the proceeds of every piece of land the district sells for the next two and a half years.

**Meeting**
Organizational and regular meeting, January 16, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**The organizational half**
The Board elects an acting chairperson to officiate until a president is elected and appoints a temporary secretary, then elects president, vice president and secretary in turn. The treasurer is appointed, fund depositories and the investment resolution established, board and district legal counsel designated, the superintendent designated deputy secretary, a person designated for posting notices of meetings, and the meeting schedule adopted. Several of these agenda-index lines carry the prior year's dates — the depositories item reads 2016/17 and 2017/18 and the schedule item reads 2017 calendar year — apparently unrevised template text in a January 2018 packet, as is the consent-agenda line reading "Treasurer's Report – November 2016."

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment recognizes the 2017-18 Superintendent Student Advisory Board, made up of student leaders from all four high schools who are nominated by teachers, counselors and administrators and whose expressed mission is "leaving the Troy School District better than it was when they entered." The day before the meeting they carried out another Martin Luther King, Junior, Day of Service at Athens High School, where community members learned about Dr. King's legacy and performed four service projects; the SSAB also runs a smaller spring service project and advises Dr. Machesky and central office staff from a high school perspective. The second item is Board of Education Recognition, marking January as the month the district celebrates the Board's work, framed around the journey begun a little over three years earlier to become a World Class School District by 2020.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the December 5, 2017 special meeting and workshop and the December 19, 2017 meeting, the Treasurer's Report, and a corrected resolution from the December 19 asbestos abatement award.

**Treasurer's Report**
General Fund check disbursements total $6,816,514.12 and total disbursements in period are $9,875,817.28.

**The corrected asbestos resolution**
The packet carries both versions of the same award, which is why it is back before the Board. An RFP sought competitive bids for asbestos abatement at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard elementary schools; Rob Carson reviewed them. The corrected resolution awards the work to **Qualified Abatement at $82,700.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The superseded December 19 version is reproduced with the contractor name struck through — "NOVA Environmental, Inc.Qualified Abatement" — and the amount rendered "$82,700.00.00", an evident transcription error in the original that the correction resolves.

**Personnel and business**
The Board ratifies an extension of the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association (TESPA), MEA/NEA contract **through June 30, 2022** — three years added to the existing collective bargaining agreement — and issues a probationary contract to Rebecca Turner as a 1.0 speech pathologist at Athens and the Troy Center for Transition.

The business item approves $853,231.22 of furniture for 4th and 5th grade classrooms through Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and the Oakland County America Saves Cooperative Purchase Program, as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, led the project team with Workspace Interiors and building administrators and staff to evaluate the use and needs for furniture in those classrooms, and an accompanying "The Learning Environment" presentation sets out the design.

These are recorded here as printed rather than corrected.

**Recognition 5.A: Superintendent Student Advisory Board and the MLK Day of Service.** The Mission Moment recognizes the 2017-18 Superintendent Student Advisory Board, described as outstanding student leaders from all four high schools in the district who come together with the expressed mission of leaving the Troy School District better than it was when they entered. Members are nominated by teachers, counselors and administrators and selected from a group of applicants. The day before this meeting the students executed another successful Martin Luther King, Junior, Day of Service at Athens High School, where members of the community came together to learn about the legacy of Dr. King and perform four service projects having a direct positive impact in his name. The SSAB students helped plan and carry out the Day of Service as well as a smaller service project each spring, give input to Dr. Machesky and central office staff from a high school perspective, and work to encourage students at their own schools to participate in district-wide activities. The recommended action is to invite the students up to receive a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

**Recognition 5.B: Board of Education Recognition.** Each January the Troy School District recognizes and celebrates the work of the Board of Education. The script frames the recognition around the district's journey, begun a little over three years earlier, to become a World Class School District by the year 2020, and the Board's role in making that ambitious goal possible.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the December 5, 2017 Special Board of Education Meeting; B. Minutes of the December 5, 2017 Board of Education Workshop; C. Minutes of the December 19, 2017 Board of Education Meeting; D. Treasurer's Report; and E. Corrected Resolution from the 12/19/17 asbestos abatement award.

**Treasurer's Report.** General Fund check disbursements total $6,816,514.12, and total disbursements in period — check disbursements together with ACH debits, outgoing wire transfers, P-Card purchases and prior period void disbursements — come to $9,875,817.28. The bulk of the packet's middle sections is the check register run by fund, with roughly 1,900 register lines across parts two and three.

**Consent item 8.E: the corrected asbestos abatement resolution.** This item exists because the resolution adopted on December 19, 2017 named the wrong contractor, and the packet reproduces both versions so the Board can see the correction. Both recite the same underlying facts: an RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for asbestos abatement work at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard Elementary Schools, and the bids were reviewed by Mr. Rob Carson, Director of Operations.

The corrected resolution reads that the bid for asbestos abatement at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard Elementary Schools be awarded to Qualified Abatement in the amount of $82,700.00, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The superseded version is reproduced showing the edit in place — the contractor line reads "NOVA Environmental, Inc.Qualified Abatement," the original name struck through and the correct one substituted — and its amount is rendered "$82,700.00.00," a transcription error carried in the original document. The dollar figure of the award itself is unchanged at $82,700.00; what changed is the name of the firm receiving it.

**Personnel 9.A: TESPA contract extension.** The Board is recommended to approve the extension of the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association (TESPA), MEA/NEA contract through June 30, 2022 — an extension of three years to the current TESPA Collective Bargaining Agreement. The resolution approves that extension.

**Personnel 9.B: elementary and secondary.** The Board is recommended to approve the issuance of a probationary contract for the 2017-2018 school year to Rebecca Turner, 1.0 Speech Pathologist serving Athens High School and the Troy Center for Transition.

**Business 11.A: furniture purchase for 4th and 5th grade classrooms.** Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, led a project team with Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and building administrators and staff to evaluate the use and needs for furniture in 4th and 5th grade classrooms. The recommendation is to approve the furniture and equipment purchase from the Oakland County America Saves Cooperative Purchase Program, and the resolution approves the furniture purchase for 4th and 5th grade classrooms in the amount of $853,231.22 through Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and the Oakland County America Saves Cooperative Purchase Program as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. An accompanying presentation titled "The Learning Environment" sets out the intended classroom design and the products selected.

Read together, the January 2018 packet pairs a long-horizon labor commitment — three additional years of the TESPA agreement, running to June 30, 2022 — with the district's continuing capital reinvestment of 2016 Capital Projects Fund money into classrooms, $853,231.22 of it in this single furniture award, alongside the smaller $82,700.00 abatement contract whose only defect was the contractor's name.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, May 16, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition — six items**

The Mission Moment honors Barnard teacher **Taryn Huang**, accepted into Columbia University's Teachers College August Writing Institute — a program for educators "committed to turning classrooms into richly literate reading and writing workshops," admitting only a small number of applicants each year.

The accompanying presentation traces what the district has already built from the same partnership. The Teachers College Reading and Writing Project is a think tank started at Columbia under Lucy Calkins. Hamilton principal **Sarah Glasser** and Hill literacy specialist **Erin Detmer** attended the January Writing Coaching Institute; the presentation quotes John Hattie — "I suggest that we should focus on the greatest source of variance that can make the difference – the teacher." Back in Troy, Glasser began working shoulder to shoulder with teachers as a coach, the takeaway being that coaching is powerful **because teachers get feedback in the midst of instruction**, so every day becomes an opportunity for professional growth. Detmer set up lab experiences at Hill where the coach models a strategy and the teacher tries it in a safe environment. Curriculum and Instruction Specialist **Natalie Haezebrouck** observed both and carried the strategies into CAT network meetings — "giving teachers time to practice makes learning 'sticky!'" The three then created a three-day **Troy Coaching Institute** for principals and literacy specialists, working in classrooms with students at Hamilton and Hill.

Sixteen support staff were nominated for the Outstanding Support Staff Award, chosen by people "who talked about the impact these employees have on the lives of those around them… when we say we ensure learning for all, ALL truly means ALL." **Erin Prendergast**, para/resource room at Troy Union, is named Employee of the Year and forwarded to the county for the Betty Campion Outstanding Support Staff Award.

Twenty-seven retirees are introduced, the longest-serving being **Gary Griffith, a teacher since 1974**, followed by Sharon Brennan (1977), Karen Hurst (1977), and Renee Fidler, Gary Mason and Valerie Pfeifer (all 1978). Monitors display a visual recognition for twenty minutes beforehand; Jordan Harris reads each name, position and length of career, and **Board Vice-President Karl Schmidt** presents each a clock.

The fourth item recognizes a **$10,000 grant from the AT&T Foundation**, secured through the Troy Community Foundation and Oakland County Commissioner Doug Tietz, used to provide **transportation for high school students in after-school tutoring programs**. The fifth recognizes the Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence, which **funded 80 grants** this year, with president Julie McClure presenting. The sixth adopts a resolution supporting National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 8-12, 2017.

Minutes of the April 11 workshop and April 18 meeting, the March 2017 Treasurer's Report, and approval of the 2017-2018 Oakland ISD budget.

**Recognition 2.A: Teachers' College.** The Board honors Barnard Elementary teacher Taryn Huang, accepted into the prestigious Teachers' College at Columbia University August Writing Institute. The Writing Institute is designed for educators, classroom teachers, school administrators and curriculum specialists who are committed to turning classrooms into richly literate reading and writing workshops; applicants must apply and only a small number are accepted each year. Huang is invited up to describe what she hopes to learn and bring back to Troy, and receives a certificate after she speaks.

The accompanying presentation, titled "University of Columbia, Teachers College Partnership: Building Capacity In TSD," sets out what the district has already built from the relationship. The Teachers College Reading and Writing Project is described as a think tank started at Columbia University under the leadership of Lucy Calkins, whose mission is to help young people become avid readers, writers and inquirers through effective instruction, working shoulder to shoulder with educators at all levels to hone literacy practices.

Under the heading "Investing in Learning: Coaching Institute at TCRWP," the presentation quotes John Hattie — "I suggest that we should focus on the greatest source of variance that can make the difference – the teacher" — and records that Sarah Glasser, Hamilton principal, and Erin Detmer, Hill literacy specialist, attended the January Writing Coaching Institute, where they learned a model for supporting teachers to provide responsive, evidence-based instruction in literacy.

Back at Troy, Glasser immediately started working shoulder to shoulder with teachers in the role of coach. The Teachers College takeaway recorded is that the role of coach is a powerful one because teachers get feedback while in the midst of instruction, so that every day becomes an opportunity for professional growth; Hamilton teachers have been honing their ability to deliver effective one-on-one conferences. At Hill, Detmer set up lab experiences in which the coach models a strategy and then the teacher tries it out in a safe environment, the takeaway being that professional learning should be frequent and provide opportunities for immediate practice.

Natalie Haezebrouck, Curriculum and Instruction Specialist for Elementary Literacy, observed both Detmer and Glasser and used strategies from the Coaching Institute at CAT meetings to make teacher learning more authentic — "giving teachers time to practice makes learning 'sticky!'" The three then created a three-day Troy Coaching Institute for principals and literacy specialists, in which participants worked in classrooms with students at Hamilton and Hill to hone their craft.

The structure of the item is worth noting: the Board is not merely congratulating one teacher on an acceptance, it is showing the return on two earlier acceptances — a single January institute attended by two staff, propagated through a building principal, a literacy specialist, a district curriculum specialist and finally a three-day institute for the district's own principals.

**Recognition 2.B: 2016-17 Outstanding Support Staff Award.** Sixteen individuals were nominated, chosen by colleagues, parents and students who talked about the impact these employees have on the lives of those around them: "They exemplify our values and help us to ensure that when we say we ensure learning for all, ALL truly means ALL."

The nominees are Rose Arnon, custodian, Costello; Nahla Asmar, ELD tutor, Boulan Park; Margaret Baines, facility manager, Athens; Dawn Copp, health care aide, Martell; Janet Davert, secretary, Baker; Maxine Japowicz, paraprofessional, Martell; Janie Kirchler, health care aide, Hamilton; Sharon Kreza, secretary, Wattles; Ivonne Mastracci, secretary, Troy Union; Karyn Mroczka, secretary, Smith; Sue Ohlert, secretary, Athens; Joni Pallas, paraprofessional, special education, Larson; Candy Parker, bus driver; Erin Prendergast, para/resource room, Troy Union; Betty Prospal, secretary, employee services; and Seth Wyatt, paraeducator, special education, Costello.

From that pool, Erin Prendergast was awarded the Troy School District Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year, and her name was also sent to the county for consideration for the county-wide Betty Campion Outstanding Support Staff Award.

The retirees are Joan Barrett, teacher, Troy High, since 1987; Sharon Brennan, teacher, Larson Middle School, since 1977; Dikki CieChanski, teacher, Martell, since 1987; Mary Curl, secretary, Morse, support staff since 1996; Janet D'Agostino, secretary, Troy Career Center, support staff since 2000; Vera Dorr, ELD paraprofessional, Wass and Costello, support staff since 1996; William Edwards, computer technician, Services, support staff since 1995; Renee Fidler, teacher, elementary music, since 1978; Karen Field, support staff since 1997; Gary Griffith, teacher since 1974; Renee Haraburda, teacher since 1988; Karen Hurst, teacher since 1977; Mary Johnson, teacher since 1991; Mary Klotz, support staff since 1997; Janet MacDonald, support staff since 1987; Susan Madej, support staff since 1999; Gary Mason, teacher, Baker Middle School, since 1978; Janice Meganck, secretary, International Academy East, support staff since 1997; Valerie Pfeifer, teacher, Troy High, since 1978; Heide Rosenberg, teacher, Troy High, since 1991; Sandra Sinnaeve, ELD paraprofessional, Troy Union, support staff since 2000; Kathleen Steinberger, ELD paraprofessional, Wattles, support staff since 2001; Hank Thoenes, teacher, Boulan Park, since 1987; Colleen Tropea, teacher, Smith Middle School, since 1985; Camille Tucci, teacher, Athens, since 1986; and Linda Worrell, teacher, Troy High, since 1989.

The accompanying slides read "Thank you for the years of dedication and support you have given to the Troy School District. We wish you all the best in your retirement! Congratulations!" followed by a slide per retiree. Gary Griffith's forty-three years is the longest tenure in the group.

The staging instructions match those used in later years: for approximately twenty minutes before the board meeting all the monitors in the room display a visual recognition of the district's retirees; a note card is placed on a chair for each retiree attending; Jordan Harris reads each name, position and length of career; the retiree comes forward and stands near the presentation table; and the retirement gift, a clock, is presented — here by Board Vice-President Karl Schmidt rather than the president, Dr. Philippart.

**Personnel 6.A: Special Education Supervisor.** The recommendation is Ms. Jessica Carrier, with an extensive 18-year career in education. She began as a middle school special education teacher for Fraser Public Schools, then served as the assistive technology consultant for special education in the Fraser School District; her career progressed to special education teacher consultant, then middle school assistant principal, then principal for Fraser Public Schools. For the last two years she has served as Director of Special Education at Fraser, managing and overseeing all special education services within the district. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in special education from Central Michigan University, a master's degree in educational administration from Saginaw Valley State University, a specialist degree in educational leadership, and Director of Special Education state certification from Saginaw Valley State.

The item's closing sentence reads that with the Board's approval "Ms. Carrier will begin her duties as Director of Technology as of July 1, 2017" — text carried over from the Soggs item that follows; the resolution itself correctly issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Jessica Carrier, who will begin her duties as Special Education Supervisor effective July 1, 2017.

The selection funnel is published in full: there were 135 applications submitted, of which 11 were granted first round interviews — Rebecca Anders, Jessica Carrier, Karly DiDocha, Tamaran Dillard, Michelle Flessa, Thomas Harwood, Jennifer Lorence, Lydia Moore, Melanie Morey, Chris Olson and Sarah Young. Of those, 4 moved to the final round: Jessica Carrier, Director of Special Education at Fraser Public Schools; Michelle Flessa, special education teacher, Troy School District; Lydia Moore, early childhood special education consultant, Oakland Schools; and Sarah Young, behavior support coordinator, Troy School District. The final selection was Jessica Carrier. (The transition line reads "Of the 7 listed above, 4 moved to the final round" while eleven names are listed — an inconsistency in the source.)

Three of the eleven first-round interviewees recur later in these packets: Sarah Young would be appointed Special Education Supervisor herself in May 2018, Melanie Morey was already principal at Barnard, and Carrier would be promoted to Director of Special Education in July 2018.

**Personnel 6.B: Director of Technology.** The recommendation is Ms. Elizabeth Soggs, with an extensive 17-year career in the technology field. She began as a technical systems coordinator for the Bloomfield Hills School District, then served as executive director of technology for the School District of the City of Pontiac. For the last seven years she has served as Director of Technology and REMC 6 at Bay-Arenac Intermediate School District, where she fulfilled many additional responsibilities including leading the district from the E-rate service provider role to the role of an internet services consortium, providing project leadership for 13 districts in the selection and implementation process of a new student management system, and creating the "REMC 6 Tech Group" comprised of teachers from three counties. She holds a bachelor's degree in business administration and computer information systems from Walsh College and a master of arts in educational technology from Central Michigan University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, with duties beginning June 5, 2017.

The funnel: there were 34 applications submitted, of which 10 were granted first round interviews — Henry Christian, John Graham, Evan Humphrey, Matthew McCarty, Andrew Piazza, Nicholas Pitrone, Wesley Prescott, Elizabeth Soggs, Andrew Steinman and Gary van Staveren. Of those, 4 moved to the final round of interviews and building visits: Andrew Piazza, Director of Technology and Instructional Integration at Northville Public Schools; Wesley Prescott, Technology Coordinator–Field Services at Oakland ISD; Elizabeth Soggs, Director of Technology and REMC6 at Bay-Arenac ISD; and Gary van Staveren, building principal at Hamlin Elementary School, Rochester Community Schools. The final selection was Elizabeth Soggs.

The contrast between the two searches is stark and is visible only because the district publishes both funnels: 135 applicants for a special education supervisor's post against 34 for a technology directorship, in the same month, at the same district. Soggs's E-rate experience proved directly relevant — she is the Beth Soggs who would run the district's fiber maintenance and network equipment RFPs through 2018, both of them turning on E-rate reimbursement.

The agenda index and the item heading both list four policies, omitting 5000.03; the body of the item lists five. The five-policy list is the operative one.

Read as a whole, the May 2017 packet is the district's annual accounting of its people. Twenty-seven employees leave, one of them after forty-three years; sixteen support staff and every teacher in the district are thanked; two administrative posts are filled from funnels the district publishes in full, showing 135 applicants for one and 34 for the other; and one teacher's acceptance to a Columbia institute is used to show what two earlier acceptances already produced — a coaching model that moved from an institute in January to two buildings, then to the district's curriculum specialists, then to a three-day institute Troy ran for itself.
